paragraphs: This paper analyzes a mathematical model of how ocular dominance columns form in mammalian visual cortex. These columns organize cells according to their preference for input from one eye. The model provides a shared framework for studying several biological mechanisms in which patterns of neural activity influence development.

The results identify conditions under which monocular cells form robustly and cortical interactions organize them into columns. In the reported sufficient conditions, inputs belonging to the same eye have locally correlated firing and are not anticorrelated within an arbor radius. Broader correlations within an eye, or anticorrelations between the eyes, make the resulting cortex more exclusively responsive to individual eyes.

Positive correlation across an arbor radius produces an almost completely monocular cortex in the model. The authors combine computational results with eigenfunction decomposition and linear stability analysis to explain most of its features. This analytical understanding allows column widths and other properties to be predicted from measurable biological parameters, linking assumptions about activity patterns to the spatial organization that develops.
summary.tldr: A mathematical model links correlations in eye-specific neural activity to ocular dominance column formation and predicts column properties from biological parameters.

title: Models of Ocular Dominance Column Formation: Analytical and Computational Results

paragraphs: The paper outlines a computational model of how specific connections between the eye and brain develop and regenerate. Its organizing problem is map formation: how a network comes to establish an arranged set of connections between these structures. Both initial development and regeneration fall within the model's intended biological scope.

The proposed network forms maps through self-organization using local Hebbian learning rules. Molecular markers constrain that process. The model therefore brings together activity-related changes at individual connections and molecular information that restricts how the map can form. These components jointly define the proposed mechanism for producing organized eye-brain circuitry.

The authors describe simulations of eye-brain map development in fish and frogs. These simulations provide the concrete setting in which the combined mechanism is explored. The contribution is a computational framework for examining how locally operating learning rules and molecular constraints can participate in a larger spatial organization. Bringing development and regeneration into that framework also places the formation and re-formation of these circuits within a common modeling approach.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing network combines local Hebbian learning with molecular constraints to model eye-brain map formation.

title: Development and Regeneration of Eye-Brain Maps: A Computational Model

abstract: We formulate the problem of optimizing the sampling of natural images using an array of linear filters. Optimization of information capacity is constrained by the noise levels of the individual channels and by a penalty for the construction of long-range interconnections in the array. At low signal-to-noise ratios the optimal filter characteristics correspond to bound states of a Schrodinger equation in which the signal spectrum plays the role of the potential. The resulting optimal filters are remarkably similar to those observed in the mammalian visual cortex and the retinal ganglion cells of lower vertebrates. The observed scale invariance of natural images plays an essential role in this construction.

paragraphs: This paper asks what an array of visual filters should look like if it is designed to preserve information from natural images. The filters are linear, and their information capacity is optimized under two constraints: noise in individual channels and a cost for building connections over long distances. These constraints make the design problem sensitive to both signal quality and wiring.

At low signal-to-noise ratios, the optimal filters can be described using bound states of a Schrödinger equation. In this mathematical correspondence, the image signal's spectrum plays the role of the potential. The equation supplies a way to derive filter shapes from image statistics and the constraints imposed on the array.

The resulting filters closely resemble ones observed in mammalian visual cortex and in retinal ganglion cells of lower vertebrates. The scale invariance of natural images is essential to the construction. The finding suggests that these biological filter shapes can be understood through constrained information optimization, with their structure linked to regularities in the visual environment.
summary.tldr: Optimizing image information under noise and wiring costs produces filters resembling biological visual filters in the low-signal regime.

title: Optimal Sampling of Natural Images: A Design Principle for the Visual System

paragraphs: The paper connects evolution, development, and learning in a system for generating neural networks. A genetic algorithm manipulates genomes, but a developmental process stands between those genomes and the networks that perform prediction. The resulting network then learns, so genetic specification and weight adjustment play separate roles in producing its final behavior.

The developmental mechanism is ONTOL, a grammar for constructing polynomial neural networks for time-series prediction. A genome contains an ordered sequence of grammar productions that is expressed to generate a network. After construction, learning modifies the network's weights, and its prediction error determines the fitness used by the genetic algorithm.

The authors present preliminary, encouraging results and identify a new gene doubling operator as apparently critical for creating new genetic alternatives. This makes the way genetic variation is produced part of the proposed mechanism. The work's central contribution is the full sequence from an evolvable grammar through network construction and learning to a prediction-based fitness assessment.
summary.tldr: ONTOL evolves grammatical descriptions that develop into trainable neural networks, with prediction error guiding genetic selection.

title: Interposing an ontogenetic model between Genetic Algorithms and Neural Networks

paragraphs: The paper addresses a representation problem in predicting biological activity: the features describing a compound can change with its position or orientation. A learning system must therefore deal with variation caused by how an example is posed, alongside variation relevant to the activity being predicted.

Dynamic reposing tackles this by alternating between learning and repositioning. It first trains a neural network, then changes the poses of the examples to increase the network's predicted outputs. New networks and new poses are repeatedly computed until both settle. The input representation and the prediction model are consequently adjusted together.

The authors compare this procedure with tangent distance, a method used to address pose variation in handwritten character recognition. Their application is activity prediction for musk compounds. The abstract begins describing a 20-fold cross-validation but ends before reporting its outcome. The supported contribution is the comparison of two ways to handle pose dependence; the supplied evidence does not establish a winning method.
summary.tldr: The paper compares iterative pose adjustment with tangent distance for predicting the biological activity of musk compounds.

title: A Comparison of Dynamic Reposing and Tangent Distance for Drug Activity Prediction

abstract: The Fourier transform of boolean functions has come to play an important role in proving many important learnability results. We aim to demonstrate that the Fourier transform techniques are also a useful and practical algorithm in addition to being a powerful theoretical tool. We describe the more prominent changes we have introduced to the algorithm, ones that were crucial and without which the performance of the algorithm would severely deterio(cid:173) rate. One of the benefits we present is the confidence level for each prediction which measures the likelihood the prediction is correct.

paragraphs: Fourier transforms of Boolean functions have been useful for proving that certain learning problems can be solved. This paper asks whether those techniques can also support a practical learning algorithm. Its focus is the transition from a mathematically useful method to an implementation whose predictions and performance make it useful in practice.

The authors describe changes to the algorithm that they identify as crucial to its performance. According to the abstract, removing these changes would cause substantial deterioration. This places implementation choices at the center of the contribution: the practical behavior depends on how the Fourier-based learning procedure is realized, alongside the theoretical justification for using it.

Another contribution is a confidence level attached to each prediction, intended to measure how likely that prediction is to be correct. This gives the output an additional interpretation beyond the predicted answer itself. Together, the implementation changes and confidence estimates support the paper's case for Fourier techniques as an operational learning method.
summary.tldr: Implementation changes and per-prediction confidence estimates help turn Fourier-based Boolean learning into a practical algorithm.

title: Implementation Issues in the Fourier Transform Algorithm

abstract: Closed-loop control relies on sensory feedback that is usually as(cid:173) sumed to be free . But if sensing incurs a cost, it may be cost(cid:173) effective to take sequences of actions in open-loop mode. We de(cid:173) scribe a reinforcement learning algorithm that learns to combine open-loop and closed-loop control when sensing incurs a cost. Al(cid:173) though we assume reliable sensors, use of open-loop control means that actions must sometimes be taken when the current state of the controlled system is uncertain. This is a special case of the hidden-state problem in reinforcement learning, and to cope, our algorithm relies on short-term memory. The main result of the pa(cid:173) per is a rule that significantly limits exploration of possible memory states by pruning memory states for which the estimated value of information is greater than its cost. We prove that this rule allows convergence to an optimal policy.

paragraphs: Feedback control usually assumes that observing the system is free. This paper studies the case where sensing has a cost, so it can be worthwhile to execute several actions before observing again. The learner must decide how to combine closed-loop behavior using current feedback with open-loop behavior between observations.

The sensors are assumed reliable, but skipping observations still makes the current state uncertain. The algorithm therefore uses short-term memory to handle this particular hidden-state problem. Memory supports decisions when fresh sensory information is unavailable, making the choice to sense part of the control problem rather than an automatic step before every action.

The main contribution is a pruning rule that sharply restricts exploration of possible memory states. It prunes states where the estimated value of obtaining information exceeds the cost of that information, identifying circumstances in which sensing is worthwhile. The authors prove that this rule preserves convergence to an optimal policy. Thus, the method reduces the memory-related search while retaining the stated optimality guarantee.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learner balances sensing costs against acting without feedback, with a memory-pruning rule that preserves optimal-policy convergence.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Mixed Open-loop and Closed-loop Control

abstract: This work investigates the representational and inductive capabili(cid:173) ties of time-delay neural networks (TDNNs) in general, and of two subclasses of TDNN, those with delays only on the inputs (IDNN), and those which include delays on hidden units (HDNN) . Both ar(cid:173) chitectures are capable of representing the same class of languages, the definite memory machine (DMM) languages, but the delays on the hidden units in the HDNN helps it outperform the IDNN on problems composed of repeated features over short time windows.

Both ar(cid:173) chitectures are capable of representing the same class of languages, the definite memory machine (DMM) languages, but the delays on the hidden units in the HDNN helps it outperform the IDNN on problems composed of repeated features over short time windows.

paragraphs: This paper examines what time-delay neural networks can represent and how effectively they learn sequence problems. It compares two architectures: networks with delays only on their inputs and networks that also place delays on hidden units. The distinction concerns where information from earlier times remains available during processing.

Both architectures can represent the same class of languages, identified as definite memory machine languages. Thus, moving delays into the hidden part of the network does not expand the language class in the stated comparison. This result separates representational capacity from the practical question of how readily an architecture learns particular patterns.

The networks with hidden-unit delays perform better on problems built from features that repeat within short time windows. This shows that architecture can affect learning performance even when the compared networks have the same stated representational reach. The advantage is tied to the temporal structure of the tasks: repeated local features favor retaining information at the hidden-unit level. The contribution combines a capacity comparison with a finding about which delay arrangement better suits those problems.
summary.tldr: Hidden-unit delays improve learning of repeated short-window features even though both compared architectures represent the same language class.

title: Representation and Induction of Finite State Machines using Time-Delay Neural Networks

paragraphs: When photographs are represented with wavelets at multiple scales, their coefficients depart from simple Gaussian statistics in two ways. Individual coefficient distributions have heavy tails, and the variability of one coefficient depends on neighboring coefficients. These dependencies can remain even when ordinary correlations are small, so second-order descriptions miss relevant structure.

The paper examines Gaussian scale mixtures as a model for both effects. Hidden scaling variables allow Gaussian components to express changing local variability. The authors show that this family can accurately describe both individual coefficient distributions and their joint distributions, connecting the two statistical observations within one modeling approach.

The model suggests a Markov structure in which hidden scale variables link coefficients through local image structure. The authors derive an estimator for those hidden variables and show that nonlinear normalization can make the coefficients Gaussian. The contribution goes beyond describing heavy tails: it provides a representation of dependencies and a way to transform the coefficients using estimates of the local scales.
summary.tldr: Gaussian scale mixtures capture heavy tails and variance dependencies in natural-image wavelets, while estimated local scales enable Gaussianizing normalization.

title: Scale Mixtures of Gaussians and the Statistics of Natural Images

abstract: When we learn a new motor skill, we have to contend with both the vari- ability inherent in our sensors and the task. The sensory uncertainty can be reduced by using information about the distribution of previously ex- perienced tasks. Here we impose a distribution on a novel sensorimotor task and manipulate the variability of the sensory feedback. We show that subjects internally represent both the distribution of the task as well as their sensory uncertainty. Moreover, they combine these two sources of information in a way that is qualitatively predicted by optimal Bayesian processing. We further analyze if the subjects can represent multimodal distributions such as mixtures of Gaussians. The results show that the CNS employs probabilistic models during sensorimotor learning even when the priors are multimodal.

The sensory uncertainty can be reduced by using information about the distribution of previously ex- perienced tasks. Here we impose a distribution on a novel sensorimotor task and manipulate the variability of the sensory feedback. We show that subjects internally represent both the distribution of the task as well as their sensory uncertainty. The results show that the CNS employs probabilistic models during sensorimotor learning even when the priors are multimodal.

paragraphs: Learning a motor skill involves uncertainty from both sensory measurements and the task itself. Previous experience can help by providing information about which task conditions are more likely. This paper investigates whether people represent both kinds of uncertainty and combine them when learning a new sensorimotor task.

The researchers impose a distribution on the task and manipulate variability in sensory feedback. This separates the statistics of prior task experience from the reliability of current sensory information. Subjects show evidence of internally representing both and combining them in a way qualitatively predicted by optimal Bayesian processing. The claim is qualitative agreement with that prediction, rather than exact numerical optimality.

The study also examines multimodal task distributions, including Gaussian mixtures, where prior experience contains multiple concentrations of probability. Results indicate that probabilistic modeling in sensorimotor learning extends to these more structured priors. This matters because the represented task knowledge need not collapse to one typical condition; it can reflect several distinct possibilities while being combined with uncertain feedback.
summary.tldr: People combine learned task distributions with sensory uncertainty in qualitative agreement with Bayesian processing, even for multimodal priors.

title: Probabilistic Inference in Human Sensorimotor Processing

abstract: When we model a higher order functions, such as learning and memory, we face a difﬁculty of comparing neural activities with hidden variables that depend on the history of sensory and motor signals and the dynam- ics of the network. Here, we propose novel method for estimating hidden variables of a learning agent, such as connection weights from sequences of observable variables. Bayesian estimation is a method to estimate the posterior probability of hidden variables from observable data sequence using a dynamic model of hidden and observable variables. In this pa- per, we apply particle ﬁlter for estimating internal parameters and meta- parameters of a reinforcement learning model. We veriﬁed the effective- ness of the method using both artiﬁcial data and real animal behavioral data.

Here, we propose novel method for estimating hidden variables of a learning agent, such as connection weights from sequences of observable variables. Bayesian estimation is a method to estimate the posterior probability of hidden variables from observable data sequence using a dynamic model of hidden and observable variables. In this pa- per, we apply particle ﬁlter for estimating internal parameters and meta- parameters of a reinforcement learning model. paragraphs: Understanding learning and memory requires reasoning about internal quantities that cannot be observed directly. Connection weights, for example, depend on the history of sensory inputs, actions, and internal dynamics. This makes it difficult to relate observed neural activity or behavior to the hidden state of a learning model.

The paper proposes estimating those hidden quantities from sequences of observable variables. It uses a Bayesian formulation in which a dynamic model connects hidden and observed variables, allowing observations over time to update a posterior distribution over internal quantities. The method applies a particle filter to internal parameters and metaparameters of a reinforcement learning model.

This approach matters because the target is the agent's evolving learning process, not just a summary of its visible behavior. The authors report that they verified the method's effectiveness with artificial data and real animal behavioral data. Those evaluations support using sequential probabilistic estimation to connect observable behavior with otherwise hidden quantities in the specified learning model.
summary.tldr: Particle filtering estimates hidden parameters of a reinforcement learning agent from observable sequences, with tests on artificial and animal data.

title: Estimating Internal Variables and Paramters of a Learning Agent by a Particle Filter

abstract: The extraction of statistically independent components from high-dimensional multi-sensory input streams is assumed to be an essential component of sensory processing in the brain. Such independent component analysis (or blind source separation) could provide a less redundant representation of information about the external world. Another powerful processing strategy is to extract preferentially those components from high-dimensional input streams that are related to other information sources, such as internal predictions or proprioceptive feedback. This strategy allows the optimization of internal representation according to the infor- mation bottleneck method. However, concrete learning rules that implement these general unsupervised learning principles for spiking neurons are still missing. We show how both information bottleneck optimization and the extraction of inde- pendent components can in principle be implemented with stochastically spiking neurons with refractoriness. The new learning rule that achieves this is derived from abstract information optimization principles.

This strategy allows the optimization of internal representation according to the infor- mation bottleneck method. paragraphs: Sensory processing may benefit from separating mixed input into statistically independent components, producing a less redundant description of the world. Another useful goal is to preferentially preserve components related to a second information source, such as an internal prediction or feedback about body position. The paper connects this second goal to information bottleneck optimization.

These are abstract objectives for unsupervised learning, but implementing them with neurons that communicate through spikes requires concrete learning rules. The authors derive a new rule from information optimization principles and show how it can support both independent component extraction and information bottleneck optimization in stochastically spiking neurons with refractoriness.

The result bridges a description of what information a representation should retain with a model of how spiking neurons could learn it. Refractoriness is part of the neuronal setting in which the construction is presented. The claim is explicitly one of possibility: these computations can in principle be implemented in the proposed kind of neuron. It does not establish that biological sensory systems necessarily use the derived rule.
summary.tldr: A derived learning rule shows how stochastic spiking neurons could implement information bottleneck optimization and independent component extraction.

title: Information Bottleneck Optimization and Independent Component Extraction with Spiking Neurons

abstract: Bayesian model averaging, model selection and their approximations such as BIC are generally statistically consistent, but sometimes achieve slower rates of con- vergence than other methods such as AIC and leave-one-out cross-validation. On the other hand, these other methods can be inconsistent. We identify the catch-up phenomenon as a novel explanation for the slow convergence of Bayesian meth- ods. Based on this analysis we deﬁne the switch-distribution, a modiﬁcation of the Bayesian model averaging distribution. We prove that in many situations model selection and prediction based on the switch-distribution is both consistent and achieves optimal convergence rates, thereby resolving the AIC-BIC dilemma. The method is practical; we give an efﬁcient algorithm.
originalAbstract: Bayesian model averaging, model selection and their approximations such as BIC are generally statistically consistent, but sometimes achieve slower rates of con- vergence than other methods such as AIC and leave-one-out cross-validation. On the other hand, these other methods can be inconsistent. We identify the catch-up phenomenon as a novel explanation for the slow convergence of Bayesian meth- ods. Based on this analysis we deﬁne the switch-distribution, a modiﬁcation of the Bayesian model averaging distribution. We prove that in many situations model selection and prediction based on the switch-distribution is both consistent and achieves optimal convergence rates, thereby resolving the AIC-BIC dilemma. The method is practical; we give an efﬁcient algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper examines a tension between statistical consistency and convergence speed in model selection and prediction. Bayesian model averaging, Bayesian model selection, and approximations such as BIC are generally consistent, yet can converge more slowly than AIC or leave-one-out cross-validation. Those faster alternatives, however, can be inconsistent.

The authors identify a catch-up phenomenon as an explanation for slow convergence in Bayesian methods. They use this analysis to construct the switch-distribution, a modification of the distribution used in Bayesian model averaging. The proposed change therefore targets a diagnosed source of slow learning rather than simply choosing one side of the consistency-versus-speed comparison.

The paper proves that selection and prediction based on the switch-distribution are both consistent and achieve optimal convergence rates in many situations. The scope of that result matters: it is not presented as an unconditional guarantee for every setting. An efficient algorithm makes the proposal practical as well as theoretical. The contribution is a route to combining two desirable properties that the compared methods do not always deliver together.
summary.tldr: The switch-distribution modifies Bayesian model averaging to achieve both consistency and optimal convergence rates in many situations.

title: Catching Up Faster in Bayesian Model Selection and Model Averaging

abstract: Distributed learning is a problem of fundamental interest in machine learning and cognitive science. In this paper, we present asynchronous distributed learning algorithms for two well-known unsupervised learning frameworks: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes (HDP). In the proposed approach, the data are distributed across P processors, and processors independently perform Gibbs sampling on their local data and communicate their information in a local asynchronous manner with other processors. We demonstrate that our asynchronous algorithms are able to learn global topic models that are statistically as accurate as those learned by the standard LDA and HDP samplers, but with significant improvements in computation time and memory. We show speedup results on a 730-million-word text corpus using 32 processors, and we provide perplexity results for up to 1500 virtual processors. As a stepping stone in the development of asynchronous HDP, a parallel HDP sampler is also introduced.

paragraphs: Learning topic models from large text collections can demand substantial computation and memory. This paper distributes that work across processors for two unsupervised modeling frameworks: Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes. The goal is to learn a shared global topic model while allowing processors to carry out much of the inference independently.

Each processor runs Gibbs sampling on its own portion of the data and exchanges information with other processors through local asynchronous communication. This organization allows learning to proceed without making every exchange part of a single synchronized update. The paper also introduces a parallel HDP sampler as an intermediate step toward the asynchronous HDP method.

The experiments show global models with statistical accuracy comparable to standard LDA and HDP samplers, alongside significant improvements in time and memory. Speedup is demonstrated on a corpus containing 730 million words using 32 processors, with perplexity results extending to 1,500 virtual processors. These results support asynchronous communication as a practical approach to scaling topic-model inference.
summary.tldr: Asynchronous distributed sampling scales LDA and HDP learning while maintaining statistical accuracy comparable to standard samplers in the reported experiments.

title: Asynchronous Distributed Learning of Topic Models

abstract: The cluster assumption is exploited by most semi-supervised learning (SSL) methods. However, if the unlabeled data is merely weakly related to the target classes, it becomes questionable whether driving the decision boundary to the low density regions of the unlabeled data will help the classification. In such case, the cluster assumption may not be valid; and consequently how to leverage this type of unlabeled data to enhance the classification accuracy becomes a challenge. We introduce Semi-supervised Learning with Weakly-Related Unlabeled Data" (SSLW), an inductive method that builds upon the maximum-margin approach, towards a better usage of weakly-related unlabeled information. Although the SSLW could improve a wide range of classification tasks, in this paper, we focus on text categorization with a small training pool. The key assumption behind this work is that, even with different topics, the word usage patterns across different corpora tends to be consistent. To this end, SSLW estimates the optimal word-correlation matrix that is consistent with both the co-occurrence information derived from the weakly-related unlabeled documents and the labeled documents. For empirical evaluation, we present a direct comparison with a number of state-of-the-art methods for inductive semi-supervised learning and text categorization; and we show that SSLW results in a significant improvement in categorization accuracy, equipped with a small training set and an unlabeled resource that is weakly related to the test beds."

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning often assumes that clusters in unlabeled data align with the classes being predicted. When the unlabeled documents are only weakly related to those classes, placing a decision boundary in low-density regions may not help. This paper addresses how such documents can still contribute to text classification when labeled training data are scarce.

The proposed SSLW method builds on maximum-margin learning and assumes that word-usage patterns tend to remain consistent across collections, even when their topics differ. It estimates a word-correlation matrix that agrees with both co-occurrence information from the unlabeled documents and information from labeled examples. Unlabeled data therefore contribute relationships among words without requiring their document clusters to match the target categories.

The method is inductive, so the learned classifier can be applied to new documents. In comparisons with existing semi-supervised and text-categorization methods, the authors report significant accuracy improvements with small labeled training sets and weakly related unlabeled resources. The findings support using cross-corpus word relationships under the stated consistency assumption.
summary.tldr: SSLW uses word correlations to improve text classification with few labels and weakly related unlabeled documents.

title: Semi-supervised Learning with Weakly-Related Unlabeled Data : Towards Better Text Categorization

abstract: We develop new techniques for time series classification based on hierarchical Bayesian generative models (called mixed-effect models) and the Fisher kernel derived from them. A key advantage of the new formulation is that one can compute the Fisher information matrix despite varying sequence lengths and sampling times. We therefore can avoid the ad hoc replacement of Fisher information matrix with the identity matrix commonly used in literature, which destroys the geometrical grounding of the kernel construction. In contrast, our construction retains the proper geometric structure resulting in a kernel that is properly invariant under change of coordinates in the model parameter space. Experiments on detecting cognitive decline show that classifiers based on the proposed kernel out-perform those based on generative models and other feature extraction routines.

paragraphs: The paper develops time-series classifiers from hierarchical Bayesian generative models, also called mixed-effect models. Its focus is longitudinal data whose sequences may have different lengths and observation times. A Fisher kernel turns information from the fitted generative model into a way of comparing sequences for classification.

The central advance is being able to compute the Fisher information matrix despite those irregular sequences. Replacing that matrix with the identity is a common shortcut, but the authors explain that it discards the geometric basis of the kernel. Their construction preserves that basis, so the resulting kernel is invariant to changes in coordinates used to express the model parameters.

This invariance means that changing the parameter representation does not improperly change the kernel’s comparison of data. The method therefore connects a practical treatment of unevenly sampled sequences with a principled kernel construction. In experiments detecting cognitive decline, classifiers using the proposed kernel outperform classifiers based on the generative models and other feature-extraction routines, supporting its practical value in that application.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Fisher kernels preserve model geometry for irregular longitudinal data and improve cognitive-decline classification in reported experiments.

title: Hierarchical Fisher Kernels for Longitudinal Data

abstract: When learning models that are represented in matrix forms, enforcing a low-rank constraint can dramatically improve the memory and run time complexity, while providing a natural regularization of the model. However, naive approaches for minimizing functions over the set of low-rank matrices are either prohibitively time consuming (repeated singular value decomposition of the matrix) or numerically unstable (optimizing a factored representation of the low rank matrix). We build on recent advances in optimization over manifolds, and describe an iterative online learning procedure, consisting of a gradient step, followed by a second-order retraction back to the manifold. While the ideal retraction is hard to compute, and so is the projection operator that approximates it, we describe another second-order retraction that can be computed efficiently, with run time and memory complexity of O((n+m)k) for a rank-k matrix of dimension m x n, given rank one gradients. We use this algorithm, LORETA, to learn a matrix-form similarity measure over pairs of documents represented as high dimensional vectors. LORETA improves the mean average precision over a passive- aggressive approach in a factorized model, and also improves over a full model trained over pre-selected features using the same memory requirements. LORETA also showed consistent improvement over standard methods in a large (1600 classes) multi-label image classification task.

paragraphs: The paper studies online learning with matrix-valued models constrained to have low rank. Such constraints can save memory and computation while regularizing the model. The difficulty is maintaining the constraint efficiently: repeated singular value decompositions can be expensive, while directly optimizing a factorized matrix representation can be numerically unstable.

The proposed algorithm, LORETA, takes a gradient step and then returns the result to the low-rank manifold using a second-order retraction. The authors construct an efficiently computable retraction to avoid harder alternatives. For an m-by-n matrix of rank k and rank-one gradients, the stated runtime and memory complexity is O((n+m)k). The rank-one-gradient condition is part of this efficiency result.

For document-pair similarity learning, LORETA improves mean average precision over a passive-aggressive factorized model and a full model using preselected features under the same memory budget. It also shows consistent improvements over standard methods in a multilabel image classification task with 1,600 classes. These evaluations support the practical value of its low-rank update procedure.
summary.tldr: LORETA efficiently updates low-rank matrix models through manifold retractions and improves results in document similarity and multilabel image classification.

title: Online Learning in The Manifold of Low-Rank Matrices

abstract: We show that matrix completion with trace-norm regularization can be significantly hurt when entries of the matrix are sampled non-uniformly, but that a properly weighted version of the trace-norm regularizer works well with non-uniform sampling. We show that the weighted trace-norm regularization indeed yields significant gains on the highly non-uniformly sampled Netflix dataset.
originalAbstract: We show that matrix completion with trace-norm regularization can be significantly hurt when entries of the matrix are sampled non-uniformly, but that a properly weighted version of the trace-norm regularizer works well with non-uniform sampling. We show that the weighted trace-norm regularization indeed yields significant gains on the highly non-uniformly sampled Netflix dataset.

paragraphs: Matrix completion uses observed entries of a matrix to estimate entries that are missing. In collaborative filtering, the observations need not be distributed evenly across the matrix. This paper examines how that uneven sampling affects a common learning approach based on trace-norm regularization, which constrains the matrix being fitted.

The authors show that non-uniform sampling can substantially damage the performance of ordinary trace-norm regularization. Their proposed response is a properly weighted version of the same regularizer. The central idea is that the sampling pattern matters to how the model should be constrained, rather than being merely a detail of which entries happen to be available.

The paper reports that the weighted approach works well under non-uniform sampling and produces significant gains on the Netflix dataset, where observations are highly uneven. This result connects the methodological change to a collaborative-filtering application. It establishes that adjusting the regularizer can make a meaningful difference in this setting, without claiming that every weighting choice will have the same effect.
summary.tldr: Properly weighting trace-norm regularization improves matrix completion under uneven sampling, with significant gains reported on Netflix data.

title: Collaborative Filtering in a Non-Uniform World: Learning with the Weighted Trace Norm

abstract: Non-linear dynamical systems (DS) have been used extensively for building generative models of human behavior. Its applications range from modeling brain dynamics to encoding motor commands. Many schemes have been proposed for encoding robot motions using dynamical systems with a single attractor placed at a predefined target in state space. Although these enable the robots to react against sudden perturbations without any re-planning, the motions are always directed towards a single target. In this work, we focus on combining several such DS with distinct attractors, resulting in a multi-stable DS. We show its applicability in reach-to-grasp tasks where the attractors represent several grasping points on the target object. While exploiting multiple attractors provides more flexibility in recovering from unseen perturbations, it also increases the complexity of the underlying learning problem. Here we present the Augmented-SVM (A-SVM) model which inherits region partitioning ability of the well known SVM classifier and is augmented with novel constraints derived from the individual DS. The new constraints modify the original SVM dual whose optimal solution then results in a new class of support vectors (SV). These new SV ensure that the resulting multi-stable DS incurs minimum deviation from the original dynamics and is stable at each of the attractors within a finite region of attraction. We show, via implementations on a simulated 10 degrees of freedom mobile robotic platform, that the model is capable of real-time motion generation and is able to adapt on-the-fly to perturbations.

paragraphs: A dynamical system with a single attractor can generate robot motion toward a target and respond to disturbances without replanning. Its destination remains fixed, however. This paper combines several systems with different attractors, allowing a reach-to-grasp controller to have several possible grasping points on an object. Multiple destinations offer greater flexibility when unexpected perturbations occur.

The proposed Augmented-SVM partitions the state space using the region-separating ability of a support vector machine. It adds constraints derived from the individual dynamical systems. These constraints change the optimization problem and introduce a new class of support vectors that governs how the component dynamics are combined.

The resulting system minimizes deviation from the original dynamics and is stable at each attractor within a finite region of attraction. That regional qualification matters: the stated stability does not cover every possible state. Implementations on a simulated mobile robot with ten degrees of freedom demonstrate real-time motion generation and adaptation to perturbations as they happen.
summary.tldr: Augmented-SVM combines robot motion systems with multiple targets while preserving local attractor stability and supporting real-time adaptation in simulation.

title: Augmented-SVM: Automatic space partitioning for combining multiple non-linear dynamics

abstract: Early stages of visual processing are thought to decorrelate, or whiten, the incoming temporally varying signals. Because the typical correlation time of natural stimuli, as well as the extent of temporal receptive fields of lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) neurons, is much greater than neuronal time constants, such decorrelation must be done in stages combining contributions of multiple neurons. We propose to model temporal decorrelation in the visual pathway with the lattice filter, a signal processing device for stage-wise decorrelation of temporal signals. The stage-wise architecture of the lattice filter maps naturally onto the visual pathway (photoreceptors -> bipolar cells -> retinal ganglion cells -> LGN) and its filter weights can be learned using Hebbian rules in a stage-wise sequential manner. Moreover, predictions of neural activity from the lattice filter model are consistent with physiological measurements in LGN neurons and fruit fly second-order visual neurons. Therefore, the lattice filter model is a useful abstraction that may help unravel visual system function.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a model of how early visual processing removes predictable temporal relationships from incoming signals. This operation, called decorrelation or whitening, reduces redundancy across time. The motivating observation is that natural visual signals and the temporal responses of LGN neurons extend over periods much longer than individual neuronal time constants, suggesting that several processing stages must contribute.

The authors use a lattice filter, a signal-processing structure that decorrelates signals progressively. Its sequence of stages maps naturally onto the pathway from photoreceptors through bipolar and retinal ganglion cells to the LGN. The filter weights can also be learned sequentially through Hebbian rules, connecting the computational architecture to a proposed mechanism for adjusting neural connections.

The model predicts neural activity consistent with physiological measurements from LGN neurons and second-order visual neurons in fruit flies. These correspondences support its usefulness as an abstraction of temporal visual processing. The contribution is a unified account linking a computational task, a staged anatomical pathway, and a learning rule, while presenting that account as a potentially helpful model of visual function.
summary.tldr: A lattice filter models temporal decorrelation across early visual stages and produces activity predictions consistent with physiological measurements.

title: A lattice filter model of the visual pathway

abstract: While finding the exact solution for the MAP inference problem is intractable for many real-world tasks, MAP LP relaxations have been shown to be very effective in practice. However, the most efficient methods that perform block coordinate descent can get stuck in sub-optimal points as they are not globally convergent. In this work we propose to augment these algorithms with an $\epsilon$-descent approach and present a method to efficiently optimize for a descent direction in the subdifferential using a margin-based extension of the Fenchel-Young duality theorem. Furthermore, the presented approach provides a methodology to construct a primal optimal solution from its dual optimal counterpart. We demonstrate the efficiency of the presented approach on spin glass models and protein interactions problems and show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art solvers.

paragraphs: Finding an exact maximum a posteriori assignment is intractable in many practical problems, motivating linear-programming relaxations. Efficient solvers for these relaxations often use block coordinate descent. However, such methods can stop at suboptimal points, so their computational speed alone does not ensure that they solve the relaxed optimization problem globally.

The paper augments these algorithms with an epsilon-descent approach. It uses a margin-based extension of Fenchel–Young duality to efficiently find a descent direction within the subdifferential. This supplies a mechanism for making progress beyond points where the original coordinate procedure can become stuck, addressing the lack of global convergence.

The framework also provides a way to construct an optimal primal solution from an optimal dual solution. That links solving the dual optimization problem to recovering a solution of the original relaxation. Experiments on spin glass models and protein interaction problems report better performance than leading solvers. The global optimization target here is the MAP linear-programming relaxation; the abstract does not equate solving it with exact MAP inference in every problem.
summary.tldr: A Fenchel–Young margin-based descent mechanism gives MAP LP relaxation solvers global convergence and a route from dual to primal solutions.

title: Globally Convergent Dual MAP LP Relaxation Solvers using Fenchel-Young Margins

abstract: Consistently matching keypoints across images, and the related problem of finding clusters of nearby images, are critical components of various tasks in Computer Vision, including Structure from Motion (SfM). Unfortunately, occlusion and large repetitive structures tend to mislead most currently used matching algorithms, leading to characteristic pathologies in the final output. In this paper we introduce a new method, Permutations Diffusion Maps (PDM), to solve the matching problem, as well as a related new affinity measure, derived using ideas from harmonic analysis on the symmetric group. We show that just by using it as a preprocessing step to existing SfM pipelines, PDM can greatly improve reconstruction quality on difficult datasets.

paragraphs: The paper tackles consistent matching of keypoints across images and the related task of grouping nearby images. Both are important for computer-vision systems such as structure from motion, which reconstructs scene structure from images. Occlusion and large repetitive structures can mislead matching methods and introduce characteristic errors into the resulting reconstruction.

The authors introduce Permutation Diffusion Maps, together with a new affinity measure for assessing image relationships. The construction draws on harmonic analysis on the symmetric group, a mathematical framework involving permutations. This supplies a new basis for the matching problem and for measuring the relationships needed to associate images.

The method can be inserted as a preprocessing stage in existing structure-from-motion pipelines. The authors show that this addition can greatly improve reconstruction quality on difficult datasets. Its practical significance is that improving image association upstream can improve a complete reconstruction pipeline, and the reported results demonstrate that benefit without requiring the method to replace the entire pipeline.
summary.tldr: Permutation Diffusion Maps improve image matching and can substantially enhance difficult structure-from-motion reconstructions as a preprocessing step.

title: Permutation Diffusion Maps (PDM) with Application to the Image Association Problem in Computer Vision

abstract: Performing interventions is a major challenge in economic policy-making. We propose \emph{causal strategic inference} as a framework for conducting interventions and apply it to large, networked microfinance economies. The basic solution platform consists of modeling a microfinance market as a networked economy, learning the parameters of the model from the real-world microfinance data, and designing algorithms for various computational problems in question. We adopt Nash equilibrium as the solution concept for our model. For a special case of our model, we show that an equilibrium point always exists and that the equilibrium interest rates are unique. For the general case, we give a constructive proof of the existence of an equilibrium point. Our empirical study is based on the microfinance data from Bangladesh and Bolivia, which we use to first learn our models. We show that causal strategic inference can assist policy-makers by evaluating the outcomes of various types of interventions, such as removing a loss-making bank from the market, imposing an interest rate cap, and subsidizing banks.

paragraphs: The paper proposes causal strategic inference as a framework for evaluating interventions in microfinance markets. It represents a market as a networked economy, learns model parameters from real microfinance data, and develops algorithms for questions about that economy. The aim is to help assess policy changes while accounting for strategic behavior within the modeled market.

The model uses Nash equilibrium as its solution concept, describing outcomes in which participants have no incentive to change their own decisions unilaterally. For a special case, the authors prove that an equilibrium exists and that equilibrium interest rates are unique. For the general model, they give a constructive existence proof. The uniqueness result is specifically confined to the special case.

Using data from Bangladesh and Bolivia, the authors learn models and evaluate interventions such as removing an unprofitable bank, capping interest rates, and subsidizing banks. Their empirical study shows how the framework can assist policy evaluation by examining the outcomes of these changes within learned strategic models.
summary.tldr: Learned network models of microfinance markets use equilibrium analysis to evaluate interventions such as interest-rate caps, subsidies, and bank removal.

title: Causal Strategic Inference in Networked Microfinance Economies

abstract: In this paper, we develop a family of algorithms for optimizing superposition-structured” or “dirty” statistical estimators for high-dimensional problems involving the minimization of the sum of a smooth loss function with a hybrid regularization. Most of the current approaches are first-order methods, including proximal gradient or Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). We propose a new family of second-order methods where we approximate the loss function using quadratic approximation. The superposition structured regularizer then leads to a subproblem that can be efficiently solved by alternating minimization. We propose a general active subspace selection approach to speed up the solver by utilizing the low-dimensional structure given by the regularizers, and provide convergence guarantees for our algorithm. Empirically, we show that our approach is more than 10 times faster than state-of-the-art first-order approaches for the latent variable graphical model selection problems and multi-task learning problems when there is more than one regularizer. For these problems, our approach appears to be the first algorithm that can extend active subspace ideas to multiple regularizers."

paragraphs: Many high-dimensional estimators combine a smooth loss with multiple regularizers that express different structural preferences. This paper studies such superposition-structured, or dirty, models. It develops a family of second-order optimization methods for problems commonly approached with first-order techniques such as proximal gradient methods or ADMM.

The method forms a quadratic approximation to the smooth loss. Combined with the structured regularizer, this produces a subproblem that can be solved efficiently through alternating minimization. A general active-subspace selection procedure further accelerates the solver by using the low-dimensional structure encouraged by the regularizers. The authors also provide convergence guarantees.

Experiments on latent-variable graphical-model selection and multi-task learning report speedups exceeding tenfold over state-of-the-art first-order approaches when multiple regularizers are present. The authors describe their method as apparently the first to extend active-subspace ideas to multiple regularizers for these problems. The contribution links richer local approximations of the loss with structure-aware computation, and the reported speed gains concern the evaluated applications rather than all regularized estimation problems.
summary.tldr: Quadratic loss approximations and active-subspace selection accelerate models with multiple regularizers, with reported speedups greater than tenfold.

title: QUIC & DIRTY: A Quadratic Approximation Approach for Dirty Statistical Models

abstract: Stochastic variational inference (SVI) uses stochastic optimization to scale up Bayesian computation to massive data. We present an alternative perspective on SVI as approximate parallel coordinate ascent. SVI trades-off bias and variance to step close to the unknown true coordinate optimum given by batch variational Bayes (VB). We define a model to automate this process. The model infers the location of the next VB optimum from a sequence of noisy realizations. As a consequence of this construction, we update the variational parameters using Bayes rule, rather than a hand-crafted optimization schedule. When our model is a Kalman filter this procedure can recover the original SVI algorithm and SVI with adaptive steps. We may also encode additional assumptions in the model, such as heavy-tailed noise. By doing so, our algorithm outperforms the original SVI schedule and a state-of-the-art adaptive SVI algorithm in two diverse domains.

This paper interprets those updates as an approximate form of parallel coordinate ascent. From that perspective, the task is to move toward the coordinate optimum that batch variational Bayes would provide, while balancing the bias and variance of noisy information.

The authors turn this balancing act into an inference problem. A model uses a sequence of noisy realizations to estimate where the next batch optimum lies. These results support filtering as a useful way to design and adapt variational updates.

title: A Filtering Approach to Stochastic Variational Inference

abstract: This article provides the first procedure for computing a fully data-dependent interval that traps the mixing time $t_{mix}$ of a finite reversible ergodic Markov chain at a prescribed confidence level. The interval is computed from a single finite-length sample path from the Markov chain, and does not require the knowledge of any parameters of the chain. This stands in contrast to previous approaches, which either only provide point estimates, or require a reset mechanism, or additional prior knowledge. The interval is constructed around the relaxation time $t_{relax}$, which is strongly related to the mixing time, and the width of the interval converges to zero roughly at a $\sqrt{n}$ rate, where $n$ is the length of the sample path. Upper and lower bounds are given on the number of samples required to achieve constant-factor multiplicative accuracy. The lower bounds indicate that, unless further restrictions are placed on the chain, no procedure can achieve this accuracy level before seeing each state at least $\Omega(t_{relax})$ times on the average. Finally, future directions of research are identified.

paragraphs: Mixing time describes how long a Markov chain takes to approach its equilibrium behavior. This paper estimates it from one finite observed trajectory of a finite, reversible, ergodic chain. The procedure produces a fully data-dependent interval with a prescribed confidence level, without requiring knowledge of the chain’s parameters.

The interval is constructed around the closely related relaxation time. Its width shrinks toward zero at approximately an inverse-square-root rate in the trajectory length. Unlike approaches that give only a point estimate, this supplies an explicit uncertainty interval. It also avoids requiring a mechanism that resets the chain or additional prior information about it.

Without further restrictions on the chain, the lower bounds require observing each state on average at least on the order of the relaxation time. This identifies a fundamental data requirement, rather than merely a weakness of the proposed estimator, and explains why a short trajectory may be insufficient for accurate mixing-time estimation.
summary.tldr: A single trajectory yields a confidence interval for a reversible ergodic chain’s mixing time, with guarantees on accuracy and necessary sample coverage.

title: Mixing Time Estimation in Reversible Markov Chains from a Single Sample Path

abstract: An important class of problems involves training deep neural networks with sparse prediction targets of very high dimension D. These occur naturally in e.g. neural language models or the learning of word-embeddings, often posed as predicting the probability of next words among a vocabulary of size D (e.g. 200,000). Computing the equally large, but typically non-sparse D-dimensional output vector from a last hidden layer of reasonable dimension d (e.g. 500) incurs a prohibitive $O(Dd)$ computational cost for each example, as does updating the $D \times d$ output weight matrix and computing the gradient needed for backpropagation to previous layers. While efficient handling of large sparse network inputs is trivial, this case of large sparse targets is not, and has thus so far been sidestepped with approximate alternatives such as hierarchical softmax or sampling-based approximations during training. In this work we develop an original algorithmic approach that, for a family of loss functions that includes squared error and spherical softmax, can compute the exact loss, gradient update for the output weights, and gradient for backpropagation, all in $O(d^2)$ per example instead of $O(Dd)$, remarkably without ever computing the D-dimensional output. The proposed algorithm yields a speedup of $\frac{D}{4d}$, i.e. two orders of magnitude for typical sizes, for that critical part of the computations that often dominates the training time in this kind of network architecture.

Sparsity in the target does not automatically make training cheap, because the predicted output is typically dense. Computing that output, updating its weight matrix, and propagating gradients can each incur costs proportional to the output dimension D times the hidden dimension d.

Exactness is a central feature, and the supported loss family is an essential qualification.

The stated speedup for this computational component is D divided by 4d, reaching about two orders of magnitude for typical dimensions discussed in the abstract. This applies to a part of training that often dominates these architectures. It does not by itself state the same speedup for every operation in the complete network.
summary.tldr: For a specified family of losses, exact training computations with huge sparse targets can avoid constructing the output and cost O(d²) per example.

title: Efficient Exact Gradient Update for training Deep Networks with Very Large Sparse Targets

abstract: Supervised deep learning has been successfully applied for many recognition problems in machine learning and computer vision. Although it can approximate a complex many-to-one function very well when large number of training data is provided, the lack of probabilistic inference of the current supervised deep learning methods makes it difficult to model a complex structured output representations. In this work, we develop a scalable deep conditional generative model for structured output variables using Gaussian latent variables. The model is trained efficiently in the framework of stochastic gradient variational Bayes, and allows a fast prediction using stochastic feed-forward inference. In addition, we provide novel strategies to build a robust structured prediction algorithms, such as recurrent prediction network architecture, input noise-injection and multi-scale prediction training methods. In experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm in comparison to the deterministic deep neural network counterparts in generating diverse but realistic output representations using stochastic inference. Furthermore, the proposed schemes in training methods and architecture design were complimentary, which leads to achieve strong pixel-level object segmentation and semantic labeling performance on Caltech-UCSD Birds 200 and the subset of Labeled Faces in the Wild dataset.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires producing outputs with internal organization, rather than only a single recognition decision. This paper addresses the difficulty of representing such outputs probabilistically with conventional supervised deep networks. It develops a conditional generative model in which Gaussian latent variables support stochastic predictions conditioned on the input.

The model is trained using stochastic gradient variational Bayes and predicts through fast stochastic feed-forward inference. This combination provides a way to learn a structured output representation and generate different outputs from it. The authors also introduce recurrent prediction networks, noise injection into inputs, and training with predictions at multiple scales as strategies for improving robustness.

Experiments show that the proposed model can generate diverse yet realistic outputs compared with deterministic deep-network counterparts. The architectural and training strategies provide complementary benefits, leading to strong pixel-level object segmentation and semantic labeling results on Caltech-UCSD Birds 200 and a subset of Labeled Faces in the Wild. The findings connect probabilistic output generation with practical structured-prediction performance in these evaluations.
summary.tldr: A deep conditional generative model uses Gaussian latent variables and stochastic inference to produce diverse structured outputs with strong reported segmentation performance.

title: Learning Structured Output Representation using Deep Conditional Generative Models

abstract: Here we introduce a new model of natural textures based on the feature spaces of convolutional neural networks optimised for object recognition. Samples from the model are of high perceptual quality demonstrating the generative power of neural networks trained in a purely discriminative fashion. Within the model, textures are represented by the correlations between feature maps in several layers of the network. We show that across layers the texture representations increasingly capture the statistical properties of natural images while making object information more and more explicit. The model provides a new tool to generate stimuli for neuroscience and might offer insights into the deep representations learned by convolutional neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper builds a model of natural textures using the internal features of convolutional neural networks trained for object recognition. The starting network was trained for a discriminative task, yet its learned feature spaces also support generating perceptually convincing textures. The work demonstrates a generative use for representations learned through recognition.

Textures are represented through correlations between feature maps at several network layers. These correlations describe relationships among the network's responses and provide the model's account of texture. Across layers, the authors find that the representations increasingly capture natural-image statistics while also making information about objects more explicit.

Samples from the model have high reported perceptual quality, supporting the usefulness of these feature relationships for texture generation. The model also provides a tool for creating neuroscience stimuli. Beyond that practical application, the authors suggest it might help explain the deep representations learned by convolutional networks. This interpretive possibility is grounded in examining what the layerwise texture representations retain and reveal about images.
summary.tldr: Correlations among features in an object-recognition CNN support high-quality texture synthesis and offer a tool for studying learned representations.

title: Texture Synthesis Using Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Recent machine learning methods for sequential behavior prediction estimate the motives of behavior rather than the behavior itself. This higher-level abstraction improves generalization in different prediction settings, but computing predictions often becomes intractable in large decision spaces. We propose the Softstar algorithm, a softened heuristic-guided search technique for the maximum entropy inverse optimal control model of sequential behavior. This approach supports probabilistic search with bounded approximation error at a significantly reduced computational cost when compared to sampling based methods. We present the algorithm, analyze approximation guarantees, and compare performance with simulation-based inference on two distinct complex decision tasks.

paragraphs: Predicting sequential behavior can involve estimating the motives behind actions instead of directly predicting the actions themselves. The paper describes this higher-level approach as helpful for generalization across prediction settings. Its computational challenge is that turning inferred motives into predictions can become intractable when the space of possible decisions is large.

Softstar addresses inference within the maximum entropy inverse optimal control model of sequential behavior. It uses a softened form of heuristic-guided search to support probabilistic inference. The method is designed to reduce computation while retaining a bound on approximation error, tying the efficiency of the search to an explicit statement about the accuracy of its output.

The authors present the algorithm, analyze its approximation guarantees, and compare it with simulation-based inference on two complex decision tasks. They report substantially reduced computational cost relative to sampling-based methods. The contribution makes motive-based prediction more computationally accessible in the stated model, with approximation bounds providing a principled way to assess the search rather than relying only on observed speed.
summary.tldr: Softstar uses heuristic-guided probabilistic search to reduce inference cost for maximum entropy inverse optimal control with bounded approximation error.

title: Softstar: Heuristic-Guided Probabilistic Inference

abstract: Even in state-spaces of modest size, planning is plagued by the “curse of dimensionality”. This problem is particularly acute in human and animal cognition given the limited capacity of working memory, and the time pressures under which planning often occurs in the natural environment. Hierarchically organized modular representations have long been suggested to underlie the capacity of biological systems to efficiently and flexibly plan in complex environments. However, the principles underlying efficient modularization remain obscure, making it difficult to identify its behavioral and neural signatures. Here, we develop a normative theory of efficient state-space representations which partitions an environment into distinct modules by minimizing the average (information theoretic) description length of planning within the environment, thereby optimally trading off the complexity of planning across and within modules. We show that such optimal representations provide a unifying account for a diverse range of hitherto unrelated phenomena at multiple levels of behavior and neural representation.

paragraphs: Planning can become difficult even when an environment has only a modest number of states. For people and animals, limited working memory and time pressure make this especially consequential. Hierarchical representations offer a possible solution by dividing an environment into modules, but that leaves a central question: which division makes planning efficient?

The paper develops a normative theory that answers this question through information-theoretic description length. It selects a partition that minimizes the average description length of planning in the environment. This objective balances two sources of complexity: planning between modules and planning inside each module. The preferred representation is the one that optimally trades off those costs under the proposed criterion.

The authors show that the resulting representations provide a common account of multiple behavioral and neural phenomena previously treated as unrelated. The significance is both computational and explanatory: a concrete efficiency principle determines the modules and connects their organization to patterns in behavior and neural representation.
summary.tldr: The paper explains modular planning representations by minimizing the information needed to plan within and between modules.

title: Efficient state-space modularization for planning: theory, behavioral and neural signatures

abstract: We consider the Frank-Wolfe (FW) method for constrained convex optimization, and we show that this classical technique can be interpreted from a different perspective: FW emerges as the computation of an equilibrium (saddle point) of a special convex-concave zero sum game. This saddle-point trick relies on the existence of no-regret online learning to both generate a sequence of iterates but also to provide a proof of convergence through vanishing regret. We show that our stated equivalence has several nice properties, as it exhibits a modularity that gives rise to various old and new algorithms. We explore a few such resulting methods, and provide experimental results to demonstrate correctness and efficiency.

We explore a few such resulting methods, and provide experimental results to demonstrate correctness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe is a method for constrained convex optimization. This paper gives it another interpretation: its optimization process can be viewed as computing an equilibrium of a particular convex-concave zero-sum game. The equilibrium is a saddle point, connecting the search for an optimization solution with the interaction between opposing objectives.

The connection relies on no-regret online learning. These learning procedures generate the sequence of iterates, while their vanishing regret also supplies a convergence argument. In this way, the same online-learning machinery explains both how the optimization updates arise and why they approach a solution in the studied formulation.

The authors emphasize that the interpretation is modular. It provides a framework from which both existing and new algorithms can emerge, rather than only a new explanation of one established method. They explore several resulting methods and report experiments demonstrating correctness and efficiency. The contribution links optimization and equilibrium computation in a form that supports algorithm design as well as analysis.
summary.tldr: Frank-Wolfe can be understood as no-regret learning toward a game equilibrium, yielding convergence proofs and a modular route to algorithms.

title: On Frank-Wolfe and Equilibrium Computation

abstract: This paper studies empirical risk minimization (ERM) problems for large-scale datasets and incorporates the idea of adaptive sample size methods to improve the guaranteed convergence bounds for first-order stochastic and deterministic methods. In contrast to traditional methods that attempt to solve the ERM problem corresponding to the full dataset directly, adaptive sample size schemes start with a small number of samples and solve the corresponding ERM problem to its statistical accuracy. The sample size is then grown geometrically -- e.g., scaling by a factor of two -- and use the solution of the previous ERM as a warm start for the new ERM. Theoretical analyses show that the use of adaptive sample size methods reduces the overall computational cost of achieving the statistical accuracy of the whole dataset for a broad range of deterministic and stochastic first-order methods. The gains are specific to the choice of method. When particularized to, e.g., accelerated gradient descent and stochastic variance reduce gradient, the computational cost advantage is a logarithm of the number of training samples. Numerical experiments on various datasets confirm theoretical claims and showcase the gains of using the proposed adaptive sample size scheme.

paragraphs: Large-scale empirical risk minimization usually begins by optimizing an objective built from the entire training dataset. This paper instead studies a staged approach that initially uses only a small sample. Each smaller problem is solved to its statistical accuracy, linking optimization effort to the accuracy supported by that amount of data.

The sample then grows geometrically, for example by doubling, and the previous solution becomes the starting point for the next problem. This warm start carries useful optimization work forward as more examples enter the objective. The scheme therefore changes the sequence of problems an optimizer solves, allowing both deterministic and stochastic first-order methods to benefit.

The theoretical analysis shows reduced total computation for reaching the statistical accuracy of the full dataset across a broad range of methods. The size of the gain depends on the optimizer: for accelerated gradient descent and stochastic variance-reduced gradient, the advantage is a factor logarithmic in the training sample count. Numerical experiments on several datasets support the analysis and demonstrate the staged scheme’s computational benefits.
summary.tldr: Solving progressively larger training problems with warm starts reduces the computation needed to reach full-dataset statistical accuracy.

title: First-Order Adaptive Sample Size Methods to Reduce Complexity of Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: Key to multitask learning is exploiting the relationships between different tasks to improve prediction performance. Most previous methods have focused on the case where tasks relations can be modeled as linear operators and regularization approaches can be used successfully. However, in practice assuming the tasks to be linearly related is often restrictive, and allowing for nonlinear structures is a challenge. In this paper, we tackle this issue by casting the problem within the framework of structured prediction. Our main contribution is a novel algorithm for learning multiple tasks which are related by a system of nonlinear equations that their joint outputs need to satisfy. We show that our algorithm can be efficiently implemented and study its generalization properties, proving universal consistency and learning rates. Our theoretical analysis highlights the benefits of non-linear multitask learning over learning the tasks independently. Encouraging experimental results show the benefits of the proposed method in practice.
