paragraphs: Multitask learning improves predictions by using relationships among tasks. Many approaches express those relationships through linear operators, but that representation can be restrictive when tasks interact in more complicated ways. This paper studies a setting where the outputs of several tasks must jointly satisfy a system of nonlinear equations.

The authors formulate the problem as structured prediction: the collection of outputs has relationships that the learner should account for together. Their algorithm incorporates the nonlinear equations connecting those outputs. This makes the relevant structure part of learning multiple tasks, allowing information about their relationships to influence the resulting predictions. The authors also show that the algorithm can be implemented efficiently.

The theoretical analysis establishes universal consistency and learning rates, addressing both long-run statistical behavior and how learning progresses with data. It also identifies benefits over learning each task independently. Encouraging experiments support practical advantages of the proposed method. The paper's contribution is thus an efficiently implementable approach with statistical analysis for a specific, nonlinear form of task relationship.
summary.tldr: The paper learns related tasks whose joint outputs obey nonlinear equations, with consistency guarantees and encouraging experimental results.

title: Consistent Multitask Learning with Nonlinear Output Relations

abstract: We propose a multiscale quantization approach for fast similarity search on large, high-dimensional datasets. The key insight of the approach is that quantization methods, in particular product quantization, perform poorly when there is large variance in the norms of the data points. This is a common scenario for real- world datasets, especially when doing product quantization of residuals obtained from coarse vector quantization. To address this issue, we propose a multiscale formulation where we learn a separate scalar quantizer of the residual norm scales. All parameters are learned jointly in a stochastic gradient descent framework to minimize the overall quantization error. We provide theoretical motivation for the proposed technique and conduct comprehensive experiments on two large-scale public datasets, demonstrating substantial improvements in recall over existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Fast similarity search often uses quantization to represent high-dimensional vectors compactly. This paper identifies a difficulty for product quantization when vector norms, or lengths, vary greatly. The issue is especially relevant to residual vectors, which represent what remains after a coarse vector quantizer has approximated the original data.

The proposed multiscale method learns a separate scalar quantizer for the scales of residual norms. This gives differences in magnitude an explicit role in the representation. All parameters are learned together with stochastic gradient descent to minimize overall quantization error, so the scale representation and the other quantization components are optimized toward the same objective.

The authors provide theoretical motivation and evaluate the method on two large public datasets. They report substantial recall improvements over existing leading methods, meaning the search retrieves more of the relevant neighbors in those comparisons. The findings support treating variation in vector magnitude as an important source of quantization error when designing compact representations for large-scale similarity search.
summary.tldr: Learning residual-vector scales jointly with quantization improves similarity-search recall on two large datasets.

title: Multiscale Quantization for Fast Similarity Search

abstract: In this paper we study the problem of learning Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) which are functions of the form $\vct{x}\mapsto \max(0,\langle \vct{w},\vct{x}\rangle)$ with $\vct{w}\in\R^d$ denoting the weight vector. We study this problem in the high-dimensional regime where the number of observations are fewer than the dimension of the weight vector. We assume that the weight vector belongs to some closed set (convex or nonconvex) which captures known side-information about its structure. We focus on the realizable model where the inputs are chosen i.i.d.~from a Gaussian distribution and the labels are generated according to a planted weight vector. We show that projected gradient descent, when initialized at $\vct{0}$, converges at a linear rate to the planted model with a number of samples that is optimal up to numerical constants. Our results on the dynamics of convergence of these very shallow neural nets may provide some insights towards understanding the dynamics of deeper architectures.

We study this problem in the high-dimensional regime where the number of observations are fewer than the dimension of the weight vector. We assume that the weight vector belongs to some closed set (convex or nonconvex) which captures known side-information about its structure. paragraphs: The paper studies learning a single rectified linear unit: a weighted sum of inputs that is replaced by zero when negative. Its focus is a high-dimensional setting with fewer observations than weight coordinates. To make learning possible in this regime, the analysis incorporates known structural information about the weights through a closed constraint set.

That set may be convex or nonconvex. The data model is realizable: inputs are independent Gaussian samples, and their labels come from a planted weight vector. Under the studied assumptions, projected gradient descent starting at the zero vector converges to the planted model at a linear rate, with sample requirements optimal up to numerical constants.

The result links structural prior information, sample efficiency, and optimization behavior for a very shallow neural model. Linear convergence means the error decreases geometrically through the iterations covered by the guarantee. The authors suggest that understanding these dynamics may offer insight into deeper networks, while the established result concerns the specified single-ReLU setting.
summary.tldr: Under structured, realizable Gaussian assumptions, projected gradient descent learns a single ReLU at a linear rate with near-optimal sample requirements.

title: Learning ReLUs via Gradient Descent

abstract: Observational data is increasingly used as a means for making individual-level causal predictions and intervention recommendations. The foremost challenge of causal inference from observational data is hidden confounding, whose presence cannot be tested in data and can invalidate any causal conclusion. Experimental data does not suffer from confounding but is usually limited in both scope and scale. We introduce a novel method of using limited experimental data to correct the hidden confounding in causal effect models trained on larger observational data, even if the observational data does not fully overlap with the experimental data. Our method makes strictly weaker assumptions than existing approaches, and we prove conditions under which it yields a consistent estimator. We demonstrate our method's efficacy using real-world data from a large educational experiment.

paragraphs: Large observational datasets can support detailed predictions, but hidden confounding can undermine attempts to interpret those predictions causally. Unobserved influences may affect both the intervention received and its outcome. Experimental data avoids this confounding problem, yet is often available only for a smaller population or a narrower range of situations.

The paper proposes using limited experimental evidence to correct causal effect models learned from larger observational datasets. The method can work even when the two sources do not fully overlap. This makes the experiment an anchor for correcting the observational model, while retaining the broader information supplied by the observational data.

The authors state that their assumptions are strictly weaker than those of existing approaches and establish conditions under which the estimator is consistent. They also demonstrate effectiveness using real data from a large educational experiment. The consistency result is conditional on the proved conditions; the empirical application provides evidence that experimental grounding can usefully correct observational causal estimates.
summary.tldr: Limited experimental data can correct hidden confounding in observational causal models, with consistency established under stated conditions.

title: Removing Hidden Confounding by Experimental Grounding

abstract: Interactive partially observable Markov decision processes (I-POMDPs) provide a principled framework for planning and acting in a partially observable, stochastic and multi-agent environment. It extends POMDPs to multi-agent settings by including models of other agents in the state space and forming a hierarchical belief structure. In order to predict other agents' actions using I-POMDPs, we propose an approach that effectively uses Bayesian inference and sequential Monte Carlo sampling to learn others' intentional models which ascribe to them beliefs, preferences and rationality in action selection. Empirical results show that our algorithm accurately learns models of the other agent and has superior performance than methods that use subintentional models. Our approach serves as a generalized Bayesian learning algorithm that learns other agents' beliefs, strategy levels, and transition, observation and reward functions. It also effectively mitigates the belief space complexity due to the nested belief hierarchy.

paragraphs: Planning among other agents requires reasoning about actions whose causes may be only partly visible. Interactive partially observable Markov decision processes address this by including models of other agents in the state. Their beliefs form a hierarchy, allowing an agent to reason about what another agent believes and how it chooses actions.

The paper combines Bayesian inference with sequential Monte Carlo sampling to learn intentional models of other agents. Such models attribute beliefs, preferences, and rational action selection to the agents being modeled. The proposed learning procedure covers beliefs and strategy levels, along with transition, observation, and reward functions, giving it a broad role within the interactive planning framework.

Empirical results show accurate learning of another agent's model and better performance than methods using subintentional models. The approach also mitigates the complexity arising from nested beliefs. Its significance is to make richer models of other decision makers more manageable: predicting behavior can draw on inferred intentions while sampling helps handle the computational burden of maintaining hierarchical uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Bayesian inference and sequential Monte Carlo learn other agents' intentional models within interactive POMDPs.

title: Learning Others' Intentional Models in Multi-Agent Settings Using Interactive POMDPs

abstract: In this paper we study the facility location problem in the model of differential privacy (DP) with uniform facility cost. Specifically, we first show that under the hierarchically well-separated tree (HST) metrics and the super-set output setting that was introduced in Gupta et. al., there is an $\epsilon$-DP algorithm that achieves an $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$(expected multiplicative) approximation ratio; this implies an $O(\frac{\log n}{\epsilon})$ approximation ratio for the general metric case, where $n$ is the size of the input metric. These bounds improve the best-known results given by Gupta et. al. In particular, our approximation ratio for HST-metrics is independent of $n$, and the ratio for general metrics is independent of the aspect ratio of the input metric. On the negative side, we show that the approximation ratio of any $\epsilon$-DP algorithm is lower bounded by $\Omega(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon}})$, even for instances on HST metrics with uniform facility cost, under the super-set output setting. The lower bound shows that the dependence of the approximation ratio for HST metrics on $\epsilon$ can not be removed or greatly improved. Our novel methods and techniques for both the upper and lower bound may find additional applications.

paragraphs: This paper studies facility location with differential privacy when every facility has the same opening cost. It measures solution quality through a multiplicative approximation ratio, which expresses how the algorithm’s cost compares with an optimal solution. The results apply under a specified super-set output setting, making that setting part of the scope of the guarantees.

For hierarchically well-separated tree metrics, the authors give an epsilon-private algorithm with an expected approximation ratio of O(1/epsilon). This implies O(log n/epsilon) for general metrics, where n is the metric’s size. Both improve previous bounds. The tree-metric guarantee is independent of n, while the general-metric guarantee avoids dependence on the input’s aspect ratio.

The paper also proves a lower bound of Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)), even for those tree metrics with uniform facility costs and the same output setting. Thus, some deterioration with stronger privacy is unavoidable. The upper and lower bounds leave a gap, but together they establish improved achievable performance and a barrier to eliminating the dependence on the privacy parameter.
summary.tldr: Improved private facility-location algorithms reduce approximation costs, while a lower bound shows that dependence on privacy strength remains unavoidable.

title: Facility Location Problem in Differential Privacy Model Revisited

abstract: We study problem-dependent rates, i.e., generalization errors that scale tightly with the variance or the effective loss at the "best hypothesis." Existing uniform convergence and localization frameworks, the most widely used tools to study this problem, often fail to simultaneously provide parameter localization and optimal dependence on the sample size. As a result, existing problem-dependent rates are often rather weak when the hypothesis class is "rich" and the worst-case bound of the loss is large. In this paper we propose a new framework based on a "uniform localized convergence" principle. We provide the first (moment-penalized) estimator that achieves the optimal variance-dependent rate for general "rich" classes; we also establish improved loss-dependent rate for standard empirical risk minimization.

paragraphs: Generalization guarantees can become more informative when they reflect the particular learning problem. This paper studies error rates that depend tightly on the variance or effective loss associated with the best hypothesis. Such rates aim to capture favorable statistical structure that a broad worst-case bound may overlook.

The authors identify a difficulty with common uniform-convergence and localization tools: they often fail to combine localization in parameter space with optimal dependence on sample size. This can produce weak guarantees for rich hypothesis classes, especially when the worst-case loss bound is large. The proposed framework addresses this combination through a principle called uniform localized convergence.

Using that framework, the paper introduces a moment-penalized estimator achieving the optimal variance-dependent rate for general rich classes. It also derives an improved loss-dependent rate for standard empirical risk minimization. These are distinct outcomes: one concerns a new estimator, while the other strengthens the analysis of an established learning rule. Together, they improve how learning guarantees account for the statistical difficulty of a particular problem.
summary.tldr: Uniform localized convergence yields optimal variance-dependent rates for a new estimator and improved loss-dependent rates for empirical risk minimization.

title: Towards Problem-dependent Optimal Learning Rates

abstract: The objective of this paper is visual-only self-supervised video representation learning. We make the following contributions: (i) we investigate the benefit of adding semantic-class positives to instance-based Info Noise Contrastive Estimation (InfoNCE) training, showing that this form of supervised contrastive learning leads to a clear improvement in performance; (ii) we propose a novel self-supervised co-training scheme to improve the popular infoNCE loss, exploiting the complementary information from different views, RGB streams and optical flow, of the same data source by using one view to obtain positive class samples for the other; (iii) we thoroughly evaluate the quality of the learnt representation on two different downstream tasks: action recognition and video retrieval. In both cases, the proposed approach demonstrates state-of-the-art or comparable performance with other self-supervised approaches, whilst being significantly more efficient to train, i.e. requiring far less training data to achieve similar performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning video representations from visual data without class supervision. It first investigates a supervised contrastive setting and finds that adding positive examples from the same semantic class improves instance-based InfoNCE training. That result motivates finding useful class-related positives through a self-supervised procedure.

The proposed co-training scheme uses two complementary views of the same videos: RGB streams and optical flow. One view identifies positive class samples for training the other. In this way, information available through one representation helps shape the contrastive learning problem faced by the other, extending how positive examples are obtained.

The authors assess the learned representations on action recognition and video retrieval. On both tasks, they report performance that is state-of-the-art or comparable with other self-supervised methods, while requiring substantially less training data to reach similar performance. The reported efficiency benefit therefore concerns data needed for training. The findings support using complementary visual streams to improve the supervision that contrastive learning can generate for itself.
summary.tldr: RGB and optical-flow views supply positives for each other’s contrastive training, producing competitive video representations with substantially less training data.

title: Self-supervised Co-Training for Video Representation Learning

abstract: In the world of big data, large but costly to label datasets dominate many fields. Active learning, a semi-supervised alternative to the standard PAC-learning model, was introduced to explore whether adaptive labeling could learn concepts with exponentially fewer labeled samples. While previous results show that active learning performs no better than its supervised alternative for important concept classes such as linear separators, we show that by adding weak distributional assumptions and allowing comparison queries, active learning requires exponentially fewer samples. Further, we show that these results hold as well for a stronger model of learning called Reliable and Probably Useful (RPU) learning. In this model, our learner is not allowed to make mistakes, but may instead answer ``I don't know.'' While previous negative results showed this model to have intractably large sample complexity for label queries, we show that comparison queries make RPU-learning at worst logarithmically more expensive in both the passive and active regimes.

paragraphs: Active learning lets a learner adaptively choose which examples to label, aiming to reduce expensive supervision. Yet prior results show that this flexibility alone need not improve sample complexity for important classes such as linear separators. This paper studies how the picture changes when the learner can also ask comparison queries under weak distributional assumptions.

With those additions, the authors show that active learning can require exponentially fewer samples. The conditions are part of the result: the improvement comes from combining comparison queries with the stated assumptions about the data distribution. The work therefore identifies additional information that can make adaptive learning substantially more efficient than label queries alone.

The results also extend to Reliable and Probably Useful learning, where the learner may abstain but is not allowed to make mistakes. Earlier label-query results made this requirement prohibitively expensive in sample complexity. With comparisons, the paper shows that this stronger learning requirement costs at most an additional logarithmic factor in both passive and active regimes, making abstention-compatible reliability much more accessible theoretically.
summary.tldr: Under weak distributional assumptions, comparison queries enable exponential active-learning savings and efficient learning with reliable abstention.

title: The Power of Comparisons for Actively Learning Linear Classifiers

abstract: We present \textproc{Gaptron}, a randomized first-order algorithm for online multiclass classification. In the full information setting we provide expected mistake bounds for \textproc{Gaptron} with respect to the logistic loss, hinge loss, and the smooth hinge loss with $O(K)$ regret, where the expectation is with respect to the learner's randomness and $K$ is the number of classes. In the bandit classification setting we show that \textproc{Gaptron} is the first linear time algorithm with $O(K\sqrt{T})$ expected regret. Additionally, the expected mistake bound of \textproc{Gaptron} does not depend on the dimension of the feature vector, contrary to previous algorithms with $O(K\sqrt{T})$ regret in the bandit classification setting. We present a new proof technique that exploits the gap between the zero-one loss and surrogate losses rather than exploiting properties such as exp-concavity or mixability, which are traditionally used to prove logarithmic or constant regret bounds.

paragraphs: Online multiclass classification requires making successive predictions while learning from feedback. This paper introduces Gaptron, a randomized first-order algorithm, and analyzes its mistakes through surrogate losses: training objectives that stand in for the discrete error of predicting the wrong class. The analysis makes direct use of the gap between those quantities.

With full information, the authors give expected mistake bounds relative to logistic, hinge, and smooth hinge losses, with regret of order K for K classes. Under bandit feedback, they establish expected regret of order K times the square root of T, where T is the number of rounds. The expectations are over the algorithm's own randomness.

The paper identifies Gaptron as the first linear-time algorithm achieving that bandit regret rate. Its expected mistake bound also avoids dependence on feature-vector dimension, unlike earlier algorithms with the same stated regret order. The proof technique is a separate contribution: exploiting the surrogate gap provides a route to strong bounds without relying on the exp-concavity or mixability properties traditionally used for such analyses.
summary.tldr: Gaptron exploits the gap between classification error and surrogate losses to obtain strong expected regret bounds with efficient online updates.

title: Exploiting the Surrogate Gap in Online Multiclass Classification

abstract: Learning depends on changes in synaptic connections deep inside the brain. In multilayer networks, these changes are triggered by error signals fed back from the output, generally through a stepwise inversion of the feedforward processing steps. The gold standard for this process --- backpropagation --- works well in artificial neural networks, but is biologically implausible. Several recent proposals have emerged to address this problem, but many of these biologically-plausible schemes are based on learning an independent set of feedback connections. This complicates the assignment of errors to each synapse by making it dependent upon a second learning problem, and by fitting inversions rather than guaranteeing them. Here, we show that feedforward network transformations can be effectively inverted through dynamics. We derive this dynamic inversion from the perspective of feedback control, where the forward transformation is reused and dynamically interacts with fixed or random feedback to propagate error signals during the backward pass. Importantly, this scheme does not rely upon a second learning problem for feedback because accurate inversion is guaranteed through the network dynamics. We map these dynamics onto generic feedforward networks, and show that the resulting algorithm performs well on several supervised and unsupervised datasets. Finally, we discuss potential links between dynamic inversion and second-order optimization. Overall, our work introduces an alternative perspective on credit assignment in the brain, and proposes a special role for temporal dynamics and feedback control during learning.

paragraphs: Learning in a multilayer network requires determining how connections inside the network contributed to an output error. Backpropagation handles this effectively in artificial networks, but the paper describes it as biologically implausible. Some alternatives learn separate feedback connections, which introduces another learning problem and makes error assignment depend on how successfully those connections learn to invert forward processing.

The proposed approach obtains inversion through network dynamics. Viewed as a feedback control process, it reuses the forward transformation and lets it interact over time with fixed or random feedback. Error signals propagate through this interaction. The authors state that the dynamics guarantee accurate inversion within their scheme, removing the need to train a separate feedback system to approximate it.

They map these dynamics onto generic feedforward networks and report good performance on several supervised and unsupervised datasets. They also discuss possible connections to second-order optimization. The contribution is an alternative mechanism for credit assignment that gives temporal dynamics and feedback control a central role; it does not establish that biological brains implement this particular algorithm.
summary.tldr: Dynamic inversion uses feedback control to propagate learning errors without training a separate set of inverse feedback connections.

title: Biological credit assignment through dynamic inversion of feedforward networks

abstract: Training multi-agent systems (MAS) to achieve realistic equilibria gives us a useful tool to understand and model real-world systems. We consider a general sum partially observable Markov game where agents of different types share a single policy network, conditioned on agent-specific information. This paper aims at i) formally understanding equilibria reached by such agents, and ii) matching emergent phenomena of such equilibria to real-world targets. Parameter sharing with decentralized execution has been introduced as an efficient way to train multiple agents using a single policy network. However, the nature of resulting equilibria reached by such agents has not been yet studied: we introduce the novel concept of Shared equilibrium as a symmetric pure Nash equilibrium of a certain Functional Form Game (FFG) and prove convergence to the latter for a certain class of games using self-play. In addition, it is important that such equilibria satisfy certain constraints so that MAS are calibrated to real world data for practical use: we solve this problem by introducing a novel dual-Reinforcement Learning based approach that fits emergent behaviors of agents in a Shared equilibrium to externally-specified targets, and apply our methods to a n-player market example. We do so by calibrating parameters governing distributions of agent types rather than individual agents, which allows both behavior differentiation among agents and coherent scaling of the shared policy network to multiple agents.

paragraphs: Multiple agents can share one policy network while choosing actions from their own information. This makes training efficient, but raises a question: what kind of equilibrium does shared training produce when agents have different types and only partial observations? The paper studies this setting in games where agents' interests need not be identical or directly opposed.

The authors define a Shared equilibrium through a symmetric pure Nash equilibrium in a related Functional Form Game. They prove that self-play converges to this equilibrium for a certain class of games. This gives a formal interpretation of shared-policy behavior while keeping the convergence claim tied to the class for which it is established.

The paper also introduces a dual reinforcement learning approach for matching emergent equilibrium behavior to externally specified targets. It calibrates parameters of agent-type distributions, allowing agents to behave differently while retaining a shared network that scales across agents. An example involving a market with multiple participants illustrates how this calibration can connect the behavior of a trained system to real-world modeling targets.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes equilibria for agents sharing a policy and calibrates their collective behavior by adjusting distributions of agent types.

title: Calibration of Shared Equilibria in General Sum Partially Observable Markov Games

abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, discovering successful collective behaviors is challenging as it requires exploring a joint action space that grows exponentially with the number of agents. While the tractability of independent agent-wise exploration is appealing, this approach fails on tasks that require elaborate group strategies. We argue that coordinating the agents' policies can guide their exploration and we investigate techniques to promote such an inductive bias. We propose two policy regularization methods: TeamReg, which is based on inter-agent action predictability and CoachReg that relies on synchronized behavior selection. We evaluate each approach on four challenging continuous control tasks with sparse rewards that require varying levels of coordination as well as on the discrete action Google Research Football environment. Our experiments show improved performance across many cooperative multi-agent problems. Finally, we analyze the effects of our proposed methods on the policies that our agents learn and show that our methods successfully enforce the qualities that we propose as proxies for coordinated behaviors.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents must discover combinations of actions that work together, but the space of joint actions grows exponentially with the number of agents. Exploring independently is more manageable, yet can fail when success requires elaborate group strategies. This paper studies whether encouraging coordination in the policies themselves can guide exploration toward useful collective behavior.

The authors introduce two policy regularizers. TeamReg encourages predictability of actions between agents, while CoachReg encourages synchronized selection of behaviors. Both use a proposed proxy for coordination to bias learning. The idea is that these policy qualities can make coordinated exploration easier to discover, even when rewards provide limited guidance.

Evaluation covers four continuous-control tasks with sparse rewards and different coordination demands, plus the discrete-action Google Research Football environment. The experiments show performance improvements across many cooperative problems. Further analysis finds that the learned policies exhibit the predictability or synchronization targeted by the methods. This connects the observed gains with the intended behavioral changes, while keeping those changes framed as proxies for coordination.
summary.tldr: TeamReg and CoachReg encourage action predictability and synchronized behavior selection, improving performance across many evaluated cooperative multi-agent tasks.

title: Promoting Coordination through Policy Regularization in Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Accurate quantification of uncertainty is crucial for real-world applications of machine learning. However, modern deep neural networks still produce unreliable predictive uncertainty, often yielding over-confident predictions. In this paper, we are concerned with getting well-calibrated predictions in regression tasks. We propose the calibrated regression method using the maximum mean discrepancy by minimizing the kernel embedding measure. Theoretically, the calibration error of our method asymptotically converges to zero when the sample size is large enough. Experiments on non-trivial real datasets show that our method can produce well-calibrated and sharp prediction intervals, which outperforms the related state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: A regression model can predict a numerical value while also expressing uncertainty about that prediction. The paper addresses the reliability of this uncertainty: deep neural networks can be overconfident, making their reported confidence a poor guide to their actual errors. Its objective is to produce predictions whose uncertainty better matches observed outcomes.

The proposed method uses maximum mean discrepancy, a measure based on representing distributions through a kernel. Calibration is pursued by minimizing this kernel-based discrepancy. This makes the agreement underlying calibrated uncertainty part of the learning objective, rather than evaluating a model solely by the accuracy of its central numerical predictions.

The authors prove that the method's calibration error approaches zero asymptotically as the sample size becomes sufficiently large. This is a large-sample result, rather than a promise of exact calibration on any finite dataset. Experiments on real datasets produce prediction intervals that are both well calibrated and sharp, meaning informative rather than unnecessarily broad. The reported comparisons outperform related state-of-the-art methods.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based discrepancy objective improves regression uncertainty, with asymptotic calibration guarantees and strong empirical prediction intervals.

title: Calibrated Reliable Regression using Maximum Mean Discrepancy

abstract: In this work, we analyze the role of the network architecture in shaping the inductive bias of deep classifiers. To that end, we start by focusing on a very simple problem, i.e., classifying a class of linearly separable distributions, and show that, depending on the direction of the discriminative feature of the distribution, many state-of-the-art deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have a surprisingly hard time solving this simple task. We then define as neural anisotropy directions (NADs) the vectors that encapsulate the directional inductive bias of an architecture. These vectors, which are specific for each architecture and hence act as a signature, encode the preference of a network to separate the input data based on some particular features. We provide an efficient method to identify NADs for several CNN architectures and thus reveal their directional inductive biases. Furthermore, we show that, for the CIFAR-10 dataset, NADs characterize the features used by CNNs to discriminate between different classes.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how a classifier’s architecture influences which features it learns to use. The authors begin with a seemingly simple task: separating distributions that are linearly separable. They find that many advanced convolutional networks struggle depending on the direction of the feature that distinguishes the classes, showing that mathematical separability alone does not make the task equally easy for these networks.

The authors introduce neural anisotropy directions, or NADs, to describe this directional preference. These vectors form an architecture-specific signature that captures which feature directions a network favors when separating inputs. An efficient identification method makes it possible to expose these preferences for several convolutional architectures.

The paper then connects this analysis to CIFAR-10, showing that NADs characterize the features CNNs use to distinguish classes in that dataset. The findings link an architecture’s directional bias to both controlled classification difficulty and feature use on image data. NADs therefore offer a way to describe architectural inductive bias through concrete directions in the input representation.
summary.tldr: Neural anisotropy directions reveal architecture-specific feature preferences that help explain CNN difficulty on simple tasks and feature use on CIFAR-10.

title: Neural Anisotropy Directions

abstract: Recommendation Systems like YouTube are vibrant ecosystems with two types of users: Content consumers (those who watch videos) and content providers (those who create videos). While the computational task of recommending relevant content is largely solved, designing a system that guarantees high social welfare for \textit{all} stakeholders is still in its infancy. In this work, we investigate the dynamics of content creation using a game-theoretic lens. Employing a stylized model that was recently suggested by other works, we show that the dynamics will always converge to a pure Nash Equilibrium (PNE), but the convergence rate can be exponential. We complement the analysis by proposing an efficient PNE computation algorithm via a combinatorial optimization problem that is of independent interest.

paragraphs: A recommendation platform connects people who consume content with people who produce it. Choosing relevant items for consumers is only one part of understanding the resulting system: providers also make strategic choices about what to create. This paper studies those content creation dynamics through game theory, motivated by the broader problem of serving all participants in a recommendation ecosystem.

Within a previously proposed stylized model, the authors prove that the dynamics always reach a pure Nash equilibrium. At such an equilibrium, no provider can benefit by changing its own strategy alone. However, the path to that outcome can take exponentially long. The result therefore separates eventual stability from the practical speed at which decentralized behavior reaches it.

The paper also develops an efficient algorithm for computing a pure Nash equilibrium through a combinatorial optimization problem. This supplies a computational route to an equilibrium even when the modeled dynamics converge slowly. The guarantee concerns equilibrium in the stated model; convergence itself does not establish that every stakeholder receives high social welfare.
summary.tldr: In a stylized recommendation ecosystem, provider dynamics always reach equilibrium but may do so slowly, while an efficient algorithm can compute an equilibrium.

title: Content Provider Dynamics and Coordination in Recommendation Ecosystems

abstract: Panoptic segmentation is posed as a new popular test-bed for the state-of-the-art holistic scene understanding methods with the requirement of simultaneously segmenting both foreground things and background stuff. The state-of-the-art panoptic segmentation network exhibits high structural complexity in different network components, i.e. backbone, proposal-based foreground branch, segmentation-based background branch, and feature fusion module across branches, which heavily relies on expert knowledge and tedious trials. In this work, we propose an efficient, cooperative and highly automated framework to simultaneously search for all main components including backbone, segmentation branches, and feature fusion module in a unified panoptic segmentation pipeline based on the prevailing one-shot Network Architecture Search (NAS) paradigm. Notably, we extend the common single-task NAS into the multi-component scenario by taking the advantages of the newly proposed intra-modular search space and problem-oriented inter-modular search space, which helps us to obtain an optimal network architecture that not only performs well in both instance segmentation and semantic segmentation tasks but also be aware of the reciprocal relations between foreground things and background stuff classes. To relieve the vast computation burden incurred by applying NAS to complicated network architectures, we present a novel path-priority greedy search policy to find a robust, transferrable architecture with significantly reduced searching overhead. Our searched architecture, namely Auto-Panoptic, achieves the new state-of-the-art on the challenging COCO and ADE20K benchmarks. Moreover, extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of path-priority policy and transferability of Auto-Panoptic across different datasets.

paragraphs: Panoptic segmentation combines identifying individual foreground objects with assigning background regions to semantic classes. Networks for this task contain several interacting components, including a backbone, separate foreground and background branches, and a feature fusion module. Designing these components together can require substantial expert effort and repeated trials.

Auto-Panoptic searches for all of these main components within a unified one-shot neural architecture search framework. It introduces search spaces for choices within modules and for relationships across modules. This makes the search sensitive both to the two segmentation tasks and to interactions between foreground objects and background classes.

To reduce the computational burden of searching such a complex system, the authors introduce a path-priority greedy search policy. They report substantially lower search overhead and a robust, transferable architecture. Auto-Panoptic achieves state-of-the-art results on COCO and ADE20K in the reported evaluation, with additional experiments supporting the search policy and transfer across datasets. The contribution links coordinated component design with a practical strategy for controlling search cost.
summary.tldr: Auto-Panoptic jointly searches interacting segmentation components and uses a greedy search policy to reduce overhead while achieving strong benchmark results.

title: Auto-Panoptic: Cooperative Multi-Component Architecture Search for Panoptic Segmentation

abstract: Typically, inversion algorithms assume that a forward model, which relates a source to its resulting measurements, is known and fixed. Using collected indirect measurements and the forward model, the goal becomes to recover the source. When the forward model is unknown, or imperfect, artifacts due to model mismatch occur in the recovery of the source. In this paper, we study the problem of blind inversion: solving an inverse problem with unknown or imperfect knowledge of the forward model parameters. We propose DeepGEM, a variational Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework that can be used to solve for the unknown parameters of the forward model in an unsupervised manner. DeepGEM makes use of a normalizing flow generative network to efficiently capture complex posterior distributions, which leads to more accurate evaluation of the source's posterior distribution used in EM. We showcase the effectiveness of our DeepGEM approach by achieving strong performance on the challenging problem of blind seismic tomography, where we significantly outperform the standard method used in seismology. We also demonstrate the generality of DeepGEM by applying it to a simple case of blind deconvolution.

paragraphs: An inverse problem starts with indirect measurements and seeks the source that produced them. Usually, reconstruction assumes that the forward model connecting source and measurements is already correct. When its parameters are unknown or inaccurate, that mismatch can introduce artifacts into the recovered source. DeepGEM addresses this blind-inversion setting.

The method uses a variational expectation-maximization framework to estimate unknown forward-model parameters without supervision. It incorporates a normalizing flow generative network to represent complex posterior distributions over the source. Capturing these distributions efficiently supports more accurate evaluation of the source uncertainty used within expectation-maximization.

This matters because uncertainty about the source and uncertainty about the measurement model are connected: estimating model parameters depends on how the possible sources are represented. The authors demonstrate strong performance on blind seismic tomography, significantly outperforming the standard seismology method in their evaluation. They also apply DeepGEM to a simple blind-deconvolution case, showing that the framework can be used beyond the seismic example.
summary.tldr: DeepGEM uses flow-based posterior modeling within expectation-maximization to reconstruct sources when the measurement model is imperfect.

title: DeepGEM: Generalized Expectation-Maximization for Blind Inversion

abstract: We study an extension of the stochastic submodular minimization problem, namely, the stochastic $L^\natural$-convex minimization problem. We develop the first polynomial-time algorithms that return a near-optimal solution with high probability. We design a novel truncation operation to further reduce the computational complexity of the proposed algorithms. When applied to a stochastic submodular function, the computational complexity of the proposed algorithms is lower than that of the existing stochastic submodular minimization algorithms. In addition, we provide a strongly polynomial approximate algorithm. The algorithm execution also does not require any prior knowledge about the objective function except the $L^\natural$-convexity. A lower bound on the computational complexity that is required to achieve a high probability error bound is also derived. Numerical experiments are implemented to demonstrate the efficiency of our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic L-natural-convex minimization, a problem that extends stochastic submodular minimization. The objective is to find a solution close to optimal despite randomness. The authors develop the first polynomial-time algorithms for this problem that return a near-optimal solution with high probability, providing both computational and probabilistic guarantees.

A new truncation operation further reduces the algorithms' computational complexity. When applied to stochastic submodular functions, the resulting complexity is lower than that of existing algorithms for that setting. The paper also provides a strongly polynomial approximation algorithm. Execution requires no prior knowledge of the objective beyond its L-natural-convex structure, making that structural assumption central to the methods.

Alongside the algorithms, the authors derive a lower bound on the computation needed to achieve a high-probability error guarantee. This supplies a benchmark for understanding the inherent difficulty of reliable approximate optimization. Numerical experiments illustrate the efficiency predicted by the theory. The contribution therefore combines broader problem coverage, reduced computational requirements, and an analysis of what obtaining reliable solutions necessarily costs.
summary.tldr: New algorithms efficiently approximate stochastic L-natural-convex minima with high-probability guarantees and improve complexity for stochastic submodular minimization.

title: Stochastic $L^\natural$-convex Function Minimization

abstract: We propose the particle dual averaging (PDA) method, which generalizes the dual averaging method in convex optimization to the optimization over probability distributions with quantitative runtime guarantee. The algorithm consists of an inner loop and outer loop: the inner loop utilizes the Langevin algorithm to approximately solve for a stationary distribution, which is then optimized in the outer loop. The method can be interpreted as an extension of the Langevin algorithm to naturally handle nonlinear functional on the probability space. An important application of the proposed method is the optimization of neural network in the mean field regime, which is theoretically attractive due to the presence of nonlinear feature learning, but quantitative convergence rate can be challenging to obtain. By adapting finite-dimensional convex optimization theory into the space of measures, we not only establish global convergence of PDA for two-layer mean field neural networks under more general settings and simpler analysis, but also provide quantitative polynomial runtime guarantee. Our theoretical results are supported by numerical simulations on neural networks with reasonable size.

paragraphs: Particle Dual Averaging extends an optimization method from ordinary convex problems to problems whose variable is a probability distribution. This matters for mean-field neural networks, where the distribution-based perspective accommodates nonlinear feature learning but makes quantitative convergence analysis challenging. The paper develops both an algorithm and guarantees on how long it takes.

The algorithm has nested loops. An inner loop uses Langevin dynamics to approximately obtain a stationary distribution, while the outer loop optimizes that distribution. The authors interpret this construction as extending the Langevin algorithm to objectives that are nonlinear functions of probability distributions.

By adapting finite-dimensional convex optimization theory to the space of measures, the authors prove global convergence for two-layer mean-field neural networks under the settings they analyze. They also provide a polynomial runtime guarantee, strengthening the result beyond an eventual-convergence statement. Numerical simulations on reasonably sized networks support the theory. The contribution connects a distribution-based training viewpoint with quantitative guarantees despite the presence of nonlinear feature learning.
summary.tldr: Particle Dual Averaging optimizes probability distributions and provides global convergence with polynomial runtime guarantees for two-layer mean-field neural networks.

title: Particle Dual Averaging: Optimization of Mean Field Neural Network with Global Convergence Rate Analysis

abstract: Large scale training requires massive parallelism to finish the training within a reasonable amount of time. To support massive parallelism, large batch training is the key enabler but often at the cost of generalization performance. Existing works explore adaptive batching or hand-tuned static large batching, in order to strike a balance between the computational efficiency and the performance. However, these methods can provide only coarse-grained adaption (e.g., at a epoch level) due to the intrinsic expensive calculation or hand tuning requirements. In this paper, we propose a fully automated and lightweight adaptive batching methodology to enable fine-grained batch size adaption (e.g., at a mini-batch level) that can achieve state-of-the-art performance with record breaking batch sizes. The core component of our method is a lightweight yet efficient representation of the critical gradient noise information. We open-source the proposed methodology by providing a plugin tool that supports mainstream machine learning frameworks. Extensive evaluations on popular benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR10, ImageNet, and BERT-Large) demonstrate that the proposed methodology outperforms state-of-the-art methodologies using adaptive batching approaches or hand-tuned static strategies in both performance and batch size. Particularly, we achieve a new state-of-the-art batch size of 78k in BERT-Large pretraining with SQuAD score 90.69 compared to 90.58 reported in previous state-of-the-art with 59k batch size.

paragraphs: Large training batches support extensive parallel computation, but they can come at a cost to generalization. Existing adaptive approaches may change batch size only at coarse intervals because their calculations are expensive or require manual tuning. SimiGrad proposes an automated, lightweight way to adjust batch size at finer intervals, potentially every mini-batch.

Its central component is an efficient representation of important gradient-noise information, with gradient similarity providing the method's organizing idea. The goal is to make frequent adaptation affordable enough for large-scale training. The authors also provide the methodology as a plugin supporting mainstream machine-learning frameworks, connecting the proposed batching strategy to practical training workflows.

Evaluations on CIFAR10, ImageNet, and BERT-Large report improvements over adaptive and manually tuned static batching approaches in both performance and supported batch size. For BERT-Large pretraining, the method uses a batch size of 78,000 with a SQuAD score of 90.69, compared with the cited previous result of 90.58 at 59,000. These findings support finer-grained adaptation in the tested workloads.
summary.tldr: SimiGrad uses lightweight gradient information to adapt batch sizes frequently, enabling larger batches with strong reported model performance.

title: SimiGrad: Fine-Grained Adaptive Batching for Large Scale Training using Gradient Similarity Measurement

abstract: The perceptual task of speech quality assessment (SQA) is a challenging task for machines to do. Objective SQA methods that rely on the availability of the corresponding clean reference have been the primary go-to approaches for SQA. Clearly, these methods fail in real-world scenarios where the ground truth clean references are not available. In recent years, non-intrusive methods that train neural networks to predict ratings or scores have attracted much attention, but they suffer from several shortcomings such as lack of robustness, reliance on labeled data for training and so on. In this work, we propose a new direction for speech quality assessment. Inspired by human's innate ability to compare and assess the quality of speech signals even when they have non-matching contents, we propose a novel framework that predicts a subjective relative quality score for the given speech signal with respect to any provided reference without using any subjective data. We show that neural networks trained using our framework produce scores that correlate well with subjective mean opinion scores (MOS) and are also competitive to methods such as DNSMOS, which explicitly relies on MOS from humans for training networks. Moreover, our method also provides a natural way to embed quality-related information in neural networks, which we show is helpful for downstream tasks such as speech enhancement.

paragraphs: Assessing speech quality is easier when a clean recording of the same utterance is available for comparison. In many real situations, that matching reference does not exist. Neural methods that predict quality scores directly offer another route, but the paper highlights problems including reliance on labeled ratings and insufficient robustness.

NORESQA instead compares the quality of a speech signal with a provided reference whose spoken content need not match. It is inspired by people’s ability to compare recordings even when they contain different speech. The framework predicts relative subjective quality without using subjective human ratings in training, allowing reference-based comparison without requiring the corresponding clean utterance.

Networks trained this way produce scores that correlate well with human mean opinion scores. The authors also report competitive results against methods such as DNSMOS, which uses human opinion scores for training. Beyond assessment, the learned networks embed quality-related information that helps speech enhancement. The findings support relative comparison as a useful training approach for both judging speech quality and learning representations useful for improving it.
summary.tldr: NORESQA learns to assess speech quality using references with different content, without subjective ratings for training.

title: NORESQA: A Framework for Speech Quality Assessment using Non-Matching References

abstract: A ubiquitous learning problem in today’s digital market is, during repeated interactions between a seller and a buyer, how a seller can gradually learn optimal pricing decisions based on the buyer’s past purchase responses. A fundamental challenge of learning in such a strategic setup is that the buyer will naturally have incentives to manipulate his responses in order to induce more favorable learning outcomes for him. To understand the limits of the seller’s learning when facing such a strategic and possibly manipulative buyer, we study a natural yet powerful buyer manipulation strategy. That is, before the pricing game starts, the buyer simply commits to “imitate” a different value function by pretending to always react optimally according to this imitative value function. We fully characterize the optimal imitative value function that the buyer should imitate as well as the resultant seller revenue and buyer surplus under this optimal buyer manipulation. Our characterizations reveal many useful insights about what happens at equilibrium. For example, a seller with concave production cost will obtain essentially 0 revenue at equilibrium whereas the revenue for a seller with convex production cost is the Bregman divergence of her cost function between no production and certain production. Finally, and importantly, we show that a more powerful class of pricing schemes does not necessarily increase, in fact, may be harmful to, the seller’s revenue. Our results not only lead to an effective prescriptive way for buyers to manipulate learning algorithms but also shed lights on the limits of what a seller can really achieve when pricing in the dark.

paragraphs: A seller learning prices from purchase responses faces a strategic problem: the buyer can shape those responses to influence future prices. This paper analyzes a manipulation strategy in which the buyer commits, before interaction begins, to act as though they had a different value function.

The authors fully characterize the best value function for the buyer to imitate within this strategy, together with the resulting seller revenue and buyer surplus. This makes the consequences of manipulation explicit. The buyer's observed responses reflect a chosen imitation, so the seller's learning process operates on strategically shaped evidence.

The equilibrium characterizations depend strongly on production costs. With concave production costs, seller revenue is essentially zero. With convex costs, it is expressed through the Bregman divergence of the cost function between no production and a specified production level. The paper also shows that a more powerful class of pricing schemes need not improve revenue and can harm it. These results identify limits to the seller's gains from pricing flexibility under the studied manipulation.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes strategic buyer imitation and shows that greater pricing flexibility can sometimes reduce seller revenue.

title: The Limits of Optimal Pricing in the Dark

abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are neural networks trained by using physical laws in the form of partial differential equations (PDEs) as soft constraints. We present a new technique for the accelerated training of PINNs that combines modern scientific computing techniques with machine learning: discretely-trained PINNs (DT-PINNs). The repeated computation of the partial derivative terms in the PINN loss functions via automatic differentiation during training is known to be computationally expensive, especially for higher-order derivatives. DT-PINNs are trained by replacing these exact spatial derivatives with high-order accurate numerical discretizations computed using meshless radial basis function-finite differences (RBF-FD) and applied via sparse-matrix vector multiplication. While in principle any high-order discretization may be used, the use of RBF-FD allows for DT-PINNs to be trained even on point cloud samples placed on irregular domain geometries. Additionally, though traditional PINNs (vanilla-PINNs) are typically stored and trained in 32-bit floating-point (fp32) on the GPU, we show that for DT-PINNs, using fp64 on the GPU leads to significantly faster training times than fp32 vanilla-PINNs with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of DT-PINNs via a series of experiments. First, we explore the effect of network depth on both numerical and automatic differentiation of a neural network with random weights and show that RBF-FD approximations of third-order accuracy and above are more efficient while being sufficiently accurate. We then compare the DT-PINNs to vanilla-PINNs on both linear and nonlinear Poisson equations and show that DT-PINNs achieve similar losses with 2-4x faster training times on a consumer GPU. Finally, we also demonstrate that similar results can be obtained for the PINN solution to the heat equation (a space-time problem) by discretizing the spatial derivatives using RBF-FD and using automatic differentiation for the temporal derivative. Our results show that fp64 DT-PINNs offer a superior cost-accuracy profile to fp32 vanilla-PINNs, opening the door to a new paradigm of leveraging scientific computing techniques to support machine learning.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions while being penalized for violating physical equations. Computing the spatial derivatives in these penalties through automatic differentiation can be expensive, especially for higher derivatives. This paper introduces discretely trained PINNs, which replace those spatial derivative calculations with accurate numerical approximations.

The method uses radial basis function finite differences to construct derivative approximations that can be applied through sparse matrix-vector multiplication. Because this technique is meshless, it also supports point samples on irregular geometries. The authors examine differentiation in networks with random weights and find that approximations of third-order accuracy or higher offer sufficient accuracy with greater efficiency in their experiments.

On linear and nonlinear Poisson equations, the proposed networks reach similar losses with training times reduced by a factor of two to four on a consumer GPU. These comparisons use 64-bit arithmetic for the proposed method and 32-bit arithmetic for conventional PINNs. Heat-equation experiments also support combining numerical spatial derivatives with automatic temporal differentiation. The findings show how scientific computing techniques can improve the measured balance between training cost and accuracy.
summary.tldr: Replacing automatic spatial differentiation with meshless numerical approximations accelerates PINN training while preserving comparable accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Accelerated Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) using Meshless Discretizations

abstract: We propose a sparse end-to-end multi-person pose regression framework, termed QueryPose, which can directly predict multi-person keypoint sequences from the input image. The existing end-to-end methods rely on dense representations to preserve the spatial detail and structure for precise keypoint localization. However, the dense paradigm introduces complex and redundant post-processes during inference. In our framework, each human instance is encoded by several learnable spatial-aware part-level queries associated with an instance-level query. First, we propose the Spatial Part Embedding Generation Module (SPEGM) that considers the local spatial attention mechanism to generate several spatial-sensitive part embeddings, which contain spatial details and structural information for enhancing the part-level queries. Second, we introduce the Selective Iteration Module (SIM) to adaptively update the sparse part-level queries via the generated spatial-sensitive part embeddings stage-by-stage. Based on the two proposed modules, the part-level queries are able to fully encode the spatial details and structural information for precise keypoint regression. With the bipartite matching, QueryPose avoids the hand-designed post-processes. Without bells and whistles, QueryPose surpasses the existing dense end-to-end methods with 73.6 AP on MS COCO mini-val set and 72.7 AP on CrowdPose test set. Code is available at https://github.com/buptxyb666/QueryPose.
originalAbstract: We propose a sparse end-to-end multi-person pose regression framework, termed QueryPose, which can directly predict multi-person keypoint sequences from the input image. However, the dense paradigm introduces complex and redundant post-processes during inference. In our framework, each human instance is encoded by several learnable spatial-aware part-level queries associated with an instance-level query. First, we propose the Spatial Part Embedding Generation Module (SPEGM) that considers the local spatial attention mechanism to generate several spatial-sensitive part embeddings, which contain spatial details and structural information for enhancing the part-level queries. Second, we introduce the Selective Iteration Module (SIM) to adaptively update the sparse part-level queries via the generated spatial-sensitive part embeddings stage-by-stage. Based on the two proposed modules, the part-level queries are able to fully encode the spatial details and structural information for precise keypoint regression. With the bipartite matching, QueryPose avoids the hand-designed post-processes. Without bells and whistles, QueryPose surpasses the existing dense end-to-end methods with 73.6 AP on MS COCO mini-val set and 72.7 AP on CrowdPose test set. paragraphs: Estimating the poses of several people requires locating keypoints while preserving each person's spatial structure. Existing end-to-end methods use dense representations for this detail, but can introduce redundant and complex inference post-processing. QueryPose proposes a sparse framework that predicts multiple people's keypoint sequences directly from an image.

Each person is represented by an instance-level query associated with several learnable queries for body parts. A Spatial Part Embedding Generation Module uses local spatial attention to produce embeddings containing spatial and structural information. A Selective Iteration Module then updates the part queries adaptively, stage by stage. Together, these modules give the sparse queries information needed for precise keypoint prediction.

The reported results reach 73.6 AP on MS COCO mini-val and 72.7 AP on the CrowdPose test set, surpassing the compared dense end-to-end methods. title: QueryPose: Sparse Multi-Person Pose Regression via Spatial-Aware Part-Level Query

abstract: Traditional causal inference techniques assume data are independent and identically distributed (IID) and thus ignores interactions among units. However, a unit’s treatment may affect another unit's outcome (interference), a unit’s treatment may be correlated with another unit’s outcome, or a unit’s treatment and outcome may be spuriously correlated through another unit. To capture such nuances, we model the data generating process using causal graphs and conduct a systematic analysis of the bias caused by different types of interactions when computing causal effects. We derive theorems to detect and quantify the interaction bias, and derive conditions under which it is safe to ignore interactions. Put differently, we present conditions under which causal effects can be computed with negligible bias by assuming that samples are IID. Furthermore, we develop a method to eliminate bias in cases where blindly assuming IID is expected to yield a significantly biased estimate. Finally, we test the coverage and performance of our methods through simulations.

paragraphs: Causal analysis often treats observations as independent samples from the same distribution. That assumption can overlook relationships between units: one unit's treatment may affect another's outcome, or connections through other units may create misleading treatment-outcome associations. The paper studies how these interactions distort estimates of causal effects using linear graphical models.

The authors represent the data-generating process with causal graphs and systematically distinguish different sources of interaction bias. They derive theorems for detecting and quantifying that bias, along with conditions under which interactions can safely be ignored. Here, safely means that treating the samples as independent and identically distributed produces negligible bias, rather than requiring that interactions literally be absent.

For cases where ignoring interactions is expected to cause substantial bias, the paper develops a method to eliminate it. Simulations assess the methods' coverage and performance. The resulting framework addresses two related decisions: whether a simpler independent-sample analysis is adequate, and how to correct the analysis when connections between units materially affect the estimated causal relationship.
summary.tldr: Linear causal graphs identify when interactions between units bias causal estimates and when those interactions can safely be ignored.

title: Causal Inference with Non-IID Data using Linear Graphical Models

abstract: Binaural audio plays a significant role in constructing immersive augmented and virtual realities. As it is expensive to record binaural audio from the real world, synthesizing them from mono audio has attracted increasing attention. This synthesis process involves not only the basic physical warping of the mono audio, but also room reverberations and head/ear related filtration, which, however, are difficult to accurately simulate in traditional digital signal processing. In this paper, we formulate the synthesis process from a different perspective by decomposing the binaural audio into a common part that shared by the left and right channels as well as a specific part that differs in each channel. Accordingly, we propose BinauralGrad, a novel two-stage framework equipped with diffusion models to synthesize them respectively. Specifically, in the first stage, the common information of the binaural audio is generated with a single-channel diffusion model conditioned on the mono audio, based on which the binaural audio is generated by a two-channel diffusion model in the second stage. Combining this novel perspective of two-stage synthesis with advanced generative models (i.e., the diffusion models), the proposed BinauralGrad is able to generate accurate and high-fidelity binaural audio samples. Experiment results show that on a benchmark dataset, BinauralGrad outperforms the existing baselines by a large margin in terms of both object and subject evaluation metrics (Wave L2: $0.128$ vs. $0.157$, MOS: $3.80$ vs. $3.61$). The generated audio samples\footnote{\url{https://speechresearch.github.io/binauralgrad}} and code\footnote{\url{https://github.com/microsoft/NeuralSpeech/tree/master/BinauralGrad}} are available online.

This requires capturing more than the basic physical transformation of a sound signal: room reverberation and filtering associated with the head and ears also matter. The paper approaches these effects through learned generation, motivated by the expense of recording binaural sound and the difficulty of accurately simulating it with traditional signal processing.

The method separates information shared by both ears from information specific to each channel. A first diffusion model takes the mono recording and generates a single-channel representation of the shared information. summary.tldr: BinauralGrad uses two diffusion stages to generate shared and channel-specific audio information, improving binaural synthesis on a benchmark.

title: BinauralGrad: A Two-Stage Conditional Diffusion Probabilistic Model for Binaural Audio Synthesis

abstract: We advance both the theory and practice of robust $\ell_p$-quasinorm regression for $p \in (0,1]$ by using novel variants of iteratively reweighted least-squares (IRLS) to solve the underlying non-smooth problem. In the convex case, $p=1$, we prove that this IRLS variant converges globally at a linear rate under a mild, deterministic condition on the feature matrix called the stable range space property. In the non-convex case, $p\in(0,1)$, we prove that under a similar condition, IRLS converges locally to the global minimizer at a superlinear rate of order $2-p$; the rate becomes quadratic as $p\to 0$. We showcase the proposed methods in three applications: real phase retrieval, regression without correspondences, and robust face restoration. The results show that (1) IRLS can handle a larger number of outliers than other methods, (2) it is faster than competing methods at the same level of accuracy, (3) it restores a sparsely corrupted face image with satisfactory visual quality.

In the non-convex case, $p\in(0,1)$, we prove that under a similar condition, IRLS converges locally to the global minimizer at a superlinear rate of order $2-p$; the rate becomes quadratic as $p\to 0$. paragraphs: Robust regression seeks useful fits even when some observations are outliers. This paper develops variants of iteratively reweighted least squares, or IRLS, for nonsmooth regression objectives based on ℓp measures with p between zero and one. IRLS approaches the difficult objective through repeated weighted least-squares problems, updating how strongly observations influence the fit.

For the convex case p = 1, the authors prove global linear convergence under a deterministic feature-matrix condition called the stable range space property. For nonconvex values between zero and one, a similar condition gives local convergence to the global minimizer at superlinear order 2 − p. The rate approaches quadratic as p approaches zero, but this guarantee is local.

Applications include real phase retrieval, regression without correspondences, and robust face restoration. The reported results show greater tolerance of outliers than other methods, faster execution at equal accuracy, and satisfactory restoration of a sparsely corrupted face image. The paper thus combines explicit convergence conditions with practical evidence for solving robust regression problems efficiently.
summary.tldr: New IRLS variants provide conditional global linear or local superlinear convergence guarantees and strong empirical results for robust regression.

title: Global Linear and Local Superlinear Convergence of IRLS for Non-Smooth Robust Regression

abstract: Spiking Neural networks (SNNs) represent and transmit information by spatiotemporal spike patterns, which bring two major advantages: biological plausibility and suitability for ultralow-power neuromorphic implementation. Despite this, the binary firing characteristic makes training SNNs more challenging. To learn the parameters of deep SNNs in an event-driven fashion as in inference of SNNs, backpropagation with respect to spike timing is proposed. Although this event-driven learning has the advantages of lower computational cost and memory occupation, the accuracy is far below the recurrent neural network-like learning approaches. In this paper, we first analyze the commonly used temporal backpropagation training approach and prove that the sum of gradients remains unchanged between fully-connected and convolutional layers. Secondly, we show that the max pooling layer meets the above invariance rule, while the average pooling layer does not, which will suffer the gradient vanishing problem but can be revised to meet the requirement. Thirdly, we point out the reverse gradient problem for time-based gradients and propose a backward kernel that can solve this problem and keep the property of the invariable sum of gradients. The experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR10 among time-based training methods. Also, this is the first time that the time-based backpropagation approach successfully trains SNN on the CIFAR100 dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhuyaoyu/SNN-event-driven-learning.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through discrete spikes over time, making them attractive for biological modeling and low-power neuromorphic computing. Their binary firing behavior also complicates training. Learning through spike timing can operate in an event-driven fashion with lower computation and memory use, but prior timing-based methods have lagged behind recurrent-network-like training in accuracy.

The paper analyzes temporal backpropagation and proves a conservation property: the sum of gradients remains unchanged between fully connected and convolutional layers. Max pooling respects this property, while average pooling does not and can suffer vanishing gradients. The authors show that average pooling can be revised to meet the requirement.

They also identify a reverse-gradient problem in timing-based learning and propose a backward kernel that resolves it while preserving the gradient-sum property. Experiments achieve state-of-the-art CIFAR10 results among time-based training methods. The authors additionally report the first successful training of an SNN on CIFAR100 using time-based backpropagation. These results connect analysis of gradient behavior to improved capability within event-driven training.
summary.tldr: Analyzing and correcting timing-gradient behavior improves event-driven spiking-network training, including leading reported CIFAR10 performance among time-based methods.

title: Training Spiking Neural Networks with Event-driven Backpropagation

abstract: We demonstrate for the first time that ill-conditioned, non-smooth, constrained distributions in very high dimension, upwards of 100,000, can be sampled efficiently \emph{in practice}. Our algorithm incorporates constraints into the Riemannian version of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and maintains sparsity. This allows us to achieve a mixing rate independent of smoothness and condition numbers. On benchmark data sets in systems biology and linear programming, our algorithm outperforms existing packages by orders of magnitude. In particular, we achieve a 1,000-fold speed-up for sampling from the largest published human metabolic network (RECON3D). Our package has been incorporated into a popular Bioinformatics library.
