paragraphs: Bayesian optimization is valued for making effective use of limited evaluations, but its focus on global optimization makes higher-dimensional problems difficult. This paper adapts that sample-efficient approach to a local search. It restricts optimization of the acquisition function, which guides the next evaluations, to the neighborhood of a Gaussian search distribution.

The search distribution moves toward regions with high objective values. Its update uses an information-theoretic approach with a Bayesian interpretation: the distribution expresses prior knowledge about where the optimum lies, and each iteration weights that knowledge by the likelihood that a location is optimal. This connects local stochastic search to probabilistic reasoning about promising locations.

The authors demonstrate the algorithm on benchmark objective functions and a continuous robotic task. In the robotic example, imitation learning supplies an informative prior. The approach therefore offers a way to use prior knowledge and sample-efficient evaluation within a moving local search region, with empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness on the tested optimization and motor-skill problems.
summary.tldr: Local Bayesian optimization searches near an adaptively updated Gaussian distribution to bring sample-efficient optimization to higher-dimensional motor-skill problems.

title: Local Bayesian Optimization of Motor Skills

abstract: We study the set of all decompositions (clusterings) of a graph through its characterization as a set of lifted multicuts. This leads us to practically relevant insights related to the definition of classes of decompositions by must-join and must-cut constraints and related to the comparison of clusterings by metrics. To find optimal decompositions defined by minimum cost lifted multicuts, we establish some properties of some facets of lifted multicut polytopes, define efficient separation procedures and apply these in a branch-and-cut algorithm.
originalAbstract: We study the set of all decompositions (clusterings) of a graph through its characterization as a set of lifted multicuts. This leads us to practically relevant insights related to the definition of classes of decompositions by must-join and must-cut constraints and related to the comparison of clusterings by metrics. To find optimal decompositions defined by minimum cost lifted multicuts, we establish some properties of some facets of lifted multicut polytopes, define efficient separation procedures and apply these in a branch-and-cut algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to divide a graph into clusters using a mathematical representation called lifted multicuts. Its starting point is a characterization of the entire collection of graph decompositions. This gives a common language for reasoning about which clusterings are possible and for searching for a clustering with the lowest specified cost.

One use of this characterization is to understand constraints that require particular elements to belong together or remain separate. These must-join and must-cut requirements define classes of acceptable decompositions. The same perspective also yields insights into metrics for comparing clusterings, connecting the description of individual solutions with ways to measure differences between them.

For optimization, the authors investigate facets of lifted multicut polytopes, geometric structures that represent the problem's feasible choices. They develop efficient separation procedures and incorporate them into a branch-and-cut algorithm for finding minimum-cost lifted multicuts. The contribution therefore combines structural analysis with an optimization method: it explains aspects of the space of graph clusterings and uses that understanding to help search it.
summary.tldr: Lifted multicuts provide a framework for analyzing constrained graph clusterings and optimizing them with a branch-and-cut algorithm.

title: Analysis and Optimization of Graph Decompositions by Lifted Multicuts

abstract: Many tasks in machine learning and data mining, such as data diversification, non-parametric learning, kernel machines, clustering etc., require extracting a small but representative summary from a massive dataset. Often, such problems can be posed as maximizing a submodular set function subject to a cardinality constraint. We consider this question in the streaming setting, where elements arrive over time at a fast pace and thus we need to design an efficient, low-memory algorithm. One such method, proposed by Badanidiyuru et al. (2014), always finds a 0.5-approximate solution. Can this approximation factor be improved? We answer this question affirmatively by designing a new algorithm Salsa for streaming submodular maximization. It is the first low-memory, singlepass algorithm that improves the factor 0.5, under the natural assumption that elements arrive in a random order. We also show that this assumption is necessary, i.e., that there is no such algorithm with better than 0.5-approximation when elements arrive in arbitrary order. Our experiments demonstrate that Salsa significantly outperforms the state of the art in applications related to exemplar-based clustering, social graph analysis, and recommender systems.

paragraphs: Choosing a small representative subset from a massive dataset appears in tasks such as clustering and recommendation. The paper studies a formulation that maximizes a submodular set function while limiting how many items may be selected. In a stream, items arrive rapidly, so a useful algorithm must make progress with little memory and limited access to past data.

The authors introduce Salsa, a low-memory algorithm that processes the stream in a single pass. Under the assumption that items arrive in random order, it improves on an approximation factor of one-half. That factor describes the guaranteed quality of the selected set relative to the best achievable selection, so exceeding it strengthens the theoretical guarantee.

The arrival-order assumption is central: the paper also proves that no algorithm of this kind can beat one-half for arbitrary ordering. Experiments report substantial improvements over existing methods in exemplar-based clustering, social graph analysis, and recommender systems. The contribution therefore pairs an improved algorithm with a result explaining when the improvement is possible.
summary.tldr: Salsa exceeds the one-half approximation guarantee for low-memory, single-pass submodular selection when stream items arrive in random order.

title: Beyond 1/2-Approximation for Submodular Maximization on Massive Data Streams

abstract: Why are classifiers in high dimension vulnerable to “adversarial” perturbations? We show that it is likely not due to information theoretic limitations, but rather it could be due to computational constraints. First we prove that, for a broad set of classification tasks, the mere existence of a robust classifier implies that it can be found by a possibly exponential-time algorithm with relatively few training examples. Then we give two particular classification tasks where learning a robust classifier is computationally intractable. More precisely we construct two binary classifications task in high dimensional space which are (i) information theoretically easy to learn robustly for large perturbations, (ii) efficiently learnable (non-robustly) by a simple linear separator, (iii) yet are not efficiently robustly learnable, even for small perturbations. Specifically, for the first task hardness holds for any efficient algorithm in the statistical query (SQ) model, while for the second task we rule out any efficient algorithm under a cryptographic assumption. These examples give an exponential separation between classical learning and robust learning in the statistical query model or under a cryptographic assumption. It suggests that adversarial examples may be an unavoidable byproduct of computational limitations of learning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether adversarial vulnerability comes from insufficient information or from the computational difficulty of learning robust classifiers. It first proves that, for a broad class of tasks, the existence of a robust classifier implies that relatively few training examples suffice to find one. The catch is that the search algorithm may require exponential time.

The authors then construct two high-dimensional binary classification tasks that separate ordinary learning from robust learning. Both permit efficient ordinary classification with a simple linear separator. Both also admit robust learning with sufficiently powerful computation, even for large perturbations. Yet efficient robust learning is ruled out even for small perturbations within the respective hardness settings.

For one construction, the barrier applies to efficient algorithms in the statistical query model. For the other, it depends on a cryptographic assumption. These results establish exponential separations under those conditions. They support computational constraints as a possible explanation for adversarial examples, rather than proving that computation explains every observed vulnerability or that robustness is universally impossible.
summary.tldr: Constructed classification tasks show that robust learning can require far more computation than ordinary learning despite needing relatively little data.

title: Adversarial examples from computational constraints

abstract: We present a provably optimal differentially private algorithm for the stochastic multi-arm bandit problem, as opposed to the private analogue of the UCB-algorithm (Mishra and Thakurta, 2015; Tossou and Dimitrakakis, 2016) which doesn’t meet the recently discovered lower-bound of $\Omega \left(\frac{K\log(T)}{\epsilon} \right)$ (Shariff and Sheffet, 2018). Our construction is based on a different algorithm, Successive Elimination (Even-Dar et al., 2002), that repeatedly pulls all remaining arms until an arm is found to be suboptimal and is then eliminated. In order to devise a private analogue of Successive Elimination we visit the problem of private stopping rule , that takes as input a stream of i.i.d samples from an unknown distribution and returns a multiplicative $(1 \pm \alpha)$-approximation of the distribution’s mean, and prove the optimality of our private stopping rule. We then present the private Successive Elimination algorithm which meets both the non-private lower bound (Lai and Robbins, 1985) and the above-mentioned private lower bound. We also compare empirically the performance of our algorithm with the private UCB algorithm.

paragraphs: The stochastic multi-arm bandit problem requires learning which choices give better rewards while deciding which choices to sample. This paper develops a differentially private algorithm with provable optimality. Its motivation is that the private UCB approach discussed in the abstract does not match an established lower bound on the cost of private learning.

The construction instead starts from Successive Elimination. This method repeatedly samples the remaining arms and removes an arm once it is identified as suboptimal. To make that process private, the authors develop a private stopping rule for a stream of independent, identically distributed samples. The rule returns a multiplicative approximation to the unknown distribution's mean, and its optimality is proved.

Using that component, the private Successive Elimination algorithm meets both the non-private lower bound and the privacy-related lower bound, whose stated dependence is K log(T) divided by epsilon. This connects a private mean-estimation primitive to an optimal bandit procedure. The paper also empirically compares its algorithm with private UCB, without specifying the comparison's outcome in the abstract.
summary.tldr: An optimal private stopping rule enables a differentially private Successive Elimination bandit algorithm that meets private and non-private lower bounds.

title: An Optimal Private Stochastic-MAB Algorithm based on Optimal Private Stopping Rule

abstract: Options have been shown to be an effective tool in reinforcement learning, facilitating improved exploration and learning. In this paper, we present an approach based on spectral graph theory and derive an algorithm that systematically discovers options without access to a specific reward or task assignment. As opposed to the common practice used in previous methods, our algorithm makes full use of the spectrum of the graph Laplacian. Incorporating modes associated with higher graph frequencies unravels domain subtleties, which are shown to be useful for option discovery. Using geometric and manifold-based analysis, we present a theoretical justification for the algorithm. In addition, we showcase its performance in several domains, demonstrating clear improvements compared to competing methods.

paragraphs: Options provide reinforcement learning agents with behaviors that can help exploration and learning. This paper asks how to discover them before a particular reward function or task has been supplied. The approach uses the structure of the domain itself, allowing option discovery to proceed without knowing which outcomes a later task will reward.

The algorithm is derived from spectral graph theory and uses the full spectrum of the graph Laplacian. Its distinguishing choice is to include modes associated with higher graph frequencies, rather than following the more restricted spectral practice described for previous methods. These higher-frequency modes reveal subtleties of the domain that the paper shows can be useful when constructing options.

Geometric and manifold-based analysis provides a theoretical justification for the algorithm. Evaluations in several domains demonstrate clear improvements over competing methods. The combined message is that reward-free option discovery can benefit from a richer account of graph structure: details represented by higher frequencies can contribute useful information alongside the rest of the spectrum.
summary.tldr: Using the full graph Laplacian spectrum enables reward-free option discovery that captures useful domain details and improves on evaluated alternatives.

title: Option Discovery in the Absence of Rewards with Manifold Analysis

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm for online linear-quadratic control in a known system subject to adversarial disturbances. Existing regret bounds for this setting scale as $\sqrt{T}$ unless strong stochastic assumptions are imposed on the disturbance process. We give the first algorithm with logarithmic regret for arbitrary adversarial disturbance sequences, provided the state and control costs are given by known quadratic functions. Our algorithm and analysis use a characterization for the optimal offline control law to reduce the online control problem to (delayed) online learning with approximate advantage functions. Compared to previous techniques, our approach does not need to control movement costs for the iterates, leading to logarithmic regret.

Our algorithm and analysis use a characterization for the optimal offline control law to reduce the online control problem to (delayed) online learning with approximate advantage functions. paragraphs: Online control requires choosing actions while disturbances arrive over time. This paper studies linear-quadratic control with known system dynamics and disturbances that may be chosen adversarially. The objective is to keep regret small: the accumulated cost disadvantage associated with making decisions online. Earlier bounds in this setting grew with the square root of the time horizon unless strong stochastic disturbance assumptions were imposed.

The authors give an algorithm with logarithmic regret for arbitrary adversarial disturbance sequences, provided the state and control costs are known quadratic functions. This changes how the bound grows with the duration of the problem. The improvement retains adversarial disturbances while relying on the stated knowledge and quadratic structure of the control problem.

The method characterizes the optimal offline control law and uses it to reduce control to delayed online learning with approximate advantage functions. Unlike earlier techniques, the analysis does not need to control movement costs between successive iterates. Avoiding that requirement is the key analytical change that enables the logarithmic regret guarantee.
summary.tldr: A reduction to delayed online learning achieves logarithmic regret for known linear-quadratic systems under arbitrary adversarial disturbances.

title: Logarithmic Regret for Adversarial Online Control

abstract: This work considers the canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) of tensors using proximally regularized sketched alternating least squares algorithms. First, it establishes a sublinear rate of convergence for proximally regularized sketched CPD algorithms under two natural conditions that are known to be satisfied by many popular forms of sketching. Second, it demonstrates that the iterative nature of CPD algorithms can be exploited algorithmically to choose more performant sketching rates. This is accomplished by introducing CPD-MWU, a proximally-regularized sketched alternating least squares algorithm that adaptively selects the sketching rate at each iteration. On both synthetic and real data we observe that for noisy tensors CPD-MWU produces decompositions of comparable accuracy to the standard CPD decomposition in less time, often half the time; for ill-conditioned tensors, given the same time budget, CPD-MWU produces decompositions with an order-of-magnitude lower relative error. For a representative real-world dataset CPD-MWU produces residual errors on average 20% lower than CPRAND-MIX and 44% lower than SPALS, two recent sketched CPD algorithms.

paragraphs: Canonical polyadic decomposition represents a tensor through simpler components. This paper studies such algorithms with proximal regularization and asks how much sketching should be used as the decomposition progresses.

title: Adaptive Sketching for Fast and Convergent Canonical Polyadic Decomposition

abstract: Modern generative models are usually designed to match target distributions directly in the data space, where the intrinsic dimension of data can be much lower than the ambient dimension. We argue that this discrepancy may contribute to the difficulties in training generative models. We therefore propose to map both the generated and target distributions to the latent space using the encoder of a standard autoencoder, and train the generator (or decoder) to match the target distribution in the latent space. Specifically, we enforce the consistency in both the data space and the latent space with theoretically justified data and latent reconstruction losses. The resulting generative model, which we call a perceptual generative autoencoder (PGA), is then trained with a maximum likelihood or variational autoencoder (VAE) objective. With maximum likelihood, PGAs generalize the idea of reversible generative models to unrestricted neural network architectures and arbitrary number of latent dimensions. When combined with VAEs, PGAs substantially improve over the baseline VAEs in terms of sample quality. Compared to other autoencoder-based generative models using simple priors, PGAs achieve state-of-the-art FID scores on CIFAR-10 and CelebA.

title: Perceptual Generative Autoencoders

abstract: We introduce a new neural network architecture that we call "grid-functioned" neural networks. It utilises a grid structure of network parameterisations that can be specialised for different subdomains of the problem, while maintaining smooth, continuous behaviour. The grid gives the user flexibility to prevent gross features from overshadowing important minor ones. We present a full characterisation of its computational and spatial complexity, and demonstrate its potential, compared to a traditional architecture, over a set of synthetic regression problems. We further illustrate the benefits through a real-world 3D skeletal animation case study, where it offers the same visual quality as a state-of-the-art model, but with lower computational complexity and better control accuracy.

paragraphs: A neural network may need to capture both broad patterns and small details that matter for a particular task. This paper introduces grid-functioned neural networks, which organize network parameterizations into a grid. Different parts of that structure can specialize in different subdomains of the problem while maintaining smooth, continuous behavior.

The grid gives users flexibility to keep large-scale features from overshadowing important minor ones. The architectural idea therefore combines specialization with continuity: different regions can receive tailored modeling capacity without giving up smooth overall behavior. The authors also characterize computational and spatial complexity, making resource requirements part of the architectural analysis.

Synthetic regression experiments compare the approach with a traditional architecture and demonstrate its potential. A real-world case study then applies it to 3D skeletal animation. There, the model matches the visual quality of a state-of-the-art system while using lower computational complexity and providing better control accuracy. The results illustrate a setting where local specialization benefits both efficiency and fine control.
summary.tldr: Grid-functioned networks combine smooth regional specialization with improved efficiency and control in a 3D skeletal-animation case study.

title: Grid-Functioned Neural Networks

abstract: This paper studies two variants of the best arm identification (BAI) problem under the streaming model, where we have a stream of n arms with reward distributions supported on [0,1] with unknown means. The arms in the stream are arriving one by one, and the algorithm cannot access an arm unless it is stored in a limited size memory. We first study the streaming \epslion-topk-arms identification problem, which asks for k arms whose reward means are lower than that of the k-th best arm by at most \epsilon with probability at least 1-\delta. For general \epsilon \in (0,1), the existing solution for this problem assumes k = 1 and achieves the optimal sample complexity O(\frac{n}{\epsilon^2} \log \frac{1}{\delta}) using O(\log^*(n)) memory and a single pass of the stream. We propose an algorithm that works for any k and achieves the optimal sample complexity O(\frac{n}{\epsilon^2} \log\frac{k}{\delta}) using a single-arm memory and a single pass of the stream. Second, we study the streaming BAI problem, where the objective is to identify the arm with the maximum reward mean with at least 1-\delta probability, using a single-arm memory and as few passes of the input stream as possible. We present a single-arm-memory algorithm that achieves a near instance-dependent optimal sample complexity within O(\log \Delta_2^{-1}) passes, where \Delta_2 is the gap between the mean of the best arm and that of the second best arm.

paragraphs: The paper studies best-arm identification when arms arrive in a stream and can be accessed only while stored in limited memory. Each arm has an unknown mean reward, with rewards bounded between zero and one. The challenge combines statistical uncertainty with restrictions on retaining and revisiting candidate arms.

For approximate top-k identification, the authors give a single-pass algorithm using single-arm memory. With probability at least 1−delta, it returns k arms whose means are no more than epsilon below the kth-best mean. Its optimal sample complexity is of order n divided by epsilon squared, multiplied by log(k/delta), extending the earlier single-best-arm setting.

For identifying the exact best arm, they again use single-arm memory but allow multiple passes. Their algorithm has nearly instance-optimal sample complexity and needs a number of passes logarithmic in the inverse gap between the best and second-best means. The two results distinguish approximate selection in one pass from exact identification, where closer leading means affect the stated pass bound.
summary.tldr: Single-arm-memory streaming algorithms achieve optimal approximate top-k sampling and nearly instance-optimal exact best-arm identification with multiple passes.

title: Optimal Streaming Algorithms for Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Continual Learning is a learning paradigm where learning systems are trained on a sequence of tasks. The goal here is to perform well on the current task without suffering from a performance drop on the previous tasks. Two notable directions among the recent advances in continual learning with neural networks are (1) variational Bayes based regularization by learning priors from previous tasks, and, (2) learning the structure of deep networks to adapt to new tasks. So far, these two approaches have been largely orthogonal. We present a novel Bayesian framework based on continually learning the structure of deep neural networks, to unify these distinct yet complementary approaches. The proposed framework learns the deep structure for each task by learning which weights to be used, and supports inter-task transfer through the overlapping of different sparse subsets of weights learned by different tasks. An appealing aspect of our proposed continual learning framework is that it is applicable to both discriminative (supervised) and generative (unsupervised) settings. Experimental results on supervised and unsupervised benchmarks demonstrate that our approach performs comparably or better than recent advances in continual learning.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a system to learn successive tasks while preserving performance on earlier ones. Two existing approaches address this through Bayesian regularization informed by past tasks and through changes to network structure. This paper brings those ideas together in a Bayesian framework that continually learns which parts of a deep network each task should use.

For each task, the framework learns a sparse subset of weights. Different tasks can use overlapping subsets, creating a route for information transfer between them. Task-specific structure and shared parameters therefore become parts of the same learning process. The framework connects decisions about which weights are active with the Bayesian approach to learning across tasks.

The method applies to both supervised discriminative learning and unsupervised generative learning. Experiments in both settings show performance comparable to or better than recent continual learning approaches. These findings support the value of combining structural adaptation with Bayesian learning across a sequence of tasks, including cases where learning involves generating data rather than predicting labels.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian continual learning framework assigns tasks overlapping sparse subsets of network weights to combine structural adaptation with knowledge transfer.

title: Bayesian Structural Adaptation for Continual Learning

abstract: We study the problem of zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where agents must independently produce strategies for a collaborative game that are compatible with novel partners not seen during training. Our first contribution is to consider the need for diversity in generating such agents. Because self-play (SP) agents control their own trajectory distribution during training, each policy typically only performs well on this exact distribution. As a result, they achieve low scores in ZSC, since playing with another agent is likely to put them in situations they have not encountered during training. To address this issue, we train a common best response (BR) to a population of agents, which we regulate to be diverse. To this end, we introduce \textit{Trajectory Diversity} (TrajeDi) – a differentiable objective for generating diverse reinforcement learning policies. We derive TrajeDi as a generalization of the Jensen-Shannon divergence between policies and motivate it experimentally in two simple settings. We then focus on the collaborative card game Hanabi, demonstrating the scalability of our method and improving upon the cross-play scores of both independently trained SP agents and BRs to unregularized populations.

paragraphs: Zero-shot coordination requires agents to collaborate with partners they did not encounter during training. Self-play can prepare an agent for a narrow range of situations because its own strategy shapes the trajectories it experiences. A new partner can create unfamiliar situations, making successful self-play a poor predictor of successful collaboration.

The paper trains a common best response against a population whose policies are explicitly encouraged to be diverse. Its Trajectory Diversity objective, or TrajeDi, is differentiable and generalizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence between policies. The approach makes diversity part of population training so that the responding agent faces a broader collection of behaviors.

The authors motivate the objective experimentally in two simple settings and then evaluate its scalability in the cooperative card game Hanabi. It improves cross-play scores over independently trained self-play agents and best responses to populations without diversity regularization. These results support deliberately shaping the training population as a means of improving coordination with previously unseen partners.
summary.tldr: TrajeDi encourages diverse training partners and improves zero-shot coordination in Hanabi by training a common response to that population.

title: Trajectory Diversity for Zero-Shot Coordination

abstract: In many real-world applications, reinforcement learning (RL) agents might have to solve multiple tasks, each one typically modeled via a reward function. If reward functions are expressed linearly, and the agent has previously learned a set of policies for different tasks, successor features (SFs) can be exploited to combine such policies and identify reasonable solutions for new problems. However, the identified solutions are not guaranteed to be optimal. We introduce a novel algorithm that addresses this limitation. It allows RL agents to combine existing policies and directly identify optimal policies for arbitrary new problems, without requiring any further interactions with the environment. We first show (under mild assumptions) that the transfer learning problem tackled by SFs is equivalent to the problem of learning to optimize multiple objectives in RL. We then introduce an SF-based extension of the Optimistic Linear Support algorithm to learn a set of policies whose SFs form a convex coverage set. We prove that policies in this set can be combined via generalized policy improvement to construct optimal behaviors for any new linearly-expressible tasks, without requiring any additional training samples. We empirically show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art competing algorithms both in discrete and continuous domains under value function approximation.

paragraphs: An agent may need to solve many tasks that differ in their reward functions. Successor features allow it to reuse previously learned policies when rewards are expressed linearly, but ordinary reuse does not guarantee an optimal solution. This paper develops a way to learn a policy collection that supports stronger transfer guarantees.

Under mild assumptions, the authors connect successor-feature transfer to multi-objective reinforcement learning. They then extend Optimistic Linear Support to learn policies whose successor features form a convex coverage set. This set provides the coverage needed for generalized policy improvement to construct optimal behavior for new tasks with linearly expressible rewards.

Once that policy collection has been learned, the stated transfer guarantee requires no additional environment interactions or training samples for the new task. The guarantee applies to the specified family of linearly expressible tasks and the framework’s assumptions. Experiments in discrete and continuous domains with value-function approximation show improvements over state-of-the-art competing methods. The key advance is to organize what gets learned in advance so that later policy reuse can support optimality, rather than merely reasonable performance.
summary.tldr: Learning a convex coverage set of successor features enables optimal transfer to new linearly expressible tasks under the framework’s assumptions.

title: Optimistic Linear Support and Successor Features as a Basis for Optimal Policy Transfer

abstract: This work is concerned with the following fundamental question in scientific machine learning: Can deep-learning-based methods solve noise-free inverse problems to near-perfect accuracy? Positive evidence is provided for the first time, focusing on a prototypical computed tomography (CT) setup. We demonstrate that an iterative end-to-end network scheme enables reconstructions close to numerical precision, comparable to classical compressed sensing strategies. Our results build on our winning submission to the recent AAPM DL-Sparse-View CT Challenge. Its goal was to identify the state-of-the-art in solving the sparse-view CT inverse problem with data-driven techniques. A specific difficulty of the challenge setup was that the precise forward model remained unknown to the participants. Therefore, a key feature of our approach was to initially estimate the unknown fanbeam geometry in a data-driven calibration step. Apart from an in-depth analysis of our methodology, we also demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on the open-access real-world dataset LoDoPaB CT.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether deep learning can solve noise-free inverse problems with nearly perfect numerical accuracy. An iterative, end-to-end network produces reconstructions close to numerical precision, comparable to classical compressed sensing strategies in the studied setup.

A distinctive difficulty was that participants did not know the exact forward model describing how the measurements were produced. The paper analyzes its methodology in depth and also reports state-of-the-art performance on the real-world LoDoPaB CT dataset. The near-exact recovery result specifically provides positive evidence for the noise-free inverse-problem question. The additional dataset evaluation establishes a separate practical result, extending the empirical assessment beyond the challenge setup without making near-perfect recovery a universal claim.
summary.tldr: An iterative network with data-driven geometry calibration achieves near-numerical-precision reconstruction in a noise-free CT setup.

title: Near-Exact Recovery for Tomographic Inverse Problems via Deep Learning

abstract: We propose Continual Repeated Annealed Flow Transport Monte Carlo (CRAFT), a method that combines a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler (itself a generalization of Annealed Importance Sampling) with variational inference using normalizing flows. The normalizing flows are directly trained to transport between annealing temperatures using a KL divergence for each transition. This optimization objective is itself estimated using the normalizing flow/SMC approximation. We show conceptually and using multiple empirical examples that CRAFT improves on Annealed Flow Transport Monte Carlo (Arbel et al., 2021), on which it builds and also on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) based Stochastic Normalizing Flows (Wu et al., 2020). By incorporating CRAFT within particle MCMC, we show that such learnt samplers can achieve impressively accurate results on a challenging lattice field theory example.

paragraphs: The paper introduces CRAFT, a sampling method that combines sequential Monte Carlo with variational inference based on normalizing flows. The sequential sampler works across annealing temperatures, while the learned transformations move samples between those stages. This brings a trainable transport mechanism into a sampling procedure rather than treating sampling and flow learning as separate tasks.

Each flow is trained using a KL-divergence objective for its particular transition between temperatures. The objective is itself estimated using the combined flow and sequential Monte Carlo approximation. Thus, the current sampling approximation supplies information for learning transformations that transport samples through the annealing sequence.

The authors provide conceptual arguments and multiple empirical examples showing improvements over Annealed Flow Transport Monte Carlo and MCMC-based Stochastic Normalizing Flows. They also incorporate CRAFT into particle MCMC and obtain highly accurate results on a challenging lattice field theory example. This last result demonstrates how a learned sampler can contribute within a broader Monte Carlo method, extending the practical role of the learned transport maps.
summary.tldr: CRAFT trains normalizing flows within sequential Monte Carlo to improve transport between annealing stages and sampling performance.

title: Continual Repeated Annealed Flow Transport Monte Carlo

abstract: Retrosynthesis prediction is one of the fundamental challenges in organic synthesis. The task is to predict the reactants given a core product. With the advancement of machine learning, computer-aided synthesis planning has gained increasing interest. Numerous methods were proposed to solve this problem with different levels of dependency on additional chemical knowledge. In this paper, we propose Retroformer, a novel Transformer-based architecture for retrosynthesis prediction without relying on any cheminformatics tools for molecule editing. Via the proposed local attention head, the model can jointly encode the molecular sequence and graph, and efficiently exchange information between the local reactive region and the global reaction context. Retroformer reaches the new state-of-the-art accuracy for the end-to-end template-free retrosynthesis, and improves over many strong baselines on better molecule and reaction validity. In addition, its generative procedure is highly interpretable and controllable. Overall, Retroformer pushes the limits of the reaction reasoning ability of deep generative models.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis works backward from a desired product to the reactants that could produce it. The paper introduces Retroformer, a Transformer architecture for predicting those reactants. Its end-to-end, template-free approach performs molecule editing without relying on cheminformatics tools, placing that part of the prediction process within the learned architecture.

The central design is a local attention head that jointly encodes a molecule’s sequence and graph representations. It lets information move between the local region involved in a reaction and the broader reaction context. This connects a representation of molecular structure with the contextual information needed to reason about the overall transformation.

The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy for end-to-end template-free retrosynthesis and improved molecule and reaction validity relative to many strong baselines. They also describe the generation procedure as highly interpretable and controllable. The stated contribution combines predictive performance with a mechanism for integrating local chemistry-related structure and global context during generation, rather than treating the molecular sequence as an isolated representation.
summary.tldr: Retroformer combines molecular sequences and graphs through local attention to improve end-to-end, template-free reactant prediction.

title: Retroformer: Pushing the Limits of End-to-end Retrosynthesis Transformer

abstract: Methods based on deep neural networks with a massive number of layers and skip-connections have made impressive improvements on single image super-resolution (SISR). The skip-connections in these complex models boost the performance at the cost of a large amount of memory. With the increase of camera resolution from 1 million pixels to 100 million pixels on mobile phones, the memory footprint of these algorithms also increases hundreds of times, which restricts the applicability of these models on memory-limited devices. A plain model consisting of a stack of 3{\texttimes}3 convolutions with ReLU, in contrast, has the highest memory efficiency but poorly performs on super-resolution. This paper aims at calculating a winning initialization from a complex teacher network for a plain student network, which can provide performance comparable to complex models. To this end, we convert the teacher model to an equivalent large plain model and derive the plain student’s initialization. We further improve the student’s performance through initialization-aware feature distillation. Extensive experiments suggest that the proposed method results in a model with a competitive trade-off between accuracy and speed at a much lower memory footprint than other state-of-the-art lightweight approaches.

paragraphs: Single-image super-resolution benefits from deep networks with many layers and skip connections, but those structures consume substantial memory. The burden becomes greater as input image resolution rises. A plain sequence of 3-by-3 convolutions and ReLU operations is highly memory-efficient, yet ordinarily gives weaker super-resolution performance. MemSR aims to improve this simpler architecture through training.

The authors then use feature distillation that accounts for this initialization to improve the student further, transferring information from the teacher into the memory-efficient model.

Extensive experiments suggest a competitive balance between accuracy and speed while using much less memory than other leading lightweight approaches. The contribution is therefore a way to make a plain architecture more capable through teacher-derived initialization and distillation. It addresses the tension between the predictive benefits of complex models and the memory demands of high-resolution image processing.
summary.tldr: MemSR transfers initialization and features from a complex teacher into a plain super-resolution network with a much smaller memory footprint.

title: MemSR: Training Memory-efficient Lightweight Model for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Batching has a fundamental influence on the efficiency of deep neural network (DNN) execution. However, for dynamic DNNs, efficient batching is particularly challenging as the dataflow graph varies per input instance. As a result, state-of-the-art frameworks use heuristics that result in suboptimal batching decisions. Further, batching puts strict restrictions on memory adjacency and can lead to high data movement costs. In this paper, we provide an approach for batching dynamic DNNs based on finite state machines, which enables the automatic discovery of batching policies specialized for each DNN via reinforcement learning. Moreover, we find that memory planning that is aware of the batching policy can save significant data movement overheads, which is automated by a PQ tree-based algorithm we introduce. Experimental results show that our framework speeds up state-of-the-art frameworks by on average 1.15x, 1.39x, and 2.45x for chain-based, tree-based, and lattice-based DNNs across CPU and GPU. The framework is open-sourced at https://github.com/gulang2019/ED-Batch.git.

Existing frameworks rely on heuristics that can make suboptimal choices. There is also a memory problem: operations grouped into a batch have adjacency requirements that can force costly movement of data.

These results support the value of coordinating learned batching decisions with memory planning. The different averages also show that the reported improvement varies with the structure of the network.
summary.tldr: ED-Batch learns network-specific batching policies and coordinates memory planning to accelerate dynamic neural network execution.

title: ED-Batch: Efficient Automatic Batching of Dynamic Neural Networks via Learned Finite State Machines

abstract: Modeling spatiotemporal dynamical systems is a fundamental challenge in machine learning. Transformer models have been very successful in NLP and computer vision where they provide interpretable representations of data. However, a limitation of transformers in modeling continuous dynamical systems is that they are fundamentally discrete time and space models and thus have no guarantees regarding continuous sampling. To address this challenge, we present the Continuous Spatiotemporal Transformer (CST), a new transformer architecture that is designed for modeling of continuous systems. This new framework guarantees a continuous and smooth output via optimization in Sobolev space. We benchmark CST against traditional transformers as well as other spatiotemporal dynamics modeling methods and achieve superior performance in a number of tasks on synthetic and real systems, including learning brain dynamics from calcium imaging data.

paragraphs: Many systems evolve continuously through space and time, while transformers represent their inputs through discrete observations. This creates a mismatch: a model built around sampled points does not automatically guarantee that its output behaves continuously between them. The paper addresses this issue with the Continuous Spatiotemporal Transformer, or CST.

CST is designed specifically for continuous dynamical systems. Its central mechanism is optimization in Sobolev space, which provides the framework’s guarantee of continuous, smooth output. Smoothness is therefore a property addressed by the model’s mathematical formulation, rather than something inferred solely from how its predictions look at the observed samples.

The authors compare CST with traditional transformers and other methods for modeling dynamics across space and time. They report superior performance on several tasks involving both synthetic and real systems, including learning brain dynamics from calcium imaging. The contribution combines a structural guarantee about output behavior with empirical evidence of predictive usefulness. The smoothness guarantee concerns continuity of the modeled output; the reported performance advantages are findings from the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: CST uses Sobolev-space optimization to guarantee smooth, continuous outputs and improves performance on several spatiotemporal modeling tasks.

title: Continuous Spatiotemporal Transformer

abstract: Recent trends in language modeling have focused on increasing performance through scaling, and have resulted in an environment where training language models is out of reach for most researchers and practitioners. While most in the community are asking how to push the limits of extreme computation, we ask the opposite question: How far can we get with a single GPU in just one day? We investigate the downstream performance achievable with a transformer-based language model trained completely from scratch with masked language modeling for a single day on a single consumer GPU. Aside from re-analyzing nearly all components of the pretraining pipeline for this scenario and providing a modified pipeline with performance close to BERT, we investigate why scaling down is hard, and which modifications actually improve performance in this scenario. We provide evidence that even in this constrained setting, performance closely follows scaling laws observed in large-compute settings. Through the lens of scaling laws, we categorize a range of recent improvements to training and architecture and discuss their merit and practical applicability (or lack thereof) for the limited compute setting. We provide code to reproduce all experiments at github.com/JonasGeiping/cramming .

The authors train a transformer from scratch using masked language modeling and evaluate its downstream performance. The motivation is to make meaningful pretraining experiments accessible when large computing resources are unavailable.

They revisit nearly every component of the pretraining pipeline and provide a modified pipeline whose performance is close to BERT. The investigation also asks why reducing the computing budget is difficult and which training or architectural changes actually help under this constraint. A technique's usefulness is therefore assessed within the specified time and hardware budget.

The authors find evidence that performance in this small-compute setting closely follows scaling laws observed with much larger budgets. They use those relationships to organize and assess recent improvements, including their practical suitability for constrained training. The result is both a concrete training pipeline and an analysis of how to spend limited computation effectively, with code provided for reproducing the experiments.
summary.tldr: A redesigned pretraining pipeline achieves performance close to BERT after one day of training from scratch on one consumer GPU.

title: Cramming: Training a Language Model on a single GPU in one day.

abstract: Neural networks have shown great potential in accelerating the solution of partial differential equations (PDEs). Recently, there has been a growing interest in introducing physics constraints into training neural PDE solvers to reduce the use of costly data and improve the generalization ability. However, these physics constraints, based on certain finite dimensional approximations over the function space, must resolve the smallest scaled physics to ensure the accuracy and stability of the simulation, resulting in high computational costs from large input, output, and neural networks. This paper proposes a general acceleration methodology called NeuralStagger by spatially and temporally decomposing the original learning tasks into several coarser-resolution subtasks. We define a coarse-resolution neural solver for each subtask, which requires fewer computational resources, and jointly train them with the vanilla physics-constrained loss by simply arranging their outputs to reconstruct the original solution. Due to the perfect parallelism between them, the solution is achieved as fast as a coarse-resolution neural solver. In addition, the trained solvers bring the flexibility of simulating with multiple levels of resolution. We demonstrate the successful application of NeuralStagger on 2D and 3D fluid dynamics simulations, which leads to an additional $10\sim100\times$ speed-up. Moreover, the experiment also shows that the learned model could be well used for optimal control.

paragraphs: Physics-constrained neural solvers learn to solve partial differential equations while respecting physical equations during training. Their constraints must resolve small-scale physics to maintain simulation accuracy and stability. That requirement can produce large inputs, outputs, and networks, making the solver expensive even when neural methods are intended to accelerate computation.

NeuralStagger divides the original learning problem across space and time into several coarser-resolution subtasks. Each subtask receives its own smaller neural solver. The outputs are arranged to reconstruct the original solution, and the solvers are trained jointly using the original physics-constrained loss. This retains the full solution as the object on which the physical constraints are enforced.

Because the component solvers can run in parallel, the approach can achieve solution speed comparable to a coarse-resolution solver. The trained components also permit simulation at multiple resolutions. Experiments on two- and three-dimensional fluid dynamics report an additional 10–100-fold speedup. The authors further show that the learned model can be used for optimal control, extending the demonstrated utility beyond simulation alone.
summary.tldr: NeuralStagger combines parallel coarse-resolution neural solvers into a physics-constrained solution, reporting 10–100-fold additional speedups in fluid simulations.

title: NeuralStagger: Accelerating Physics-constrained Neural PDE Solver with Spatial-temporal Decomposition

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) learn the representation of graph-structured data, and their expressiveness can be further enhanced by inferring node relations for propagation. Attention-based GNNs infer neighbor importance to manipulate the weight of its propagation. Despite their popularity, the discussion on deep graph attention and its unique challenges has been limited. In this work, we investigate some problematic phenomena related to deep graph attention, including vulnerability to over-smoothed features and smooth cumulative attention. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we show that various attention-based GNNs suffer from these problems. Motivated by our findings, we propose AERO-GNN, a novel GNN architecture designed for deep graph attention. AERO-GNN provably mitigates the proposed problems of deep graph attention, which is further empirically demonstrated with (a) its adaptive and less smooth attention functions and (b) higher performance at deep layers (up to 64). On 9 out of 12 node classification benchmarks, AERO-GNN outperforms the baseline GNNs, highlighting the advantages of deep graph attention. Our code is available at https://github.com/syleeheal/AERO-GNN.

paragraphs: Attention-based graph neural networks learn how much influence neighboring nodes should have during information propagation. Increasing depth raises particular difficulties for this mechanism. The paper investigates vulnerability to over-smoothed features and excessive smoothness in cumulative attention, examining how these phenomena affect the attention used across many graph-processing layers.

Through theoretical and empirical analysis, the authors show that various attention-based GNNs suffer from these problems. They then propose AERO-GNN, an architecture designed specifically for deep graph attention. The method provably mitigates the identified issues, connecting the architectural remedy to the same problems established by the analysis.

Experiments further show adaptive, less smooth attention functions and stronger performance at deep layers, including networks with up to 64 layers. AERO-GNN outperforms the baseline GNNs on nine of twelve node classification benchmarks. The results support the usefulness of deep graph attention when its specific smoothing problems are addressed. The claim combines a theoretical mitigation result with empirical improvements across most, rather than all, of the evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: AERO-GNN mitigates smoothing problems in deep graph attention and outperforms baseline GNNs on nine of twelve node classification benchmarks.

title: Towards Deep Attention in Graph Neural Networks: Problems and Remedies

abstract: Recently, unsupervised representation learning (URL) has improved the sample efficiency of Reinforcement Learning (RL) by pretraining a model from a large unlabeled dataset. The underlying principle of these methods is to learn temporally predictive representations by predicting future states in the latent space. However, an important challenge of this approach is the representational collapse, where the subspace of the latent representations collapses into a low-dimensional manifold. To address this issue, we propose a novel URL framework that causally predicts future states while increasing the dimension of the latent manifold by decorrelating the features in the latent space. Through extensive empirical studies, we demonstrate that our framework effectively learns predictive representations without collapse, which significantly improves the sample efficiency of state-of-the-art URL methods on the Atari 100k benchmark. The code is available at https://github.com/dojeon-ai/SimTPR.

paragraphs: Unsupervised pretraining can help reinforcement learning agents use interaction data more efficiently. One approach learns state representations by predicting future states in a latent space from a large unlabeled dataset. However, these representations can collapse into a low-dimensional structure, leaving the model with fewer distinct feature directions than its representation could otherwise support.

The paper proposes a framework that combines causal prediction of future states with feature decorrelation. The predictive objective encourages the representation to capture information about what comes next. Decorrelation reduces dependence between latent features, aiming to increase the dimension of the latent manifold and address the collapse that can accompany predictive representation learning.

Extensive empirical studies show that the framework learns predictive representations without collapse and significantly improves the sample efficiency of state-of-the-art unsupervised representation methods on Atari 100k. The findings connect an internal property of the representation to downstream learning behavior. In the evaluated setting, maintaining a richer set of feature directions works alongside temporal prediction to make the pretrained representation more useful for reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Combining future-state prediction with latent feature decorrelation prevents representation collapse in the reported studies and improves Atari 100k sample efficiency.

title: On the Importance of Feature Decorrelation for Unsupervised Representation Learning in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Knowing the features of a complex system that are highly relevant to a particular target variable is of fundamental interest in many areas of science. Existing approaches are often limited to linear settings, sometimes lack guarantees, and in most cases, do not scale to the problem at hand, in particular to images. We propose DRCFS, a doubly robust feature selection method for identifying the causal features even in nonlinear and high dimensional settings. We provide theoretical guarantees, illustrate necessary conditions for our assumptions, and perform extensive experiments across a wide range of simulated and semi-synthetic datasets. DRCFS significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, selecting robust features even in challenging highly non-linear and high-dimensional problems.

paragraphs: Identifying which features matter causally to a target variable is a central problem in studying complex systems. The paper focuses on settings where relationships can be nonlinear and the number of available features can be large. It argues that existing approaches often rely on linearity, lack guarantees, or struggle to scale to data such as images.

The authors introduce DRCFS, a doubly robust method for selecting causal features in these more demanding settings. They provide theoretical guarantees and examine necessary conditions for the assumptions behind their analysis. This makes the assumptions part of the method’s justification: the causal interpretation is supported by a stated theoretical framework rather than by predictive relevance alone.

The empirical evaluation covers a broad collection of simulated and semi-synthetic datasets. DRCFS significantly outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches and selects robust features in challenging nonlinear, high-dimensional problems. Together, the theoretical and experimental contributions support extending causal feature selection beyond simpler linear settings, with the reported practical evidence grounded in those controlled and partially constructed datasets.
summary.tldr: DRCFS combines theoretical guarantees with strong simulated and semi-synthetic results for causal feature selection in nonlinear, high-dimensional settings.

title: DRCFS: Doubly Robust Causal Feature Selection

abstract: Humans have the ability to adapt the type of information they use, the procedure they employ, and the amount of time they spend when solving problems. However, most standard neural networks have a fixed function type and computation budget regardless of the sample’s nature or difficulty. Adaptivity is a powerful paradigm as it not only imbues practitioners with flexibility pertaining to the downstream usage of these models but can also serve as a powerful inductive bias for solving certain challenging classes of problems. In this work, we introduce a new approach called AdaTape, which allows for dynamic computation in neural networks through adaptive tape tokens. AdaTape utilizes an elastic input sequence by equipping an architecture with a dynamic read-and-write tape. Specifically, we adaptively generate input sequences using tape tokens obtained from a tape bank which can be either trainable or derived from input data. We examine the challenges and requirements to obtain dynamic sequence content and length, and propose the Adaptive Tape Reading (ATR) algorithm to achieve both goals. Through extensive experiments on image recognition tasks, we show that AdaTape can achieve better performance while maintaining the computational cost. To facilitate further research, we have released code at https://github.com/google-research/scenic/tree/main/scenic/projects/adatape.

paragraphs: Standard neural networks usually apply a fixed kind and amount of computation regardless of how difficult an example is. AdaTape introduces flexibility by allowing the input sequence itself to change. This gives the network a way to adapt the information it processes, rather than requiring every example to use an identical sequence structure.

The method equips an architecture with a dynamic read-and-write tape built from additional tape tokens. These tokens come from a bank that can be learned during training or constructed from the input data. The proposed Adaptive Tape Reading algorithm controls both which content enters the sequence and how long that sequence becomes.

Experiments on image recognition show that AdaTape can improve performance while maintaining computational cost. The result supports adaptive sequence construction as a useful way to allocate computation without simply increasing the overall budget. Its contribution is therefore both an architecture mechanism and an algorithm for making sequence content and length responsive to the example being processed.
summary.tldr: AdaTape adapts input sequence content and length to improve image recognition performance at maintained computational cost.

title: Adaptive Computation with Elastic Input Sequence

abstract: We study Bayesian optimization (BO) in high-dimensional and non-stationary scenarios. Existing algorithms for such scenarios typically require extensive hyperparameter tuning, which limits their practical effectiveness. We propose a framework, called BALLET, which adaptively filters for a high-confidence region of interest (ROI) as a superlevel-set of a nonparametric probabilistic model such as a Gaussian process (GP). Our approach is easy to tune, and is able to focus on local region of the optimization space that can be tackled by existing BO methods. The key idea is to use two probabilistic models: a coarse GP to identify the ROI, and a localized GP for optimization within the ROI. We show theoretically that BALLET can efficiently shrink the search space, and can exhibit a tighter regret bound than standard BO without ROI filtering. We demonstrate empirically the effectiveness of BALLET on both synthetic and real-world optimization tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization becomes challenging when the search space has many dimensions or the objective behaves differently across regions. Existing approaches for these settings can require extensive hyperparameter tuning. BALLET addresses this difficulty by adaptively identifying a promising part of the search space and directing optimization toward that region.

The framework uses two probabilistic models with different jobs. A coarse Gaussian process identifies a high-confidence region of interest through a superlevel set, meaning a region selected according to a modeled level threshold. A localized Gaussian process then handles optimization inside that region. This separates the problem of deciding where to search from the problem of choosing evaluations within the selected area.

The theoretical analysis shows that BALLET can efficiently reduce the search space and can obtain a tighter regret bound than standard Bayesian optimization without filtering. This is a possible advantage established by the analysis, rather than an unconditional improvement. Experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks support its effectiveness, while the framework is described as easy to tune and compatible with existing local optimization methods.
summary.tldr: BALLET uses a coarse model to find promising regions and a local model to focus Bayesian optimization within them.

title: Learning Regions of Interest for Bayesian Optimization with Adaptive Level-Set Estimation

abstract: Multi-timestep simulation of brain-inspired Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) boost memory requirements during training and increase inference energy cost. Current training methods cannot simultaneously solve both training and inference dilemmas. This work proposes a novel Temporal Reversible architecture for SNNs (T-RevSNN) to jointly address the training and inference challenges by altering the forward propagation of SNNs. We turn off the temporal dynamics of most spiking neurons and design multi-level temporal reversible interactions at temporal turn-on spiking neurons, resulting in a $\mathcal{O}(L)$ training memory. Combined with the temporal reversible nature, we redesign the input encoding and network organization of SNNs to achieve $\mathcal{O}(1)$ inference energy cost. Then, we finely adjust the internal units and residual connections of the basic SNN block to ensure the effectiveness of sparse temporal information interaction. T-RevSNN achieves excellent accuracy on ImageNet, while the memory efficiency, training time acceleration and inference energy efficiency can be significantly improved by $8.6 \times$, $2.0 \times$ and $1.6 \times$, respectively. This work is expected to break the technical bottleneck of significantly increasing memory cost and training time for large-scale SNNs while maintaining both high performance and low inference energy cost.

T-RevSNN changes the network’s forward computation to address both costs together. These findings support an architectural approach to reducing the costs of multi-timestep computation while retaining high performance. The broader ambition is to ease the memory and training-time bottlenecks of large spiking networks while keeping inference energy low.
summary.tldr: T-RevSNN uses sparse, reversible temporal interactions to improve spiking-network memory use, training speed, and inference-energy efficiency while retaining strong ImageNet accuracy.

title: High-Performance Temporal Reversible Spiking Neural Networks with $\mathcalO(L)$ Training Memory and $\mathcalO(1)$ Inference Cost

abstract: Neural networks whose weights are the output of a predictor (HyperNetworks) achieve excellent performance on many tasks. In ConvNets, kernel prediction layers are a popular type of HyperNetwork. Previous theoretical work has argued that a hierarchy of multiplicative interactions exists in which gating is at the bottom and full weight prediction, as in HyperNetworks, is at the top. In this paper, we constructively demonstrate an equivalence between gating combined with fixed weight layers and weight prediction, relativizing the notion of a hierarchy of multiplicative interactions. We further derive an equivalence between a restricted type of HyperNetwork and factorization machines. Finally, we find empirically that gating layers can learn to imitate weight prediction layers with an SGD variant and show a novel practical application in image denoising using kernel prediction networks. Our reformulation of predicted kernels, combining fixed layers and gating, reduces memory requirements.

paragraphs: HyperNetworks produce the weights used by another network, and kernel prediction applies this idea to convolutional filters. Earlier theoretical work placed full weight prediction above simpler gating in a hierarchy of multiplicative interactions. This paper reexamines that distinction by asking what gating can express when combined with fixed-weight layers.

The authors give a constructive equivalence between that combination and weight prediction. This qualifies the proposed hierarchy: the surrounding fixed layers matter when comparing the power of gating with generated weights. They also establish an equivalence between a restricted form of HyperNetwork and factorization machines, connecting another pair of model formulations.

The paper complements these constructions with empirical evidence that gating layers can learn to imitate weight prediction layers using a variant of stochastic gradient descent. It also applies the reformulation to image denoising with kernel prediction networks, reducing memory requirements. The contribution therefore links representational equivalence to a practical alternative implementation, while separately testing whether the equivalent behavior can be learned.
summary.tldr: Gating combined with fixed-weight layers can express weight prediction, and the reformulation reduces memory in a denoising application.

title: Is Kernel Prediction More Powerful than Gating in Convolutional Neural Networks?

abstract: Modeling unsteady, fast transient, and advection-dominated physics problems is a pressing challenge for physics-aware deep learning (PADL). The physics of complex systems is governed by large systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) and ancillary constitutive models with nonlinear structures, as well as evolving state fields exhibiting sharp gradients and rapidly deforming material interfaces. Here, we investigate an inductive bias approach that is versatile and generalizable to model generic nonlinear field evolution problems. Our study focuses on the recent physics-aware recurrent convolutions (PARC), which incorporates a differentiator-integrator architecture that inductively models the spatiotemporal dynamics of generic physical systems. We extend the capabilities of PARC to simulate unsteady, transient, and advection-dominant systems. The extended model, referred to as PARCv2, is equipped with differential operators to model advection-reaction-diffusion equations, as well as a hybrid integral solver for stable, long-time predictions. PARCv2 is tested on both standard benchmark problems in fluid dynamics, namely Burgers and Navier-Stokes equations, and then applied to more complex shock-induced reaction problems in energetic materials. We evaluate the behavior of PARCv2 in comparison to other physics-informed and learning bias models and demonstrate its potential to model unsteady and advection-dominant dynamics regimes.

paragraphs: Rapidly changing physical systems are difficult for learned simulators, especially when motion transports sharp boundaries or produces steep spatial gradients. Their behavior can involve large nonlinear systems of partial differential equations and additional constitutive models. This paper extends a physics-aware neural architecture to better represent these demanding forms of evolution.

The starting point is PARC, which uses a differentiator-integrator architecture to model change over space and time. PARCv2 adds differential operators for advection-reaction-diffusion equations and a hybrid integral solver intended to support stable predictions over long periods. These architectural choices encode structure associated with physical evolution into the model's computation.

They compare its behavior with other physics-informed and learning-bias models. The results demonstrate its potential for unsteady and advection-dominated dynamics. The contribution is an extension of the architecture's physical modeling capabilities, supported by evaluations spanning standard equations and a more complex application.
summary.tldr: PARCv2 adds physical differential operators and a hybrid integrator to model rapidly changing, advection-dominated systems.

title: PARCv2: Physics-aware Recurrent Convolutional Neural Networks for Spatiotemporal Dynamics Modeling

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as state-of-the-art generative models for image generation. However, sampling from diffusion models is usually time-consuming due to the inherent autoregressive nature of their sampling process. In this work, we propose a novel approach that accelerates the sampling of diffusion models by parallelizing the autoregressive process. Specifically, we reformulate the sampling process as solving a system of triangular nonlinear equations through fixed-point iteration. With this innovative formulation, we explore several systematic techniques to further reduce the iteration steps required by the solving process. Applying these techniques, we introduce ParaTAA, a universal and training-free parallel sampling algorithm that can leverage extra computational and memory resources to increase the sampling speed. Our experiments demonstrate that ParaTAA can decrease the inference steps required by common sequential sampling algorithms such as DDIM and DDPM by a factor of 4$\sim$14 times. Notably, when applying ParaTAA with 100 steps DDIM for Stable Diffusion, a widely-used text-to-image diffusion model, it can produce the same images as the sequential sampling in only 7 inference steps. The code is available at https://github.com/TZW1998/ParaTAA-Diffusion.

paragraphs: Diffusion models typically generate an image through a sequence of dependent sampling steps. Because later steps depend on earlier ones, this process can take substantial time even after the model has been trained. This paper asks how to reorganize those dependencies so that more of the sampling work can happen in parallel.

The authors express sampling as a system of triangular nonlinear equations and solve it through fixed-point iteration. This formulation gives them a systematic way to develop techniques that reduce the number of solver iterations. Their resulting algorithm, ParaTAA, requires no model training and uses additional computation and memory to accelerate sampling.

Experiments report a four- to fourteen-fold reduction in inference steps relative to common sequential samplers, including DDIM and DDPM. In the highlighted Stable Diffusion example, ParaTAA reproduces the images from a 100-step DDIM run using seven inference steps. These results concern fewer sequential inference steps; the approach explicitly trades extra computational and memory resources for faster generation.
summary.tldr: ParaTAA reformulates diffusion sampling as a parallel equation-solving problem, reducing inference steps without retraining while using extra computation and memory.

title: Accelerating Parallel Sampling of Diffusion Models

abstract: With the emergence of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), considerable efforts have been devoted to fine-tuning them for downstream tasks. Despite the progress made in designing efficient fine-tuning methods, such methods require access to the model’s parameters, which can be challenging as model owners often opt to provide their models as a black box to safeguard model ownership. This paper proposes a Collaborative Fine-Tuning (CraFT) approach for fine-tuning black-box VLMs to downstream tasks, where one only has access to the input prompts and the output predictions of the model. CraFT comprises two modules, a prompt generation module for learning text prompts and a prediction refinement module for enhancing output predictions in residual style. Additionally, we introduce an auxiliary prediction-consistent loss to promote consistent optimization across these modules. These modules are optimized by a novel collaborative training algorithm. Extensive experiments on few-shot classification over 15 datasets demonstrate the superiority of CraFT. The results show that CraFT achieves a decent gain of about 12% with 16-shot datasets and only 8,000 queries. Moreover, CraFT trains faster and uses only about 1/80 of the memory footprint for deployment, while sacrificing only 1.62% compared to the white-box method. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mrflogs/CraFT.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained vision-language model usually requires access to its parameters. That access may be unavailable when a model owner exposes only prompts and predictions. CraFT addresses adaptation in this black-box setting, learning how to interact with the model and improve its outputs using only the permitted input and output interface.

CraFT has two trainable modules. One learns text prompts, and the other refines the resulting predictions through residual adjustments. An additional prediction-consistency loss helps align their optimization, while a collaborative training algorithm coordinates their learning. This makes adaptation a joint problem of choosing useful prompts and correcting the predictions those prompts produce.

Experiments cover few-shot classification on 15 datasets. The authors report a gain of about 12% with 16-shot datasets using 8,000 queries. They also report faster training and a deployment memory footprint of roughly one eightieth of the white-box comparison, with a reported performance sacrifice of 1.62%. These results show a practical adaptation tradeoff when direct access to a model's weights is unavailable.
summary.tldr: CraFT adapts black-box vision-language models by jointly learning prompts and prediction refinements, with strong reported few-shot results and low deployment memory use.

title: Connecting the Dots: Collaborative Fine-tuning for Black-Box Vision-Language Models

abstract: Exploration remains a critical issue in deep reinforcement learning for an agent to attain high returns in unknown environments. Although the prevailing exploration Random Network Distillation (RND) algorithm has been demonstrated to be effective in numerous environments, it often needs more discriminative power in bonus allocation. This paper highlights the “bonus inconsistency” issue within RND, pinpointing its primary limitation. To address this issue, we introduce the Distributional RND (DRND), a derivative of the RND. DRND enhances the exploration process by distilling a distribution of random networks and implicitly incorporating pseudo counts to improve the precision of bonus allocation. This refinement encourages agents to engage in more extensive exploration. Our method effectively mitigates the inconsistency issue without introducing significant computational overhead. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over the original RND algorithm. Our method excels in challenging online exploration scenarios and effectively serves as an anti-exploration mechanism in D4RL offline tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yk7333/DRND.
