paragraphs: Exploration methods give reinforcement learning agents additional incentives to investigate unfamiliar experience. Random Network Distillation is an established approach, but the paper identifies a problem in how it assigns these exploration bonuses. Its bonuses can be inconsistent, limiting how precisely they distinguish which experiences deserve further exploration.

Distributional Random Network Distillation, or DRND, changes the object being distilled to a distribution of random networks. It also implicitly incorporates pseudo counts into bonus allocation. These changes make the exploration signal more discriminating and encourage broader exploration. The authors report that the refinement mitigates bonus inconsistency without adding significant computational overhead.

Both theory and experiments support improvements over the original RND algorithm. The method performs well in challenging online exploration settings and also works as an anti-exploration mechanism on D4RL offline tasks. These are different uses of the same underlying refinement: encouraging exploration during online learning and supporting anti-exploration during offline learning. The results suggest that more precise bonus allocation can be useful across both settings.
summary.tldr: DRND distills a distribution of random networks to improve exploration-bonus consistency and supports both online exploration and offline anti-exploration.

title: Exploration and Anti-Exploration with Distributional Random Network Distillation

abstract: Rooting in the scarcity of most attributes, realistic pedestrian attribute datasets exhibit unduly skewed data distribution, from which two types of model failures are delivered: (1) label imbalance: model predictions lean greatly towards the side of majority labels; (2) semantics imbalance: model is easily overfitted on the under-represented attributes due to their insufficient semantic diversity. To render perfect label balancing, we propose a novel framework that successfully decouples label-balanced data re-sampling from the curse of attributes co-occurrence, i.e., we equalize the sampling prior of an attribute while not biasing that of the co-occurred others. To diversify the attributes semantics and mitigate the feature noise, we propose a Bayesian feature augmentation method to introduce true in-distribution novelty. Handling both imbalances jointly, our work achieves best accuracy on various popular benchmarks, and importantly, with minimal computational budget.

To render perfect label balancing, we propose a novel framework that successfully decouples label-balanced data re-sampling from the curse of attributes co-occurrence, i.e., we equalize the sampling prior of an attribute while not biasing that of the co-occurred others. To diversify the attributes semantics and mitigate the feature noise, we propose a Bayesian feature augmentation method to introduce true in-distribution novelty. Handling both imbalances jointly, our work achieves best accuracy on various popular benchmarks, and importantly, with minimal computational budget.

paragraphs: This paper addresses two consequences of rare attributes in pedestrian-recognition datasets. Label imbalance pushes predictions toward common labels. Semantic imbalance leaves rare attributes with too little variety, encouraging overfitting. Because an image can contain several attributes simultaneously, changing how frequently one attribute is sampled can also change the sampling of others.

The proposed framework separates label balancing from this co-occurrence problem. It equalizes an attribute’s sampling prior without biasing the priors of attributes that appear alongside it. This directly targets the difficulty of balancing a multi-label dataset, where examples cannot be treated as belonging to only one independent category.

To address limited semantic diversity, the authors introduce Bayesian feature augmentation intended to add variation within the data distribution while reducing feature noise. The method therefore handles both how often attributes are represented and how varied their learned representations are. Jointly addressing these imbalances produces the best reported accuracy on several popular benchmarks with a small computational budget. The findings support treating frequency and semantic diversity as distinct, complementary training concerns.
summary.tldr: The method combines co-occurrence-aware label balancing with Bayesian feature augmentation to improve pedestrian attribute recognition.

title: Pedestrian Attribute Recognition as Label-balanced Multi-label Learning

abstract: Test-Time Training has emerged as a promising solution to address distribution shifts in 3D point cloud classification. However, existing methods often rely on computationally expensive backpropagation during adaptation, limiting their applicability in real-world, time-sensitive scenarios. In this paper, we introduce SMART-PC, a skeleton-based framework that enhances resilience to corruptions by leveraging the geometric structure of 3D point clouds. During pre-training, our method predicts skeletal representations, enabling the model to extract robust and meaningful geometric features that are less sensitive to corruptions, thereby improving adaptability to test-time distribution shifts. Unlike prior approaches, SMART-PC achieves real-time adaptation by eliminating backpropagation and updating only BatchNorm statistics, resulting in a lightweight and efficient framework capable of achieving high frame-per-second rates while maintaining superior classification performance. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including ModelNet40-C, ShapeNet-C, and ScanObjectNN-C, demonstrate that SMART-PC achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing methods such as MATE in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The implementation is available at: https://github.com/AliBahri94/SMART-PC.

paragraphs: Point-cloud classifiers can face corrupted inputs whose distribution differs from their training data. Test-time training adapts models to these changes, but backpropagation during adaptation can be expensive. SMART-PC addresses both robustness and adaptation speed by combining geometric representation learning with lightweight updates at test time.

During pre-training, the model predicts skeletal representations of three-dimensional point clouds. This encourages features that capture meaningful geometric structure and are less sensitive to corruption. At test time, adaptation updates only BatchNorm statistics, avoiding backpropagation. The framework therefore links the features learned before deployment to a low-cost mechanism for responding to changed inputs.

Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ShapeNet-C, and ScanObjectNN-C report state-of-the-art classification results and better computational efficiency than existing methods, including MATE. The authors also report real-time adaptation at high frame rates. These findings support the combination of skeletal supervision and statistics-only adaptation as a way to improve corruption resilience while keeping test-time computation lightweight.
summary.tldr: SMART-PC learns skeletal point-cloud features and adapts only BatchNorm statistics, improving reported corruption robustness and efficiency without test-time backpropagation.

title: SMART-PC: Skeletal Model Adaptation for Robust Test-Time Training in Point Clouds

abstract: The ability to acquire high-resolution, large-scale geospatial data at an unprecedented using LiDAR and other related technologies has intensified the need for scalable algorithms for terrain analysis, including shortest-path-distance (SPD) queries on large-scale terrain digital elevation models (DEMs). In this paper, we present a neural data structure for efficiently answering SPD queries approximately on a large terrain DEM, which is based on the recently proposed neural geodesic field (NeuroGF) framework (Zhang et al., 2023)—the state-of-the-art neural data structure for estimating geodesic distance. In particular, we propose a decoupled-NeuroGF data structure combined with an efficient two-stage mixed-training strategy, which significantly reduces computational bottlenecks and enables efficient training on terrain DEMs at a scale not feasible before. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by performing detailed experiments on both synthetic and real data sets. For instance, we can train a small model with around 70000 parameters on a terrain DEM with 16 million nodes in a matter of hours that can answer SPD queries with 1% relative error in at most 10ms per query.

paragraphs: High-resolution terrain data make it possible to represent landscapes in great detail, but they also create very large graphs for distance calculations. This paper tackles shortest-path-distance queries on digital elevation models. Its goal is to answer these queries approximately and quickly using a compact learned data structure.

The method builds on neural geodesic fields, which use a neural representation to estimate distances. The authors introduce a decoupled version of NeuroGF together with a two-stage mixed-training procedure. These changes reduce computational bottlenecks during learning, allowing the method to train on terrain models at scales that the earlier approach could not feasibly handle.

Experiments cover synthetic and real terrain datasets. One reported example trains a model with roughly 70,000 parameters on a terrain containing 16 million nodes within hours. It answers distance queries with 1% relative error in at most 10 milliseconds per query. This example illustrates the central benefit: a small learned representation can provide fast approximate distance answers even when the underlying terrain graph is very large.
summary.tldr: A decoupled neural distance representation and two-stage training make fast approximate shortest-path queries feasible on terrain graphs with millions of nodes.

title: De-coupled NeuroGF for Shortest Path Distance Approximations on Large Terrain Graphs

abstract: Deep networks are prone to catastrophic forgetting during sequential task learning, i.e., losing the knowledge about old tasks upon learning new tasks. To this end, continual learning (CL) has emerged, whose existing methods focus mostly on regulating or protecting the parameters associated with the previous tasks. However, parameter protection is often impractical, since the size of parameters for storing the old-task knowledge increases linearly with the number of tasks, otherwise it is hard to preserve the parameters related to the old-task knowledge. In this work, we bring a dual opinion from neuroscience and physics to CL: in the whole networks, the pathways matter more than the parameters when concerning the knowledge acquired from the old tasks. Following this opinion, we propose a novel CL framework, learning without isolation (LwI), where model fusion is formulated as graph matching and the pathways occupied by the old tasks are protected without being isolated. Thanks to the sparsity of activation channels in a deep network, LwI can adaptively allocate available pathways for a new task, realizing pathway protection and addressing catastrophic forgetting in a parameter-effcient manner. Experiments on popular benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed LwI.

paragraphs: When a neural network learns tasks sequentially, learning a new task can erase knowledge needed for earlier ones. Many continual learning methods respond by protecting parameters associated with old tasks. The paper identifies a difficulty with this approach: preserving old knowledge can require parameter storage that grows with the task count, while limiting that storage makes protection harder.

Learning without Isolation, or LwI, instead emphasizes the pathways used to express learned knowledge. It formulates model fusion as graph matching and protects pathways occupied by earlier tasks without isolating them. Because activation channels are sparse, the framework can adaptively assign available pathways to a new task.

Experiments on popular benchmark datasets demonstrate the method's superiority in the evaluated settings. The proposed contribution is a parameter-efficient approach to addressing forgetting by preserving how information travels through the network. Its central design decision shifts protection toward task-relevant pathways, using sparse activation structure to make room for new learning while maintaining routes associated with previous tasks.
summary.tldr: LwI addresses continual-learning forgetting by protecting existing task pathways and adaptively allocating available pathways to new tasks.

title: Learning without Isolation: Pathway Protection for Continual Learning

abstract: Foundation models have revolutionized language modeling, while whether this success is replicated in scientific computing remains unexplored. We present OmniArch, the first prototype aiming at solving multi-scale and multi-physics scientific computing problems with physical alignment. We addressed all three challenges with one unified architecture. Its pre-training stage contains a Fourier Encoder-decoder fading out the disharmony across separated dimensions and a Transformer backbone integrating quantities through temporal dynamics, and the novel PDE-Aligner performs physics-informed fine-tuning under flexible conditions. As far as we know, we first conduct 1D-2D-3D united pre-training on the PDEBench, and it sets not only new performance benchmarks for 1D, 2D, and 3D PDEs but also demonstrates exceptional adaptability to new physics via in-context and zero-shot learning approaches, which supports realistic engineering applications and foresight physics discovery.

paragraphs: OmniArch explores whether a unified foundation-model approach can support scientific computing across multiple scales, physical systems, and spatial dimensions. The paper presents a prototype that combines shared pre-training with physics-informed adaptation, aiming to bring these requirements together in one architecture.

During pre-training, a Fourier encoder-decoder addresses differences across dimensions, while a Transformer backbone integrates quantities through their temporal dynamics. A separate PDE-Aligner provides physics-informed fine-tuning under flexible conditions. These components assign complementary roles to representing scientific data, learning its evolution, and adapting the model in accordance with physical information.

The authors report joint pre-training across one-, two-, and three-dimensional problems on PDEBench, describing it as a first to their knowledge. They report new performance benchmarks in all three dimensional settings and adaptability to new physics through in-context and zero-shot learning. The findings support the prototype’s ambition to share capabilities across scientific problems, with engineering applications and physics discovery presented as potential uses of that broader adaptability.
summary.tldr: OmniArch combines joint multidimensional PDE pre-training with physics-informed adaptation to support scientific computing across scales and physical systems.

title: OmniArch: Building Foundation Model for Scientific Computing

abstract: We study contextual bandits with general constraints, where a learner observes contexts and aims to maximize cumulative rewards while satisfying a wide range of general constraints. We introduce the Optimistic$^3$ framework, a novel learning and decision-making approach that integrates optimistic design into parameter learning, primal decision, and dual violation adaptation (i.e., triple-optimism), combined with an efficient primal-dual architecture. Optimistic$^3$ achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret and constraint violation for contextual bandits with general constraints. This framework not only outperforms the state-of-the-art results that achieve $\tilde{O}(T^{\frac{3}{4}})$ guarantees when Slater’s condition does not hold but also improves on previous results that achieve $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T}/\delta)$ when Slater’s condition holds ($\delta$ denotes the Slater’s condition parameter), offering a $O(1/\delta)$ improvement. Note this improvement is significant because $\delta$ can be arbitrarily small when constraints are particularly challenging. Moreover, we show that Optimistic$^3$ can be extended to classical multi-armed bandits with both stochastic and adversarial constraints, recovering the best-of-both-worlds guarantee established in the state-of-the-art works, but with significantly less computational overhead.

paragraphs: A constrained contextual-bandit learner observes context, chooses actions, and tries to accumulate reward while respecting constraints. This paper introduces Optimistic³, which applies optimistic design to three linked parts of that process: learning parameters, making the primary decision, and adapting the dual variables associated with constraint violations.

Within an efficient primal-dual architecture, the framework achieves regret and constraint-violation bounds that grow as the square root of the number of rounds, up to logarithmic factors. Without Slater’s condition, this improves on prior bounds growing with the three-quarter power. When that condition holds, it also removes a previous inverse dependence on the condition’s parameter, delta.

The delta improvement matters because the parameter can become arbitrarily small for difficult constraints, making the earlier bound much larger. The authors also extend the framework to classical multi-armed bandits with stochastic and adversarial constraints. That extension recovers established best-of-both-worlds guarantees with substantially less computational overhead, combining improved contextual-bandit bounds with a more efficient route to existing guarantees in another setting.
summary.tldr: Optimistic³ coordinates optimism across learning, decisions, and constraint adaptation to improve constrained-bandit guarantees and computational efficiency.

title: Triple-Optimistic Learning for Stochastic Contextual Bandits with General Constraints

abstract: The message-passing mechanism of graph convolutional networks (i.e., GCNs) enables label information to reach more unlabeled neighbors, thereby increasing the utilization of labels. However, the additional label information does not always contribute positively to the GCN. To address this issue, we propose a new two-step framework called ELU-GCN. In the first stage, ELU-GCN conducts graph learning to learn a new graph structure (i.e., ELU-graph), which allows the additional label information to positively influence the predictions of GCN. In the second stage, we design a new graph contrastive learning on the GCN framework for representation learning by exploring the consistency and mutually exclusive information between the learned ELU graph and the original graph. Moreover, we theoretically demonstrate that the proposed method can ensure the generalization ability of GCNs. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of our method.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks spread information between connected nodes, allowing labels to influence predictions for nearby unlabeled nodes. However, making more label information available does not always improve predictions. ELU-GCN addresses this problem by changing the graph through which information travels and then learning representations from both the modified and original structures.

The first stage learns an ELU graph intended to make the additional influence of labels beneficial. The second stage uses graph contrastive learning to examine information shared by the two graphs as well as information that is mutually exclusive between them. Both relationships contribute to representation learning, so the learned graph and the original graph provide distinct sources of training information.

The authors provide a theoretical result supporting the method’s ability to ensure generalization and report experimental superiority over the compared approaches. The central contribution is to treat the usefulness of propagated label information as a graph-learning problem. It couples that structural change with a representation-learning objective that explicitly considers how the two graph views agree and differ.
summary.tldr: ELU-GCN learns a graph that makes label propagation more useful, then combines it with the original graph through contrastive learning.

title: Enhancing the Influence of Labels on Unlabeled Nodes in Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: Utilizing the complex inter-variable causal relationships within multivariate time-series provides a promising avenue toward more robust and reliable multivariate time-series anomaly detection (MTSAD) but remains an underexplored area of research. This paper proposes Causality-Aware contrastive learning for RObust multivariate Time-Series (CAROTS), a novel MTSAD pipeline that incorporates the notion of causality into contrastive learning. CAROTS employs two data augmentors to obtain causality-preserving and -disturbing samples that serve as a wide range of normal variations and synthetic anomalies, respectively. With causality-preserving and -disturbing samples as positives and negatives, CAROTS performs contrastive learning to train an encoder whose latent space separates normal and abnormal samples based on causality. Moreover, CAROTS introduces a similarity-filtered one-class contrastive loss that encourages the contrastive learning process to gradually incorporate more semantically diverse samples with common causal relationships. Extensive experiments on five real-world and two synthetic datasets validate that the integration of causal relationships endows CAROTS with improved MTSAD capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/kimanki/CAROTS.

paragraphs: An unusual reading in a collection of time series can involve more than an unexpected value: it can also involve a change in how variables relate to one another. CAROTS builds an anomaly detector around this idea, using causal relationships between variables to shape what its learned representation treats as normal or abnormal.

The method creates two kinds of altered training samples. One preserves causal relationships and supplies varied examples of normal behavior; the other disturbs those relationships to produce synthetic anomalies. Contrastive learning then trains an encoder to distinguish these groups in its internal representation. This makes the distinction between preserved and disrupted relationships part of the training signal.

CAROTS also introduces a similarity-filtered loss that gradually admits more semantically diverse samples sharing causal relationships. This broadens the normal variations considered during learning. Experiments on five real-world and two synthetic datasets support improved anomaly detection from incorporating causal relationships. The findings suggest that how variables interact can provide useful detection information alongside their individual time-series patterns.
summary.tldr: CAROTS improves time-series anomaly detection by teaching an encoder to distinguish variations that preserve causal relationships from those that disrupt them.

title: Causality-Aware Contrastive Learning for Robust Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection

abstract: We propose a novel class of language models, Latent Thought Models (LTMs), which incorporate explicit latent thought vectors that follow an explicit prior model in latent space. These latent thought vectors guide the autoregressive generation of ground tokens through a Transformer decoder. Training employs a dual-rate optimization process within the classical variational Bayes framework: fast learning of local variational parameters for the posterior distribution of latent vectors (inference-time computation), and slow learning of global decoder parameters. Empirical studies reveal that LTMs possess additional scaling dimensions beyond traditional Large Language Models (LLMs), such as the number of iterations in inference-time computation and number of latent thought vectors. Higher sample efficiency can be achieved by increasing training compute per token, with further gains possible by trading model size for more inference steps. Designed based on these scaling properties, LTMs demonstrate superior sample and parameter efficiency compared to autoregressive models and discrete diffusion models. They significantly outperform these counterparts in validation perplexity and zero-shot language modeling tasks. Additionally, LTMs exhibit emergent few-shot in-context reasoning capabilities that scale with model size, and achieve competitive performance in conditional and unconditional text generation. The project page is available at https://deqiankong.github.io/blogs/ltm.

paragraphs: Latent Thought Models introduce explicit hidden vectors that guide a Transformer decoder’s token generation. These vectors follow a specified prior in latent space. The architecture adds a set of internal variables that can be refined through computation, giving the model ways to scale beyond changing the decoder’s parameter count.

Training uses variational Bayes with two learning rates: local parameters describing the posterior over latent vectors are updated quickly, while shared decoder parameters are learned slowly. The local updates provide the inference-time computation. Both the number of refinement iterations and the number of latent thought vectors become adjustable dimensions of the model.

Experiments find that spending more training computation per token can improve sample efficiency, with further gains possible by exchanging model size for additional inference steps. Models designed around these properties outperform the evaluated autoregressive and discrete diffusion models in validation perplexity and zero-shot language modeling, with better sample and parameter efficiency. The authors also report few-shot in-context reasoning that scales with model size and competitive conditional and unconditional text generation.
summary.tldr: Latent Thought Models refine hidden vectors through variational inference, adding computation-based scaling options that improve reported sample and parameter efficiency.

title: Latent Thought Models with Variational Bayes Inference-Time Computation

abstract: Spatially Resolved Transcriptomics (SRT) is a cutting-edge technique that captures the spatial context of cells within tissues, enabling the study of complex biological networks. Recent graph-based methods leverage both gene expression and spatial information to identify relevant spatial domains. However, these approaches fall short in obtaining meaningful spot representations, especially for spots near spatial domain boundaries, as they heavily emphasize adjacent spots that have minimal feature differences from an anchor node. To address this, we propose Spotscape, a novel framework that introduces the Similarity Telescope module to capture global relationships between multiple spots. Additionally, we propose a similarity scaling strategy to regulate the distances between intra- and inter-slice spots, facilitating effective multi-slice integration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of Spotscape in various downstream tasks, including single-slice and multi-slice scenarios.

paragraphs: Spatially resolved transcriptomics combines gene-expression measurements with information about where those measurements occur in tissue. Learning useful representations of these spatial spots helps identify tissue domains. The paper argues that existing graph-based approaches place too much emphasis on nearby spots with very similar features, making representations especially problematic near domain boundaries.

The proposed Spotscape framework introduces a Similarity Telescope module to capture relationships among spots at a global level. This expands the information available when representing a spot beyond the local relationships emphasized by previous methods. The authors also introduce similarity scaling to regulate distances among spots within a tissue slice and across different slices, supporting their integration into a shared analysis.

Experiments show improved performance on downstream tasks involving both single slices and multiple slices. These findings support the value of combining global relationships with explicit control of within-slice and across-slice similarity. The approach matters because a useful spatial representation must account for tissue-wide context while still allowing measurements from different slices to be brought together effectively.
summary.tldr: Spotscape uses global spot relationships and similarity scaling to improve spatial transcriptomics representations and integration across tissue slices.

title: Global Context-aware Representation Learning for Spatially Resolved Transcriptomics

abstract: Feature learning in neural networks is crucial for their expressive power and inductive biases, motivating various theoretical approaches. Some approaches describe network behavior after training through a change in kernel scale from initialization, resulting in a generalization power comparable to a Gaussian process. Conversely, in other approaches training results in the adaptation of the kernel to the data, involving directional changes to the kernel. The relationship and respective strengths of these two views have so far remained unresolved. This work presents a theoretical framework of multi-scale adaptive feature learning bridging these two views. Using methods from statistical mechanics, we derive analytical expressions for network output statistics which are valid across scaling regimes and in the continuum between them. A systematic expansion of the network’s probability distribution reveals that mean-field scaling requires only a saddle-point approximation, while standard scaling necessitates additional correction terms. Remarkably, we find across regimes that kernel adaptation can be reduced to an effective kernel rescaling when predicting the mean network output in the special case of a linear network. However, for linear and non-linear networks, the multi-scale adaptive approach captures directional feature learning effects, providing richer insights than what could be recovered from a rescaling of the kernel alone.

paragraphs: Theories of neural-network feature learning describe training in different ways. Some characterize it through a change in the overall scale of a kernel, while others describe directional changes that adapt the kernel to the data. This paper develops a framework connecting these views and examining what each captures about the trained network.

Using statistical-mechanics methods, the authors derive expressions for network output statistics across scaling regimes and the continuum between them. A systematic expansion shows that mean-field scaling needs only a saddle-point approximation, whereas standard scaling requires additional corrections. This provides a shared analytical treatment while preserving meaningful differences between the regimes.

For linear networks, predicting the mean output admits a notable simplification: kernel adaptation can be represented by an effective rescaling across the regimes studied. That result applies to this particular prediction target and network case. The fuller framework captures directional feature-learning effects in both linear and nonlinear networks, revealing structure that kernel rescaling alone cannot recover.
summary.tldr: A multi-scale theory connects kernel rescaling and directional adaptation while identifying feature-learning effects that rescaling alone misses.

title: From Kernels to Features: A Multi-Scale Adaptive Theory of Feature Learning

abstract: Driven by steady progress in deep generative modeling, simulation-based inference (SBI) has emerged as the workhorse for inferring the parameters of stochastic simulators. However, recent work has demonstrated that model misspecification can harm SBI’s reliability, preventing its adoption in important applications where only misspecified simulators are available. This work introduces robust posterior estimation (RoPE), a framework that overcomes model misspecification with a small real-world calibration set of ground truth parameter measurements. We formalize the misspecification gap as the solution of an optimal transport (OT) problem between learned representations of real-world and simulated observations, allowing RoPE to learn a model of the misspecification without placing additional assumptions on its nature. RoPE shows how the calibration set and OT together offer a controllable balance between calibrated uncertainty and informative inference even under severely misspecified simulators. Results on four synthetic tasks and two real-world problems with ground-truth labels demonstrate that RoPE outperforms baselines and consistently returns informative and calibrated credible intervals.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference estimates the parameters behind observations using a simulator. Its reliability can suffer when that simulator does not adequately represent the real process. Robust posterior estimation, or RoPE, addresses this mismatch using a small calibration set of real observations with ground-truth parameter measurements.

RoPE represents the difference between simulated and real observations as an optimal transport problem between learned representations. This lets it learn a model of the mismatch without imposing additional assumptions about the mismatch's nature. The calibration examples provide real-world grounding, while the transport formulation connects them to the simulator-based inference process.

Together, these components offer a controllable balance between informative estimates and calibrated uncertainty, including when simulators are severely misspecified. On four synthetic tasks and two real-world problems with ground-truth labels, RoPE outperforms the evaluated baselines and consistently produces informative, calibrated credible intervals. The contribution is therefore both a way to account for simulator error and a way to retain useful uncertainty estimates, with real parameter measurements supplying the necessary calibration evidence.
summary.tldr: RoPE uses real-world calibration measurements and optimal transport to improve parameter inference when simulators are misspecified.

title: Addressing Misspecification in Simulation-based Inference through Data-driven Calibration

abstract: Human decision-making in cognitive tasks and daily life exhibits considerable variability, shaped by factors such as task difficulty, individual preferences, and personal experiences. Understanding this variability across individuals is essential for uncovering the perceptual and decision-making mechanisms that humans rely on when faced with uncertainty and ambiguity. We propose a systematic Boundary Alignment Manipulation (BAM) framework for studying human perceptual variability through image generation. BAM combines perceptual boundary sampling in ANNs and human behavioral experiments to systematically investigate this phenomenon. Our perceptual boundary sampling algorithm generates stimuli along ANN perceptual boundaries that intrinsically induce significant perceptual variability. The efficacy of these stimuli is empirically validated through large-scale behavioral experiments involving 246 participants across 116,715 trials, culminating in the variMNIST dataset containing 19,943 systematically annotated images. Through personalized model alignment and adversarial generation, we establish a reliable method for simultaneously predicting and manipulating the divergent perceptual decisions of pairs of participants. This work bridges the gap between computational models and human individual difference research, providing new tools for personalized perception analysis. Code and data for this work are publicly available.

paragraphs: People can interpret the same ambiguous image differently, reflecting differences in experience, preferences, and task difficulty. This paper introduces Boundary Alignment Manipulation, or BAM, to study that variability systematically. It combines image generation using artificial neural networks with behavioral experiments involving human participants.

BAM samples images along neural-network perceptual boundaries, producing stimuli that induce substantial variation in human judgments. The authors validate these stimuli in experiments with 246 participants across 116,715 trials. The resulting variMNIST dataset contains 19,943 systematically annotated images, grounding the computational approach in a substantial collection of observed perceptual decisions.

The framework also aligns models to individuals and uses adversarial generation to predict and manipulate differences between pairs of participants' decisions. The authors report a reliable method for doing both within their study. The contribution is a way to make perceptual disagreement an experimental target: generated images reveal where individuals diverge, and personalized models help investigate and influence those divergences. This connects neural-network boundaries with tools for analyzing individual differences in human perception.
summary.tldr: BAM generates ambiguous images at neural-network perceptual boundaries to study, predict, and manipulate differences in human judgments.

title: Synthesizing Images on Perceptual Boundaries of ANNs for Uncovering and Manipulating Human Perceptual Variability

abstract: We study private prediction where differential privacy is achieved by adding noise to the outputs of a non-private model. Existing methods rely on noise proportional to the global sensitivity of the model, often resulting in sub-optimal privacy-utility trade-offs compared to private training. We introduce a novel approach for computing dataset-specific upper bounds on prediction sensitivity by leveraging convex relaxation and bound propagation techniques. By combining these bounds with the smooth sensitivity mechanism, we significantly improve the privacy analysis of private prediction compared to global sensitivity-based approaches. Experimental results across real-world datasets in medical image classification and natural language processing demonstrate that our sensitivity bounds are can be orders of magnitude tighter than global sensitivity. Our approach provides a strong basis for the development of novel privacy preserving technologies.

paragraphs: This paper studies protecting predictions by adding noise to the outputs of a model trained without privacy protection. How much noise is needed depends on prediction sensitivity: how much a prediction could change when the training data change. Existing approaches use global sensitivity, which can lead to unfavorable privacy–utility tradeoffs compared with private training.

The authors develop dataset-specific upper bounds on prediction sensitivity using convex relaxation and bound propagation. Rather than relying only on a global bound, their analysis accounts for the particular dataset. They then combine these bounds with the smooth sensitivity mechanism, providing the privacy machinery needed to use this more tailored sensitivity information.

Experiments on real-world medical image classification and natural-language-processing datasets show that the resulting bounds can be orders of magnitude tighter than global-sensitivity bounds. The reported advance is therefore a substantially sharper analysis of private prediction. It supports improving the amount of noise justified by sensitivity analysis, while the stated empirical comparison concerns bound tightness rather than a universal advantage over private training.
summary.tldr: Dataset-specific sensitivity bounds combined with smooth sensitivity sharpen privacy analysis for noisy predictions from non-private models.

title: Certification for Differentially Private Prediction in Gradient-Based Training

abstract: Various data modalities are common in real-world applications. (e.g., EHR, medical images and clinical notes in healthcare). Thus, it is essential to develop multimodal learning methods to aggregate information from multiple modalities. The main challenge is appropriately aligning and fusing the representations of different modalities into a joint distribution. Existing methods mainly rely on concatenation or the Kronecker product, oversimplifying interactions structure between modalities and indicating a need to model more complex interactions. Additionally, the joint distribution of latent representations with higher-order interactions is underexplored. Copula is a powerful statistical structure in modelling the interactions between variables, as it bridges the joint distribution and marginal distributions of multiple variables. In this paper, we propose a novel copula modelling-driven multimodal learning framework, which focuses on learning the joint distribution of various modalities to capture the complex interaction among them. The key idea is interpreting the copula model as a tool to align the marginal distributions of the modalities efficiently. By assuming a Gaussian mixture distribution for each modality and a copula model on the joint distribution, our model can also generate accurate representations for missing modalities. Extensive experiments on public MIMIC datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our model over other competitors. The code is anonymously available at https://github.com/HKU-MedAI/CMCM.

paragraphs: Combining information from different modalities requires representing how those sources relate to one another. In healthcare, for example, records, images, and notes provide different views of a case. This paper focuses on learning their joint distribution, arguing that common combination operations can oversimplify the interactions among their representations.

The proposed framework uses a copula, a statistical structure connecting the individual distributions of variables to their joint distribution. Here, the individual distributions describe the modalities, and the copula models their relationships. Treating this structure as an alignment mechanism gives the framework a way to capture complex interactions rather than relying only on concatenating representations or taking their Kronecker product.

The model assumes a Gaussian mixture distribution for each modality and a copula structure for their joint distribution. Under this design, it can also generate representations for missing modalities. Experiments on public MIMIC datasets report better performance than the competing methods evaluated. The findings support explicitly modeling cross-modal dependencies as a useful approach to both combining available information and representing an absent modality.
summary.tldr: A copula-based framework models relationships among modalities and can generate missing-modality representations under its distributional assumptions.

title: Cross-Modal Alignment via Variational Copula Modelling

abstract: Reward design in reinforcement learning and optimal control is challenging. Preference-based alignment addresses this by enabling agents to learn rewards from ranked trajectory pairs provided by humans. However, existing methods often struggle from poor robustness to unknown false human preferences. In this work, we propose a robust and efficient reward alignment method based on a novel and geometrically interpretable perspective: hypothesis space batched cutting. Our method iteratively refines the reward hypothesis space through “cuts” based on batches of human preferences. Within each batch, human preferences, queried based on disagreement, are grouped using a voting function to determine the appropriate cut, ensuring a bounded human query complexity. To handle unknown erroneous preferences, we introduce a conservative cutting method within each batch, preventing erroneous human preferences from making overly aggressive cuts to the hypothesis space. This guarantees provable robustness against false preferences, while eliminating the need to explicitly identify them. We evaluate our method in a model predictive control setting across diverse tasks. The results demonstrate that our framework achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art methods in error-free settings while significantly outperforming existing methods when handling a high percentage of erroneous human preferences.

paragraphs: Learning rewards from human comparisons avoids requiring people to write a reward function directly. However, mistaken preferences can mislead the learning process. This paper represents reward alignment as progressively narrowing a space of candidate reward functions, with each batch of human judgments providing evidence for which candidates to remove.

The method queries preferences based on disagreement and combines judgments within a batch using a voting function. Those votes determine a geometric cut to the reward hypothesis space, with bounded human query complexity. To handle unknown errors, the authors introduce conservative cuts that prevent mistaken preferences from eliminating too much of the space. The method does not need to explicitly identify which judgments are false.

The paper provides a robustness guarantee against false preferences and evaluates the approach in model predictive control across diverse tasks. Results are comparable or superior to state-of-the-art methods with error-free feedback, and substantially better when many preferences are erroneous. The findings support conservative aggregation as a way to make preference-based reward learning more reliable.
summary.tldr: Conservative cuts based on batches of human preferences narrow candidate reward functions while providing robustness to erroneous feedback.

title: Robust Reward Alignment via Hypothesis Space Batch Cutting

abstract: The Influence Function (IF) is a widely used technique for assessing the impact of individual training samples on model predictions. However, existing IF methods often fail to provide reliable influence estimates in deep neural networks, particularly when applied to noisy training data. This issue does not stem from inaccuracies in parameter change estimation, which has been the primary focus of prior research, but rather from deficiencies in loss change estimation, specifically due to the sharpness of validation risk. In this work, we establish a theoretical connection between influence estimation error, validation set risk, and its sharpness, underscoring the importance of flat validation minima for accurate influence estimation. Furthermore, we introduce a novel estimation form of Influence Function specifically designed for flat validation minima. Experimental results across various tasks validate the superiority of our approach.

paragraphs: Influence functions estimate how individual training examples affect a model’s predictions. The paper investigates why these estimates can be unreliable for deep neural networks, especially with noisy training data. Its diagnosis focuses on estimating the resulting change in validation loss, rather than on estimating how model parameters change.

The authors connect influence-estimation error theoretically to validation risk and its sharpness. Sharpness describes how sensitively the validation loss responds to nearby parameter changes. This connection highlights why a good estimate of parameter movement can still lead to an unreliable estimate of its consequences for validation performance. Flatter validation minima become important for accurate influence estimation.

The paper introduces a new influence-function estimation form designed for flat validation minima. Experiments across several tasks report advantages over existing approaches. The contribution shifts attention to the geometry of the validation objective and its role in translating parameter changes into loss changes. That distinction matters because improving one stage of an influence calculation does not necessarily resolve error introduced by the next.
summary.tldr: The paper links unreliable influence estimates to sharp validation loss and proposes an estimator designed for flat validation minima.

title: Towards Robust Influence Functions with Flat Validation Minima

abstract: Existing prompt-based approaches have demonstrated impressive performance in continual learning, leveraging pre-trained large-scale models for classification tasks; however, the tight coupling between foreground-background information and the coupled attention between prompts and image-text tokens present significant challenges in incremental medical object detection tasks, due to the conceptual gap between medical and natural domains. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the iDPA framework, which comprises two main components: 1) Instance-level Prompt Generation (IPG), which decouples fine-grained instance-level knowledge from images and generates prompts that focus on dense predictions, and 2) Decoupled Prompt Attention (DPA), which decouples the original prompt attention, enabling a more direct and efficient transfer of prompt information while reducing memory usage and mitigating catastrophic forgetting. We collect 13 clinical, cross-modal, multi-organ, and multi-category datasets, referred to as ODinM-13, and experiments demonstrate that iDPA outperforms existing SOTA methods, with FAP improvements of f 5.44%, 4.83%, 12.88%, and 4.59% in full data, 1-shot, 10-shot, and 50-shot settings, respectively.

paragraphs: Incremental medical object detection requires models to keep learning detection tasks while retaining earlier knowledge. The paper identifies challenges in adapting prompt-based continual learning from classification: foreground and background information are tightly coupled, and prompts interact with image-text tokens through coupled attention. Differences between medical and natural imagery make this transfer especially difficult.

iDPA addresses these issues with two components. Instance-level Prompt Generation extracts fine-grained knowledge about individual objects and creates prompts suited to dense prediction. Decoupled Prompt Attention changes how prompt information enters the model, supporting more direct transfer while reducing memory use and mitigating catastrophic forgetting, the loss of previously learned capabilities.

The authors assemble ODinM-13 from 13 clinical datasets spanning modalities, organs, and categories. They report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in full-data and 1-shot, 10-shot, and 50-shot settings. These evaluations support the usefulness of designing prompts around individual detection instances and revising their attention interactions when extending pretrained models to incremental medical detection.
summary.tldr: iDPA combines instance-focused prompts with decoupled attention to improve incremental medical object detection and mitigate forgetting.

title: iDPA: Instance Decoupled Prompt Attention for Incremental Medical Object Detection

abstract: Normalizing Flows (NFs) are likelihood-based models for continuous inputs. They have demonstrated promising results on both density estimation and generative modeling tasks, but have received relatively little attention in recent years. In this work, we demonstrate that NFs are more powerful than previously believed. We present TarFlow: a simple and scalable architecture that enables highly performant NF models. TarFlow can be thought of as a Transformer-based variant of Masked Autoregressive Flows (MAFs): it consists of a stack of autoregressive Transformer blocks on image patches, alternating the autoregression direction between layers. TarFlow is straightforward to train end-to-end, and capable of directly modeling and generating pixels. We also propose three key techniques to improve sample quality: Gaussian noise augmentation during training, a post training denoising procedure, and an effective guidance method for both class-conditional and unconditional settings. Putting these together, TarFlow sets new state-of-the-art results on likelihood estimation for images, beating the previous best methods by a large margin, and generates samples with quality and diversity comparable to diffusion models, for the first time with a stand-alone NF model. We make our code available at https://github.com/apple/ml-tarflow.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows model probabilities for continuous data and can also generate samples. This paper revisits their capabilities through TarFlow, a scalable architecture that directly models and generates image pixels. The work asks how far a standalone flow model can go with a modern architecture and techniques aimed at sample quality.

TarFlow uses a stack of autoregressive Transformer blocks operating on image patches, with the autoregressive direction alternating between layers. It is trained end to end. Three additional techniques improve generation: Gaussian noise augmentation during training, denoising after training, and guidance that works in both class-conditional and unconditional settings.

The combined system reports new state-of-the-art image likelihood estimates, exceeding previous methods by a large margin. It also produces samples whose quality and diversity are comparable to diffusion models. These findings address both probability modeling and generation, supporting the claim that normalizing flows have greater practical capability than previously recognized. The reported comparison is achieved with a standalone normalizing-flow model equipped with the proposed architecture and sampling improvements.
summary.tldr: TarFlow combines autoregressive Transformers with sample-quality improvements to achieve strong image likelihoods and generation comparable to diffusion models.

title: Normalizing Flows are Capable Generative Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as scalable judges in pairwise evaluation, but they remain prone to miscalibration and biases. We propose SCOPE (Selective Conformal Optimized Pairwise Evaluation), a framework that calibrates an acceptance threshold so that, under exchangeability, the error rate among non-abstained judgments is at most a user-specified level $\alpha$. To supply SCOPE with a bias-neutral uncertainty signal, we introduce Bidirectional Preference Entropy (BPE), which queries the judge under both response positions and converts the order-averaged preference probability into an entropy-based score. Across various pairwise judging benchmarks, BPE outperforms standard confidence proxies in calibration and discrimination, while SCOPE consistently satisfies the target risk bound (empirical FDR $\approx 0.097$–$0.099$ at $\alpha=0.10$) and retains substantial coverage. Compared to vanilla baselines, SCOPE accepts up to $2.4\times$ more judgments under the same risk constraint, demonstrating that BPE enables reliable and high-coverage LLM-based evaluation.

paragraphs: Language models can compare two responses at scale, but their judgments may be biased or poorly calibrated. SCOPE addresses this by deciding which judgments to accept and which to abstain from. It calibrates an acceptance threshold so that, under exchangeability, the error rate among accepted judgments stays at or below a user-chosen level.

Its uncertainty signal is Bidirectional Preference Entropy. The judge evaluates both response orderings, and the method averages the resulting preference probabilities before converting them into an entropy score. This is designed to neutralize position bias in the uncertainty estimate, giving the acceptance procedure a more informative signal than ordinary confidence proxies.

Across pairwise-judging benchmarks, this signal improves calibration and discrimination. At a target error level of 0.10, SCOPE reports empirical false discovery rates around 0.097–0.099 while retaining substantial coverage. It accepts up to 2.4 times as many judgments as vanilla baselines under the same risk constraint. The result links calibrated abstention to a larger usable set of judgments, with exchangeability remaining the stated assumption.
summary.tldr: SCOPE combines order-averaged uncertainty with calibrated abstention to control accepted LLM-judgment errors under exchangeability.

title: SCOPE: Selective Conformal Optimized Pairwise LLM Judging

abstract: We propose CLoVE (Clustering of Loss Vector Embeddings), a novel algorithm for Clustered Federated Learning (CFL). In CFL, clients are naturally grouped into clusters based on their data distribution. However, identifying these clusters is challenging, as client assignments are unknown. CLoVE utilizes client embeddings derived from model losses on client data, and leverages the insight that clients in the same cluster share similar loss values, while those in different clusters exhibit distinct loss patterns. Based on these embeddings, CLoVE is able to iteratively identify and separate clients from different clusters and optimize cluster-specific models through federated aggregation. Key advantages of CLoVE over existing CFL algorithms are (1) its simplicity, (2) its applicability to both supervised and unsupervised settings, and (3) the fact that it eliminates the need for near-optimal model initialization, which makes it more robust and better suited for real-world applications. We establish theoretical convergence bounds, showing that CLoVE can recover clusters accurately with high probability in a single round and converges exponentially fast to optimal models in a linear setting. Our comprehensive experiments comparing with a variety of both CFL and generic Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) algorithms on different types of datasets and an extensive array of non-IID settings demonstrate that CLoVE achieves highly accurate cluster recovery in just a few rounds of training, along with state-of-the-art model accuracy, across a variety of both supervised and unsupervised PFL tasks.

paragraphs: Federated learning clients can have different data distributions, making a single shared model an imperfect fit. Clustered federated learning instead learns models for groups of similar clients, but those groups are initially unknown. CLoVE identifies them using patterns in the losses that models incur on client data.

The method turns these losses into client embeddings. Its guiding observation is that clients from the same cluster have similar loss patterns, while clients from different clusters tend to differ. CLoVE repeatedly uses those embeddings to separate groups and updates each group’s model through federated aggregation. It supports supervised and unsupervised tasks without requiring a nearly optimal initial model.

Across experiments with varied data heterogeneity, CLoVE recovers clusters accurately within a few training rounds and reports state-of-the-art model accuracy. These results support loss patterns as a useful basis for learning both client groupings and personalized models.
summary.tldr: CLoVE groups federated clients by their model-loss patterns and learns cluster-specific models without near-optimal initialization.

title: CLoVE: Personalized Federated Learning through Clustering of Loss Vector Embeddings

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly capable, but the mechanisms of their thinking and decision-making processes remain unclear. Chain-of-thoughts (CoTs) have been commonly utilized to externalize LLMs’ thinking, but this strategy fails to accurately reflect LLMs’ thinking process. Techniques based on LLMs’ hidden representations provide an inner perspective to improve the monitorability of their latent thinking. However, previous methods only try to develop external modules instead of making LLMs themselves easier to monitor. In this paper, we propose a novel method, TELLME, improving the transparency of LLMs and helping monitors identify unsuitable and sensitive behaviors. Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of TELLME on detoxification tasks, where LLMs achieve consistent improvement among multimodal test sets, distinct architectures, and varying parameter scales. We further analyze TELLME’s improvement on LLMs’ generalization ability from both optimal transport theory and empirical perspectives.

paragraphs: TELLME addresses the difficulty of monitoring what language models are doing internally. Written chains of thought are often used as a window into model reasoning, but the paper argues that they do not accurately reflect the underlying process. Hidden representations offer another source of information for identifying unsuitable or sensitive behavior.

The authors shift attention from building external monitoring modules to making the language model itself easier to monitor. TELLME is designed to improve model transparency so that monitors can better identify problematic behavior. The central contribution is therefore a change to the model being observed, alongside the broader use of its internal representations for monitoring.

The reported evaluation focuses on detoxification. Improvements are consistent across multimodal test sets, different architectures, and varying model sizes. The authors also examine improved generalization through both optimal transport theory and empirical analysis. These results support enhancing monitorability within the model as a useful approach to behavior detection, with evidence spanning several tested model and evaluation settings.
summary.tldr: TELLME makes language models easier to monitor and reports consistent improvements on detoxification evaluations.

title: Beyond External Monitors: Enhancing Transparency of Large Language Models for Easier Monitoring

abstract: Human ratings are central to learning and inference across several application domains, but they are also subject to inter-rater biases and judgment errors. Quantifying the uncertainty of these human ratings would require repeated measurements, which are expensive and rarely available at scale. We propose a Bayesian graphical model to estimate the instance-level and item-level uncertainty of (subjective) human ratings by leveraging auxiliary (objective) data. Our model learns a shared latent content representation that explains factors common to both the human rating and auxiliary data and a latent uncertainty variable that captures fluctuations in the human assessments via a data-conditioned prior. We develop a scalable amortized variational inference procedure that uses modality-appropriate neural encoders and decoders to represent the posterior factors. Experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that our framework can accurately recover the latent uncertainty under targeted ablations and stress tests. We further demonstrate our approach on a real-world dataset of paired functional MRI scans and behavioral testing for autism, thus highlighting the need for uncertainty quantification.

paragraphs: Human ratings mix information about the subject being assessed with variation in how people judge it. Repeated assessments can help reveal that uncertainty, but collecting them is expensive. This paper proposes a Bayesian model that instead uses paired objective measurements to estimate uncertainty at both the instance and item levels.

The model separates two hidden components. A shared content representation captures factors that explain both the human assessment and the auxiliary measurements. A separate uncertainty variable accounts for fluctuations in the assessment, with its prior distribution conditioned on the data. Neural encoders and decoders tailored to each modality support an amortized variational inference procedure, making estimation scalable.

Synthetic experiments show that the method can recover latent uncertainty under the tested ablations and stress conditions. The authors also apply it to paired functional MRI and behavioral assessments for autism. That application illustrates the relevance of quantifying uncertainty in subjective measurements; the stated recovery evidence comes from the synthetic experiments, where the hidden uncertainty can be checked.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model uses auxiliary objective measurements to estimate uncertainty in human ratings without relying on repeated assessments.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Quantify the Uncertainty of Human Ratings in a Single-Instance Multimodal Framework

abstract: Causal Abstraction (CA) theory provides a principled framework for relating causal models that describe the same system at different levels of granularity while ensuring interventional consistency between them. Recent methods for learning CAs, however, assume fixed and well-specified exogenous distributions, leaving them vulnerable to environmental shifts and model misspecification. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing the first class of distributionally robust CAs and their associated learning algorithms. The latter cast robust causal abstraction learning as a constrained min-max optimization problem with Wasserstein ambiguity sets. We provide theoretical guarantees for both empirical and Gaussian environments, enabling principled selection of ambiguity-set radii and establish quantitative guarantees on worst-case abstraction error. Furthermore, we present empirical evidence across different problems and CA learning methods, demonstrating our framework’s robustness not only to environmental shifts but also to structural and intervention mapping misspecification.

paragraphs: Causal abstraction connects detailed and coarse descriptions of the same system while seeking agreement about the effects of interventions. Existing learning methods assume that the distributions of external influences are fixed and correctly specified. This paper addresses the resulting vulnerability when environments change or those distributional assumptions are inaccurate.

The authors introduce distributionally robust causal abstractions and algorithms for learning them. Their formulation uses constrained min-max optimization: it seeks an abstraction while accounting for unfavorable distributions within a specified set. These Wasserstein ambiguity sets describe the distributional alternatives considered during learning, making the range of uncertainty part of the optimization problem.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for empirical and Gaussian environments, including guidance for choosing ambiguity-set radii and quantitative bounds on worst-case abstraction error. Experiments across different problems and abstraction-learning methods show robustness to environmental changes. They also provide evidence of robustness when causal structure or intervention mappings are misspecified. The contribution therefore extends causal abstraction learning from a single assumed environment toward explicitly accounting for uncertainty in the environments being related.
summary.tldr: This framework learns causal abstractions against distributional uncertainty, with worst-case error guarantees and empirical robustness to several forms of misspecification.

title: Distributionally Robust Causal Abstractions

abstract: Diagnosing complex diseases is inherently a sequential and iterative medical investigation process, in which a clinician strategically requests multiple rounds of diagnostic tests to differentiate among similar diseases until reaching a definitive diagnosis. Although large language models show great potential as clinical assistants, they often struggle to navigate this complex interactive process, suffering from premature diagnostic closure. Furthermore, optimizing LLMs for such multi-round environments is frequently hindered by the challenge of reward sparsity and hacking. In this paper, we introduce $\textbf{CompDiag-Bench}$, a benchmark that formalizes diagnosis as a sequential decision-making process where a clinician must strategically request diagnostic tests from a dynamic environment in order to reach a definitive diagnosis. To address this task, we propose $\texttt{Salus}$, a multi-agent framework that decouples diagnostic reasoning into three specialized functional roles: a Differential Reasoner, a Strategic Controller, and a Workup Proposer. $\texttt{Salus}$ is optimized via multi-agent reinforcement learning employing structured rewards to calibrate strategic diagnostic behavior. Specifically, we leverage an LLM-as-a-Judge reward mechanism to provide dense, semantically-grounded feedback, designed to penalize premature closure and incentivize accurate differential diagnoses. Experimental results show that our model, $\texttt{Salus-7B}$, attains state-of-the-art Top-1 accuracy of $83.64%$ on complex cases, outperforming DeepSeek-V3.2 ($71.38%$) and achieving performance on par with GPT-5.2 ($80.30%$).

paragraphs: Complex diagnosis involves repeated decisions about which tests can distinguish between plausible diseases. Language models can struggle with this interactive process by settling on a diagnosis too early. The paper introduces CompDiag-Bench, which frames diagnosis as sequential decision-making in a dynamic environment where the model requests tests before reaching a final diagnosis.

Salus divides this process among three specialized roles: a Differential Reasoner, a Strategic Controller, and a Workup Proposer. Multi-agent reinforcement learning trains their diagnostic behavior using structured rewards. On the evaluated complex cases, Salus-7B achieves 83.64% Top-1 accuracy, compared with 71.38% for DeepSeek-V3.2 and 80.30% for GPT-5.2. The authors describe its performance as state of the art and on par with GPT-5.2. The result supports coordinating diagnostic reasoning and test selection through specialized roles in the benchmark’s sequential investigation setting.
summary.tldr: Salus trains specialized agents to coordinate differential diagnosis and sequential testing, reaching 83.64% Top-1 accuracy on evaluated complex cases.

title: Salus: Strategic Diagnostic Testing for Complex Diagnosis via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Category-level 6D object pose estimation is typically formulated as a multi-category joint learning problem with fully shared model parameters. However, pronounced geometric heterogeneity across categories entangles incompatible optimization signals in shared modules, resulting in gradient conflicts and negative transfer during training. To address this challenge, we first introduce gradient-based diagnostics to quantify module-level cross-category contention. Building on results of diagnostics, we propose DecomPose, a difficulty-aware decomposition framework that mitigates optimization contention via: (1) difficulty-aware gradient decoupling, which groups categories using a data-driven difficulty proxy and routes each instance to a group-specific correspondence branch to isolate incompatible updates; and (2) stability-driven asymmetric branching, which assigns higher-capacity branches to structurally simple categories as stable optimization anchors while constraining complex categories with lightweight branches to suppress noisy updates and alleviate negative transfer. Extensive experiments on REAL275, CAMERA25, and HouseCat6D demonstrate that DecomPose effectively reduces cross-category optimization contention and delivers superior pose estimation performance across multiple benchmarks.

To address this challenge, we first introduce gradient-based diagnostics to quantify module-level cross-category contention. Building on results of diagnostics, we propose DecomPose, a difficulty-aware decomposition framework that mitigates optimization contention via: (1) difficulty-aware gradient decoupling, which groups categories using a data-driven difficulty proxy and routes each instance to a group-specific correspondence branch to isolate incompatible updates; and (2) stability-driven asymmetric branching, which assigns higher-capacity branches to structurally simple categories as stable optimization anchors while constraining complex categories with lightweight branches to suppress noisy updates and alleviate negative transfer. Extensive experiments on REAL275, CAMERA25, and HouseCat6D demonstrate that DecomPose effectively reduces cross-category optimization contention and delivers superior pose estimation performance across multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: Category-level 6D pose estimation learns to recover object position and orientation across object categories. The paper identifies a problem with fully shared models: categories with very different geometry can push shared parameters in incompatible directions. These conflicting training updates can cause negative transfer, where learning across categories harms performance.

DecomPose begins with gradient-based diagnostics that locate this conflict within model modules. It then groups categories using a data-derived measure of difficulty and routes examples through separate correspondence branches. This separates incompatible updates. Its capacity allocation is deliberately asymmetric: structurally simpler categories receive larger branches to act as stable training anchors, while complex categories receive lightweight branches to limit noisy updates.

Experiments on REAL275, CAMERA25, and HouseCat6D report reduced conflict between categories and improved pose estimation across the benchmarks. The contribution connects an observed training problem to a targeted architectural change. In particular, the results support assigning branch capacity according to optimization stability, rather than assuming that geometrically more complex categories should always receive more capacity.
summary.tldr: DecomPose separates conflicting category updates and allocates branch capacity by training stability to improve object pose estimation.

title: DecomPose: Disentangling Cross-Category Optimization Contention for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation

abstract: Despite their remarkable general capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with the precise grounding required for embodied task planning. To bridge this gap, neuro-symbolic approaches have emerged, leveraging action languages like BC+ for their formal expressiveness and reasoning flexibility. However, prior methods that naively couple LLMs with BC+ typically depend on one-shot program generation, which is brittle in dynamic environments and prone to sequential omission and causal inconsistency. To address these limitations, we propose DecoVer, a Decompose-and-Verify neuro-symbolic framework that systematically adapts BC+ to embodied task planning. Specifically, DecoVer employs a cascading decomposition strategy to partition complex knowledge into hierarchical subspaces and integrates a dual verification mechanism for syntactic and executable correctness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoVer consistently outperforms LLM-based baselines across the majority of evaluation metrics, achieving a 12.9% success rate gain over the highly capable Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and a 60.9% improvement over GPT-5.1 on logically complex test cases.
