paragraphs: DecoVer addresses the precision needed when language models plan tasks for embodied agents. A plan must connect actions to their conditions and consequences, and missing a step or breaking a causal relationship can make it unusable. The paper identifies these problems in approaches that generate an entire BC+ program in one attempt.

The framework combines language-model capabilities with the formal action language BC+. It first decomposes complex knowledge into hierarchical subspaces through a cascading process. It then applies two forms of verification: one checks syntactic correctness, and the other checks whether the resulting representation is executable. This gives program construction explicit structure and correctness checks.

Across the reported experiments, DecoVer outperforms language-model baselines on most evaluation metrics. The abstract reports a 12.9% success-rate gain over Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and a 60.9% improvement over GPT-5.1 on logically complex cases. These findings support decomposition and verification as useful components for translating broad language-model knowledge into more dependable embodied plans, particularly where sequential completeness and causal consistency matter.
summary.tldr: DecoVer improves embodied task planning by decomposing BC+ knowledge representations and verifying both their syntax and executability.

title: DecoVer: A Decompose-and-Verify Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Embodied Task Planning with BC+

abstract: Web-based agents powered by large language models are increasingly used for tasks such as email management or professional networking. Their reliance on dynamic web content, however, makes them vulnerable to prompt injection attacks: adversarial instructions hidden in interface elements that persuade the agent to divert from its original task. We introduce the Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark (TRAP), a benchmark for studying how persuasion techniques misguide autonomous web agents on realistic tasks. Across six frontier models, agents are susceptible to prompt injection in 25% of tasks on average (13% for GPT-5 to 43% for DeepSeek-R1), with small interface or contextual changes often doubling success rates and revealing systemic, psychologically driven vulnerabilities in web-based agents. We also provide a modular social-engineering injection framework with controlled experiments on high-fidelity website clones, allowing for further benchmark expansion.
originalAbstract: Web-based agents powered by large language models are increasingly used for tasks such as email management or professional networking. Their reliance on dynamic web content, however, makes them vulnerable to prompt injection attacks: adversarial instructions hidden in interface elements that persuade the agent to divert from its original task. We introduce the Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark (TRAP), a benchmark for studying how persuasion techniques misguide autonomous web agents on realistic tasks. Across six frontier models, agents are susceptible to prompt injection in 25% of tasks on average (13% for GPT-5 to 43% for DeepSeek-R1), with small interface or contextual changes often doubling success rates and revealing systemic, psychologically driven vulnerabilities in web-based agents. We also provide a modular social-engineering injection framework with controlled experiments on high-fidelity website clones, allowing for further benchmark expansion.

paragraphs: Web agents read changing interface content while carrying out requests such as managing email or professional networking. That content can contain adversarial instructions intended to pull the agent away from its assigned task. TRAP is a benchmark for studying how persuasive instructions embedded in web interfaces cause this kind of task redirection.

The benchmark uses controlled experiments on high-fidelity website clones. It also includes a modular social-engineering injection framework, allowing researchers to vary persuasive content and extend the benchmark. This setup makes it possible to examine how interface and contextual changes affect whether an agent follows an attacker’s instructions.

Across six frontier models, prompt injections succeed on an average of 25% of evaluated tasks, ranging from 13% for GPT-5 to 43% for DeepSeek-R1. Small changes to the interface or context often double attack success rates. These results show substantial sensitivity to how adversarial content is presented in the tested environments. The benchmark provides a way to investigate that sensitivity systematically, including the psychologically driven persuasion mechanisms highlighted by the authors.
summary.tldr: TRAP benchmarks persuasive prompt injections against web agents, finding successful task redirection in 25% of evaluated tasks on average across six models.

title: It’s a TRAP! Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark for Web Agents

abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently achieved strong results in text generation. However, their multi-step sampling leads to slow inference, limiting practical use. To address this, we extend Inverse Distillation, a technique originally developed to accelerate continuous diffusion models, to the discrete setting. Nonetheless, this extension introduces both theoretical and practical challenges. From a theoretical perspective, the inverse distillation objective lacks uniqueness guarantees, which may lead to suboptimal solutions. From a practical standpoint, backpropagation in the discrete space is non-trivial and often unstable. To overcome these challenges, we first provide a theoretical result demonstrating that our inverse formulation admits a unique solution, thereby ensuring valid optimization. We then introduce gradient-stable relaxations to support effective training. As a result, experiments on multiple DLMs show that our method, Inverse-distilled Diffusion Language Models (IDLM), reduces the number of inference steps by $4 \times$-$64 \times$, while preserving the teacher model’s generation quality. We provide the code, model checkpoints, and video tutorials on the project page: https://david-cripto.com/idlm

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text through multiple sampling steps, which can make inference slow. IDLM adapts inverse distillation, previously developed for continuous diffusion, to discrete language generation. Its purpose is to preserve the quality of an existing teacher model while reducing the number of steps needed to produce text.

Moving the method into a discrete setting creates two distinct problems. The inverse objective needs a uniqueness guarantee to avoid ambiguity in its solution, and propagating training gradients through discrete operations can be unstable. The authors provide a theoretical result establishing a unique solution for their inverse formulation. They also introduce relaxations designed to make gradient-based training stable.

Experiments across multiple diffusion language models report reductions of 4 to 64 times in inference step counts while preserving teacher generation quality. These results concern the number of sampling steps, rather than establishing the same numerical improvement in elapsed runtime. The work connects a theoretical foundation for discrete inverse distillation with a practical training method for accelerating existing diffusion language models.
summary.tldr: IDLM extends inverse distillation to discrete text generation, cutting sampling steps by 4–64 times while preserving teacher quality in reported experiments.

title: IDLM: Inverse-distilled Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Synthetic data becomes crucial for large language model training, but its effectiveness is highly inconsistent. We provide an information-theoretic account of this inconsistency: synthetic data improves a model only when the generation-training loop is information-open, i.e., shaped by external signals (verifiers, environments, or rubrics) that inject task-relevant information beyond the model’s current distribution. When the loop is information-closed (relying on the model’s own outputs without such signals), the data processing inequality ensures that task-relevant information can only decrease, making collapse a predicted outcome. Among information-open pipelines, both efficiency and generalization hinge on the meta-level of supervision: a coarser signal such as binary correctness treats all acceptable outputs as equivalent, so the behavior it teaches is not tied to any particular domain or surface form and generalizes naturally across tasks and domains. These observations lead to a guiding thesis: learning preferentially converges to the most information-efficient signal component available, which accelerates learning when that component is the intended one, but causes reward hacking when a spurious pattern happens to be simpler.

paragraphs: This paper asks why synthetic training data can help language models in some settings yet fail in others. Its information-theoretic account centers on whether the generation-and-training process receives task-relevant information beyond the model’s existing distribution. Verifiers, environments, and rubrics are examples of external signals that can make this process information-open.

The authors argue that such openness is necessary for improvement. In an information-closed loop that relies on the model’s own outputs, they invoke the data processing inequality to explain why task-relevant information can only decrease, making collapse a predicted outcome. Openness is a condition for useful information to enter, rather than a guarantee that any synthetic-data pipeline will succeed.

The paper also argues that the level of supervision affects efficiency and transfer. A coarse correctness signal groups acceptable outputs together, encouraging behavior less tied to particular wording or domains. Its guiding thesis is that learning favors the most information-efficient available signal. This can accelerate intended learning, but it can also produce reward hacking when a simpler, spurious pattern is available.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that useful synthetic-data learning requires external task information and depends on which supervision signals are easiest to learn.

title: An Information-Theoretic Criterion for Efficient Data Synthesis

abstract: Embodied agents replan frequently to recover from execution drift, partial observability, and coordination hazards, but each LLM-based replanning call can consume an accumulated textual context that grows over time and across agents. Once this context becomes large, replanning latency develops heavy tails and can miss real-time deadlines even when task success remains high, a failure mode that is hard to detect from average latency or success alone. We present BRACE, a controller that formulates replanning as a budgeted control loop by deciding whether to replan, selecting a replanning mode, and allocating an explicit token budget and latency service-level objective (SLO) while accounting for optional efficiency modules. As a reusable component, we introduce E-RECAP, a cost-aware progressive token pruning method that predicts token utility and prunes replanning contexts across transformer layers while preserving critical head and tail tokens. Across Meta Habitat, RoboFactory, and AirSim, BRACE with E-RECAP reduces replanning-call token counts by 62–92% and SLO violation rates from 85.5–100.0% to 4.7–50.0% in settings where task success is already saturated. In a harder RoboFactory setting where open-loop, frozen-plan, and No BRACE all fail, BRACE + E-RECAP reaches 80.0% success with 4.6% SLO violations, demonstrating that tail-aware per-call budgeting is effective across embodied platforms.

paragraphs: Embodied agents replan to handle execution drift, incomplete observations, and coordination problems. As accumulated textual context grows, some replanning calls become exceptionally slow and miss real-time deadlines, even when overall task success remains high. The paper focuses on these latency tails, which averages and success rates alone can conceal.

In a harder RoboFactory setting where the reported comparison methods fail, it reaches 80.0% success with 4.6% violations. These findings show that explicit per-call budgeting can improve timing reliability and, in the harder setting, task completion.
summary.tldr: BRACE budgets each replanning call and prunes context to reduce deadline violations while supporting embodied-agent task success.

title: When Replanning Becomes the Bottleneck: Budgeted Replanning for Embodied Agents

abstract: Adapting pre-trained vision models using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) remains challenging, as it aims to achieve performance comparable to full fine-tuning using a minimal number of trainable parameters. When applied to complex dense prediction tasks, existing methods exhibit limitations, including input-agnostic modeling and redundant cross-layer representations. To this end, we propose ParaX, a new adapter-style method featuring a simple mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture. Specifically, we introduce shared expert centers, where each expert is a trainable parameter matrix. During a feedforward pass, each ParaX module in the network dynamically generates weight matrices tailored for the current module via a simple dynamic parameter routing mechanism, which selectively aggregates parameter matrices in the corresponding expert center. Dynamic weight matrices in ParaX modules facilitate low-rank adaptation in an input-dependent manner, thus generating more customized and powerful feature representations. Moreover, since ParaX modules across multiple network layers share the same expert center, they improve feature diversity by promoting implicit cross-layer feature interaction. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the superiority of ParaX across diverse visual recognition tasks. Code is publicly released at: https://github.com/LMMMEng/ParaX.

paragraphs: ParaX adapts pretrained vision models while training relatively few parameters. The paper targets two weaknesses of existing efficient adaptation methods: their behavior can be insufficiently responsive to the input, and different layers can learn redundant representations. These issues are particularly relevant to complex dense prediction tasks.

The method treats trainable parameter matrices as experts in a shared collection called an expert center. During a forward pass, each adapter module selectively combines matrices from its corresponding center to construct weights suited to that module and the current input. These dynamically generated weights provide input-dependent low-rank adaptation. Multiple layers share an expert center, creating implicit interaction between their representations and encouraging feature diversity.

Experiments across diverse visual recognition tasks report superior performance for ParaX. The distinctive contribution is that routing determines the parameters used for adaptation, enabling customization without separately learning a complete set of weights for every layer and input. The reported findings support dynamic parameter assembly and cross-layer sharing as useful mechanisms for efficient vision-model adaptation.
summary.tldr: ParaX assembles input-dependent adapter weights from shared parameter experts to improve efficient adaptation of vision models.

title: Parameters as Experts: Adapting Vision Models with Dynamic Parameter Routing

abstract: Time series reasoning demands both the perception of complex dynamics and logical depth. However, existing LLM-based approaches exhibit two limitations: they often treat time series merely as text or images, failing to capture the patterns like trends and seasonalities needed to answer specific questions; and when trained on a mix of simple and complex tasks, simpler objectives often dominate the learning process, hindering the development of deep reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose the Pattern-Aware Alignment and Balanced Reasoning model (PATRA), introducing a pattern-aware mechanism that extracts trend and seasonality patterns from time series to achieve deep alignment. Furthermore, we design a task-aware balanced reward to harmonize learning across tasks of varying difficulty, incentivizing the generation of coherent Chains of Thought. Extensive experiments show that PATRA outperforms strong baselines across diverse Time Series Question Answering (TSQA) tasks, demonstrating superior cross-modal understanding and reasoning capability.

paragraphs: PATRA addresses two obstacles in answering questions about time series. A language model needs to recognize temporal patterns relevant to the question, and it needs sufficient reasoning ability to use them. Treating measurements only as text or images can obscure trends and seasonal behavior, while mixed-difficulty training can allow easier objectives to dominate.

The model introduces a pattern-aware mechanism that extracts trends and seasonality from time series to improve alignment with the language-based task. It also uses a task-aware balanced reward to harmonize learning across difficulty levels. This reward encourages coherent chains of thought while addressing the imbalance that can prevent more demanding reasoning tasks from receiving effective training.

Experiments report that PATRA outperforms strong baselines across diverse time-series question-answering tasks, with better cross-modal understanding and reasoning. The approach matters because it addresses both the representation of temporal evidence and the incentives used to learn from it. Its reported gains support combining explicit temporal-pattern extraction with rewards that account for differences in task difficulty.
summary.tldr: PATRA combines trend and seasonality extraction with difficulty-aware rewards to improve time-series question answering.

title: PATRA: Pattern-Aware Alignment and Balanced Reasoning for Time Series Question Answering

abstract: Autoregressive models generate sequences monotonically, where any sampled token, even if erroneous or sub-optimal, becomes a permanent condition for all subsequent steps. This structural limitation means that autoregressive models cannot revisit or revise earlier decisions, i.e., a capability essential for complex generation tasks where exploration and correction are necessary. To this end, we propose N-MARS, a Non-Monotonic AutoregRessive Sequence modeling framework that enables models to generate, evaluate, and revise tokens within a single forward pass, effectively allowing exploration before commitment. We operationalize this framework through a learned erase token that retracts the previous token, enabling on-the-fly revision within standard autoregressive decoding. To train the model, we introduce a sequence augmentation method that constructs error-correction trajectories from model-generated deviations paired with ground-truth references. We then propose masked supervised fine-tuning (mSFT) that exposes the model to errors as context for learning when to revise, without optimizing their likelihood. Finally, we refine the model with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) that incentivizes judicious usage, i.e., rewarding effective corrections while penalizing unsuccessful ones. We conduct comprehensive theoretical and empirical analysis to validate the effectiveness of N-MARS, demonstrating a robust foundation for non-monotonic sequence modeling.

paragraphs: Standard autoregressive generation makes each sampled token part of the context for later tokens, including tokens that are mistaken or suboptimal. N-MARS changes this commitment structure by allowing generation to retract a previous token. Its goal is to let a model explore and correct decisions as decoding proceeds.

The mechanism is a learned erase token integrated into standard autoregressive decoding. Training uses augmented sequences that combine model-generated deviations with ground-truth references to form error-correction trajectories. Masked supervised fine-tuning presents erroneous tokens as context for learning when to revise, while avoiding training the model to increase the likelihood of those errors.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical analyses supporting the framework’s effectiveness. The central contribution is a training and decoding scheme that treats correction as a learned action within sequence generation. The erase operation specifically retracts the preceding token, giving the model an explicit way to reconsider its latest decision.
summary.tldr: N-MARS teaches autoregressive models to retract previous tokens through a learned erase action and correction-focused training.

title: Non-Monotonic Autoregressive Sequence Model

abstract: Time series reasoning tasks often start with a natural language question and require targeted analysis of a time series. Evidence may span the full series or appear in a few short intervals, so the model must decide what to inspect. Most existing approaches encode the entire time series into a fixed representation before inference, regardless of relevance. We introduce ARTIST, which formulates time-series reasoning as a sequential decision problem. ARTIST interleaves reasoning with adaptive temporal segment selection. It adopts a controller-reasoner architecture and uses reinforcement learning to train the controller role to select informative segments and the reasoner role to generate segment-conditioned reasoning traces and final answers. During inference, the model actively acquires task-relevant information instead of relying on a static summary of the full sequence. We use a novel hierarchical policy optimization approach for post-training that allows the model to excel in both segment selection and question-answering behavior. We evaluate ARTIST on six time-series reasoning benchmarks and compare it with large language models, vision-language models, and prior time-series reasoning systems. ARTIST improves average accuracy by 6.46 absolute percentage points over the strongest baseline. The largest gains appear on rare event localization and multi-segment reasoning tasks. Supervised fine-tuning improves performance, and reinforcement learning provides additional gains by optimizing question-adaptive segment selection, showing that selective data use drives effective time-series reasoning.

paragraphs: Answering a question about a time series requires deciding where the relevant evidence lies. Some questions need the full sequence, while others depend on brief events or several separated intervals. ARTIST addresses this selection problem directly, instead of requiring every question to use a fixed representation of the entire series.

The method alternates between choosing temporal segments and reasoning about their contents. A controller selects informative intervals, and a reasoner uses those intervals to develop reasoning traces and answers. Reinforcement learning trains both roles, with a hierarchical policy optimization procedure coordinating segment selection and question answering. This makes information gathering part of the reasoning process itself.

Its largest gains concern rare-event localization and reasoning across multiple segments. Supervised fine-tuning helps, while reinforcement learning adds further improvements through question-dependent selection. These findings support the value of learning what to inspect alongside learning how to answer.
summary.tldr: ARTIST improves time-series question answering by learning to select relevant intervals as it reasons.

title: Adaptive Time Series Reasoning via Segment Selection

abstract: Dataset Distillation aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one while maintaining predictive performance. We show that as different demographic groups exhibit distinct predictive patterns, the distillation process struggles to simultaneously preserve informative signals for all subgroups, regardless of whether group sizes are mildly or severely imbalanced. Consequently, models trained on distilled data can experience substantial performance drops for certain subgroups, leading to fairness gaps. Crucially, these gaps do not disappear by merely correcting group imbalance, since they stem from fundamental mismatches in subgroup predictive patterns rather than from sample-size disparities alone. We therefore formally analyze the interaction between these two sources of bias and cast the solution as identifying a group-imbalance-agnostic barycenter of the predictive information that induces similar representations across all subgroups. By distilling toward this shared aggregate representation, we show that group fairness concerns can be reduced. Our approach is compatible with existing distillation methods, and empirical results show that it substantially reduces bias introduced by dataset distillation. Code is available at https://github.com/mhmoslemi/COBRA.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses a large training set into a small synthetic one while trying to preserve predictive performance. This paper shows that the compression can preserve useful information unevenly across demographic groups. When groups have different predictive patterns, a distilled dataset can lose signals that matter to particular subgroups and create substantial performance gaps.

The authors distinguish two sources of this problem: unequal group sizes and mismatched subgroup predictive patterns. Correcting the first does not eliminate the second, so balancing the dataset alone cannot resolve the demonstrated fairness gaps. Their formal analysis examines how these sources interact and motivates a shared target for the information retained during distillation.

That target is a barycenter: an aggregate representation of predictive information designed to be independent of group imbalance and to induce similar representations across subgroups. Distilling toward this shared representation can reduce fairness concerns while remaining compatible with existing distillation methods. Empirical results show substantial reductions in bias introduced by compression, supporting the importance of aligning predictive information as well as considering group counts.
summary.tldr: Aligning subgroup predictive information during dataset distillation reduces fairness gaps that balancing group sizes alone does not remove.

title: Fair Dataset Distillation via Cross-Group Barycenter Alignment

abstract: Leveraging future observation modeling to facilitate action generation presents a promising avenue for enhancing the capabilities of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing approaches struggle to strike a balance between maintaining efficient, predictable future representations and preserving sufficient fine-grained information to guide precise action generation. To address this limitation, we propose WoG (World Guidance), a framework that maps future observations into compact conditions by injecting them into the action inference pipeline. The VLA is then trained to simultaneously predict these compressed conditions alongside future actions, thereby achieving effective world modeling within the condition space for action inference. We demonstrate that modeling and predicting this condition space not only facilitates fine-grained action generation but also exhibits superior generalization capabilities. Moreover, it learns effectively from substantial human manipulation videos. Extensive experiments across both simulation and real-world environments validate that WoG significantly outperforms existing methods based on future prediction. Project page is available at: https://selen-suyue.github.io/WoGNet/.

paragraphs: Predicting future observations can help vision-language-action models choose actions, but the prediction target must balance compactness with useful detail. A representation that is easy to predict may omit information needed for precise movement. World Guidance, or WoG, addresses this trade-off by representing future observations as compact conditions used within action inference.

The framework maps future observations into those conditions and injects them into the action-generation pipeline. The model is trained to predict both the compressed conditions and future actions. This places world modeling in the same condition space that guides action generation, linking what the model predicts about the future with how it determines its actions.

The authors report that modeling this space supports fine-grained action generation and stronger generalization. They also find that the approach learns effectively from substantial human manipulation video data. Experiments in simulation and real-world environments show significant improvements over existing future-prediction methods. The findings support compact, action-relevant future representations as a useful way to combine world modeling with action prediction.
summary.tldr: WoG predicts compact future-observation conditions alongside actions, improving fine-grained action generation and generalization in simulated and real-world evaluations.

title: World Guidance: World Modeling in Condition Space for Action Generation

abstract: Unifying the complementary strengths of diverse Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) into a single efficient model is highly desirable but challenged by the negative transfer inherent in monolithic distillation. To address these feature conflicts, we introduce PRISM, a novel dual-stream Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that synergizes VFMs via modular specialization. We propose a two-stage paradigm: (1) expertise deconstruction, where a teacher-conditional router guides experts to specialize in distinct representational subspaces to mitigate interference, followed by (2) dynamic recomposition, where the router learns to assemble these experts into tailored computational pathways for downstream tasks. Experiments on PASCAL-Context and NYUD-v2 show that PRISM establishes a new state of the art, validating that sparse, emergent specialization is a scalable approach for integrating diverse visual knowledge.

paragraphs: Different vision foundation models contain complementary knowledge, but combining them into one model can create interference between their representations. This paper addresses negative transfer during distillation, where learning from multiple teachers can make their strengths harder to preserve within a single undifferentiated model.

PRISM uses a dual-stream mixture-of-experts architecture to organize that knowledge into specialized modules. In its first stage, a router conditioned on the teacher directs experts toward distinct representational subspaces. This expertise deconstruction is intended to reduce conflicts during learning. In the second stage, the router learns to recombine those experts into computational pathways suited to downstream tasks.

The design makes specialization and task-dependent assembly central to integrating visual knowledge. Experiments on PASCAL-Context and NYUD-v2 report new state-of-the-art results. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that sparse, emergent specialization offers a scalable approach to combining diverse vision models, while addressing the feature conflicts that make monolithic distillation difficult.
summary.tldr: PRISM combines knowledge from multiple vision models by training specialized experts and dynamically assembling them for downstream tasks.

title: PRISM: Synergizing Vision Foundation Models via Self-organized Expert Specialization

abstract: As large language models grow increasingly capable, concerns about their safe deployment have intensified. While numerous alignment strategies aim to restrict harmful behavior, these defenses can still be circumvented through carefully designed adversarial prompts. In this work, we introduce a theoretical framework that formalizes a game between an attacker hiding its intent via compositional skills and a defender. Within this framework, we design a theoretical best-response attack strategy and show that it is closely related to many existing adversarial prompting methods. We further analyze the resulting game, characterize its equilibria, and reveal inherent advantages for the attacker. Drawing on our theoretical analysis, we also derive a provably optimal defense strategy. Empirically, we evaluate a practical instantiation of the theoretically optimal attack and observe stronger performance relative to existing adversarial prompting approaches in diverse settings encompassing different LLMs and benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies adversarial prompting as a strategic interaction between an attacker and a defender. The attacker conceals its intent through combinations of skills, while the defender tries to prevent harmful behavior. Formalizing that interaction makes it possible to analyze how the two sides respond to each other, rather than treating each attack prompt as an isolated trick.

Within the proposed game, the authors construct a theoretical best-response attack and connect it to several existing prompting methods. They also characterize the game's equilibria and identify advantages available to the attacker. The same analysis produces a provably optimal defense strategy. That optimality belongs to the theoretical framework being analyzed; it is not a claim that the defense defeats every possible real-world attack.

The empirical part implements a practical version of the theoretically optimal attack and reports stronger performance than existing adversarial prompting approaches across different models and benchmarks. Together, the theory and experiments offer a common explanation for related attack methods and a principled basis for studying defensive responses.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic framework explains attacks that conceal intent through skill composition and derives optimal attack and defense strategies within that framework.

title: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Attacks on Large Language Models via Compositional Skills

abstract: Agent memory systems must accommodate continuously growing information while supporting efficient, context-aware retrieval for downstream tasks. Abstraction is essential for scaling agent memory, yet it often comes at the cost of specificity, obscuring the fine-grained details required for effective reasoning. We introduce Memora, a harmonic memory representation that structurally balances abstraction and specificity. Memora organizes information via its primary abstractions that index concrete memory values and consolidate related updates into unified memory entries, while cue anchors expand retrieval access across diverse aspects of the memory and connect related memories. Building on this structure, we employ a retrieval policy that actively exploits these memory connections to retrieve relevant information beyond direct semantic similarity. Theoretically, we show that standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Knowledge Graph (KG)-based memory systems emerge as special cases of our framework. Empirically, Memora establishes a new state-of-the-art on the LoCoMo and LongMemEval benchmarks, demonstrating better retrieval relevance and reasoning effectiveness as memory scales.

paragraphs: Agent memory must grow without making relevant information difficult to retrieve. Abstracting information helps manage that growth, but can hide details needed for later reasoning. Memora proposes a memory representation that combines broad organization with access to specific stored values, addressing this tension within the structure of memory itself.

Its primary abstractions index concrete memory values and consolidate related updates into unified entries. Cue anchors provide additional ways to access a memory through its different aspects and connect it to related memories. A retrieval policy actively follows these connections, allowing retrieval to reach useful information beyond items that directly resemble the query in semantic space.

The authors theoretically show that standard retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge-graph memory systems arise as special cases of their framework. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, Memora achieves reported state-of-the-art results, with better retrieval relevance and reasoning effectiveness as memory scales. The findings support combining abstraction, preserved detail, and connected retrieval rather than relying on a single route from a query to a stored memory.
summary.tldr: Memora organizes detailed memories under abstractions and connected retrieval cues to improve retrieval and reasoning as agent memory grows.

title: Memora: A Harmonic Memory Representation Balancing Abstraction and Specificity

abstract: Humans are born with vision-based 4D spatial-temporal intelligence, which enables us to perceive and reason about the evolution of 3D space over time from purely visual inputs. Despite its importance, this capability remains a significant bottleneck for current multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To tackle this challenge, we introduce MLLM-4D, a comprehensive framework designed to bridge the gaps in training data curation and model post-training for spatiotemporal understanding and reasoning. On the data front, we develop a cost-efficient data curation pipeline that repurposes existing stereo video datasets into high-quality 4D spatiotemporal instructional data. This results in the MLLM4D-2M and MLLM4D-R1-30k datasets for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT), alongside MLLM4D-Bench for comprehensive evaluation. Regarding model training, our post-training strategy establishes a foundational 4D understanding via SFT and further catalyzes 4D reasoning capabilities by employing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with specialized Spatiotemporal Chain of Thought (ST-CoT) prompting and Spatiotemporal reward functions (ST-reward) without involving the modification of architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MLLM-4D achieves state-of-the-art spatial-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities from purely 2D RGB inputs. Project page: https://github.com/GVCLab/MLLM-4D.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene over time requires reasoning about how three-dimensional space changes from one moment to the next. MLLM-4D targets this capability in multimodal language models using visual inputs. It addresses both the supply of suitable instructional data and the post-training process used to teach spatial and temporal reasoning.

The data pipeline repurposes existing stereo video datasets into instructions about space and time. It produces MLLM4D-2M for supervised fine-tuning, MLLM4D-R1-30k for reinforcement fine-tuning, and MLLM4D-Bench for evaluation. Reusing stereo video provides a cost-efficient route to constructing training material for a capability that the paper identifies as a bottleneck.

Training first establishes foundational understanding through supervised fine-tuning. A second stage uses Group Relative Policy Optimization with specialized spatiotemporal chain-of-thought prompts and rewards to develop reasoning further. This process does not require architectural modifications. Experiments report state-of-the-art spatial-temporal understanding and reasoning from purely 2D RGB inputs, supporting the value of combining targeted data curation with specialized post-training for reasoning about 3D scenes over time.
summary.tldr: MLLM-4D combines curated video instruction data and specialized post-training to improve reasoning about 3D space over time from RGB inputs.

title: MLLM-4D: Towards Visual-based Spatial-Temporal Intelligence

abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) has recently emerged as a promising approach for learning compressed and discrete representations for graph-structured data. However, a fundamental challenge, i.e., codebook collapse, remains underexplored in the graph domain, significantly limiting the expressiveness and generalization of graph tokens. In this paper, we present an empirical study and observe that codebook collapse consistently occurs when training VQ jointly with Graph Neural Networks under graph reconstruction tasks, even with mitigation strategies proposed in vision or language domains. Moreover, we provide a diagnosis of collapse from data and optimization perspectives, showing that collapse is associated with graph data properties such as feature redundancy and connectivity density, and is further reinforced by the training dynamics of deterministic hard assignment. To address these issues, we propose RGVQ, a novel framework that integrates graph topology and feature similarity as explicit regularization signals to enhance codebook utilization and promote token diversity. RGVQ introduces soft assignments via Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization, ensuring that all codewords receive gradient updates. In addition, RGVQ incorporates a structure-aware contrastive regularization to penalize assigning the same token to dissimilar node pairs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RGVQ substantially improves codebook utilization and consistently boosts the performance of state-of-the-art graph VQ backbones across multiple downstream tasks, enabling more expressive and transferable graph token representations.

paragraphs: Vector quantization compresses graph representations into discrete tokens chosen from a codebook. Its usefulness suffers when training collapses onto a small subset of available codewords. The paper empirically finds this collapse when graph neural networks and quantization are trained jointly for graph reconstruction, including when existing mitigation techniques from vision or language are applied.

The diagnosis connects collapse with feature redundancy, connectivity density, and training dynamics driven by deterministic hard assignment. RGVQ responds by using graph structure and feature similarity as explicit regularizers. Gumbel-Softmax soft assignments give all codewords gradient updates, while a structure-aware contrastive term penalizes assigning the same token to dissimilar node pairs.

Experiments show substantially improved codebook utilization and consistent downstream performance gains for state-of-the-art graph quantization backbones. These findings indicate that the graph itself supplies useful signals for preserving token diversity. The approach makes the discrete representation more expressive and transferable by addressing both how codewords receive training and which nodes should share them.
summary.tldr: RGVQ uses graph structure, feature similarity, and soft assignments to reduce codebook collapse and improve discrete graph representations.

title: Graph is a Natural Regularization: Revisiting Vector Quantization for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Differentiable optimization studies how to embed a mathematical program as a differentiable layer in machine learning pipelines. However, existing approaches typically rely on implicit differentiation, involving expensive Hessian computation while differentiating through optimality conditions. To address this challenge, we formulate the differentiable optimization problem as a bilevel optimization instance. We construct a new active-set Lagrangian as a proxy to compute an $\epsilon$-approximate hypergradient using only near-constant $O(\log (1/\epsilon))$ first-order information. We also show that applying this efficient hypergradient oracle to constrained bilevel optimization improves the overall gradient complexity to $\tilde{O}(\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ to reach a $(\delta, \epsilon)$-Goldstein stationary point. We implement our method FFOLayer, as a drop-in Python library compatible with existing differentiable optimization solvers. Our algorithm shows significantly faster computation with similar convergence compared to other existing solvers. The source code is available at https://github.com/GT-KOALA/FFOLayer.

paragraphs: A differentiable optimization layer lets a machine learning system use the solution of a mathematical optimization problem as part of its computation. Training then requires tracking how that solution changes when its inputs change. Existing methods commonly do this through implicit differentiation, which can require expensive second-order information involving Hessians.

This paper recasts the task as bilevel optimization: one optimization problem sits inside another. It constructs an active-set Lagrangian proxy to estimate the hypergradient, the gradient needed to train through the inner problem. The estimate uses only first-order information, with a requirement that grows logarithmically as the requested approximation becomes more accurate.

The authors also show that this gradient estimator improves the theoretical gradient complexity of constrained bilevel optimization for reaching a specified Goldstein stationarity criterion. Their implementation, FFOLayer, is a Python library designed to work with existing differentiable optimization solvers. Reported experiments show substantially faster computation with similar convergence, connecting the theoretical reduction in derivative costs to practical training efficiency.
summary.tldr: FFOLayer trains through optimization problems using first-order gradient estimates, reducing computation while retaining similar reported convergence.

title: A Fully First-Order Layer for Differentiable Optimization

abstract: Accurate weather forecast reporting enables individuals and communities to better plan daily activities, agricultural operations, and transportation. However, the current reporting process primarily relies on manual analysis of multi-source data, which often leads to information overload and reduced efficiency. With the rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), leveraging data-driven models to analyze and generate reports in the weather forecasting domain remains largely underexplored. In this work, we propose the Weather Forecasting Report (WFR) task and construct the first instruction-tuning dataset for this task, named WSInstruct, which covers 31 cities in America and 8 weather aspects. Based on this corpus, we develop the first model, WeatherSyn, specialized in generating weather forecast reports. Evaluation across multiple metrics on our dataset shows that WeatherSyn consistently outperforms leading closed-source MLLMs, particularly on structurally complex weather aspects. We further analyze its performance across diverse geographic regions and weather aspects. WeatherSyn demonstrates strong transferability across different regions, highlighting its zero-shot generalization capability. WeatherSyn offers valuable insight for developing MLLMs specialized in weather report generation.

This paper defines weather forecasting report generation as a task for multimodal language models. Its focus is generating reports from weather information, addressing the analysis and communication work involved in reporting.

The authors construct WSInstruct, an instruction-tuning dataset covering 31 cities in America and eight weather aspects. They use it to develop WeatherSyn, a model specialized for the reporting task. This pairing of task-specific data and instruction tuning provides a concrete foundation for studying automated weather-report generation.

On their dataset, WeatherSyn consistently outperforms leading closed-source multimodal models across multiple metrics, with particularly strong results for structurally complex weather aspects. The authors also analyze variation across regions and aspects, reporting strong regional transfer and zero-shot generalization. These findings support specialization for this reporting setting and suggest that learned reporting capabilities can transfer geographically. The comparative performance claims are grounded in evaluation on the authors' dataset.
summary.tldr: WeatherSyn uses specialized instruction tuning to generate weather reports, outperforming leading closed-source models on the authors' dataset.

title: WeatherSyn: An Instruction Tuning MLLM For Weather Forecasting Report Generation

abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates inference for (M)LLMs, yet a training-decoding discrepancy persists: while existing methods optimize single greedy trajectories, decoding involves verifying and ranking multiple sampled draft paths. We propose Variational Speculative Decoding (VSD), formulating draft training as variational inference over latent proposals (draft paths). VSD maximizes the marginal probability of target-model acceptance, yielding an ELBO that promotes high-quality latent proposals while minimizing divergence from the target distribution. To enhance quality and reduce variance, we incorporate a path-level utility and optimize via an Expectation-Maximization procedure. The E-step draws MCMC samples from an oracle-filtered posterior, while the M-step maximizes weighted likelihood using Adaptive Rejection Weighting (ARW) and Confidence-Aware Regularization (CAR). Theoretical analysis confirms that VSD increases expected acceptance length and speedup. Extensive experiments across LLMs and MLLMs show that VSD achieves up to a 9.58% speedup over EAGLE-3 and 8.80% over ViSpec, significantly improving decoding efficiency.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds generation by having a draft model propose token sequences for a target model to verify. This paper identifies a mismatch: draft training often optimizes a single greedy trajectory, while decoding verifies and ranks multiple sampled paths. Variational Speculative Decoding trains around the probability that proposed sequences will be accepted.

VSD treats draft paths as latent proposals and derives a variational lower-bound objective that rewards useful proposals while reducing divergence from the target distribution. It adds a path-level utility and uses expectation-maximization. The expectation step samples an oracle-filtered posterior using MCMC; the maximization step fits weighted likelihood with adaptive rejection weighting and confidence-aware regularization.

The theoretical analysis establishes increases in expected acceptance length and speedup. Experiments across language and multimodal language models report speedups of up to 9.58% over EAGLE-3 and 8.80% over ViSpec. These are maximum reported improvements. The central contribution is aligning draft training with sequence acceptance, the behavior that directly determines how much speculative decoding can accelerate generation.
summary.tldr: VSD trains speculative draft models for sequence acceptance and reports up to 9.58% speedup over EAGLE-3 and 8.80% over ViSpec.

title: Variational Speculative Decoding: Rethinking Draft Training from Token Likelihood to Sequence Acceptance

abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning has advanced large language models (LLMs) to reason through long chain-of-thought trajectories while interleaving external tool use. Existing approaches assume a fixed inventory of tools, which limits the adaptability of LLM agents to new or evolving toolsets. We present AutoTool, a training framework that equips LLM agents with dynamic tool-selection capabilities throughout their reasoning trajectories. AutoTool employs a dual-phase optimization pipeline: (i) SFT and RL-based trajectory stabilization for coherent reasoning, and (ii) KL-regularized Plackett–Luce Ranking to refine consistent multi-step tool selection. We further build a 200k dataset with explicit tool-selection rationales across 1,000+ tools and 100+ tasks spanning mathematics, science, code generation, and multimodal reasoning. Across ten diverse benchmarks, we train two base models, Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, with AutoTool. With fewer parameters, AutoTool consistently outperforms advanced LLM agents and tool-integration methods, yielding average gains of 6.4% in math & science reasoning, 4.5% in search-based QA, 7.7% in code generation, and 6.9% in multimodal understanding. In addition, AutoTool exhibits stronger generalization by dynamically leveraging unseen tools from evolving toolsets during inference.

paragraphs: Language-model agents often learn to reason with a fixed collection of external tools. That setup makes adaptation harder when tools change or unfamiliar ones become available. AutoTool trains agents to choose tools dynamically throughout a reasoning process, treating tool selection as a repeated decision that must remain consistent across multiple steps.

Training has two phases. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning first stabilize reasoning trajectories. A regularized ranking objective then refines tool choices. The authors also construct 200,000 examples containing explicit explanations for tool selections, covering more than 1,000 tools and over 100 tasks in mathematics, science, programming, and multimodal reasoning.

Across ten benchmarks, AutoTool-trained Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B models outperform the compared agents and integration methods despite using fewer parameters. Reported average gains range from 4.5% for search-based question answering to 7.7% for code generation. The models also use previously unseen tools during inference, supporting the claim that training can improve adaptability to evolving tool collections.
summary.tldr: AutoTool trains language-model agents to select tools throughout reasoning and reports stronger performance and generalization to unseen tools.

title: AutoTool: Dynamic Tool Selection and Integration for Agentic Reasoning

abstract: In this position paper, we enumerate a number of problems with the current peer-review process based on extensive empirical evidence. We argue for two structural reforms: (1) separating publication from presentation via a four-step process that first evaluates correctness, publishes all sound papers, then uses community-based ratings to select presentations; and (2) offering parallel anonymous and non-anonymous review tracks, where the non-anonymous track releases all review data publicly to increase accountability and generate valuable research datasets. We argue how our proposed policies can mitigate these problems. We urge the community to leverage the learnings from the experiments conducted in peer-review processes and incorporate evidence-based policy design.

paragraphs: This paper uses empirical evidence about peer review to motivate two structural reforms for machine-learning and AI conferences. The first separates the decision to publish a paper from the decision to present it at a conference. The authors propose a four-step process centered on checking correctness, publishing sound work, and using community ratings to select presentations.

This arrangement gives publication and presentation different functions. Soundness determines whether work enters the published record, while community assessment helps decide which papers receive presentation opportunities. The proposal therefore changes how conference selection relates to access to publication, with the aim of mitigating problems identified in the existing review process.

The second reform offers anonymous and non-anonymous review tracks in parallel. The non-anonymous track would make all review data public to support accountability and provide material for research on peer review itself. The authors argue for incorporating lessons from prior peer-review experiments into policy design. These are proposed institutional changes grounded in existing evidence, with their expected benefits presented as arguments for reform.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes publishing all sound papers, selecting presentations separately, and offering a public non-anonymous review track alongside anonymous review.

title: Position: Peer Review in ML/AI Conferences Should Separate Publication from Presentation and Offer Non-Anonymous Review Tracks

abstract: This position paper argues that to obtain reliable embodied reward models, the community must invest in "bad" robot data: failed, suboptimal, error-prone, and even hazardous behaviors. While reward models are central to any foundation model’s lifecycle, today’s embodied reward models are trained primarily on successful behaviors. We analyze three state-of-the-art embodied reward models and find that they systematically over-reward behaviors that real human evaluators would penalize, including unsafe interactions, poor execution, and shortcut strategies that only superficially satisfy tasks. We attribute these failures to a key data gap: the scarcity of negative embodied data which is costly to collect and often filtered out or withheld in existing robotics datasets. Furthermore, we show that even modest exposure to real bad behavior data can improve alignment with human preferences and reduce costly false positives. We therefore call on the embodied AI community to curate and release their bad robot data, build synthetic bad data generation engines, develop more decentralized physical evaluation systems, and design benchmarks for fine-grained embodied reward model evaluations.

paragraphs: Reward models assess the quality of robot behavior, but the paper argues that learning primarily from successful examples leaves them poorly prepared to recognize important failures. The authors examine three leading embodied reward models and find that they systematically assign excessive rewards to behavior human evaluators would penalize. These behaviors include unsafe interactions, poor execution, and shortcuts that only appear to satisfy a task.

The authors attribute these failures to a shortage of negative embodied data. Failed, suboptimal, and hazardous behavior is expensive to collect, and existing robotics datasets often remove or withhold it. That creates a gap between the behavior reward models learn from and the problematic behavior they need to evaluate.

The paper also shows that even modest exposure to real examples of bad behavior can improve agreement with human preferences and reduce costly false positives. It calls for releasing such data, generating synthetic negative examples, developing more decentralized physical evaluation systems, and building detailed reward-model benchmarks. The findings support treating failure examples as valuable training evidence.
summary.tldr: The authors find that embodied reward models overvalue problematic robot behavior and can improve with modest exposure to real failure data.

abstract: Predictive state representations (PSRs) are a recently-developed way to model discretetime, controlled dynamical systems. We present and describe two algorithms for learning a PSR model: a Monte Carlo algorithm and a temporal difference (TD) algorithm. Both of these algorithms can learn models for systems without requiring a reset action as was needed by the previously available general PSR-model learning algorithm. We present empirical results that compare our two algorithms and also compare their performance with that of existing algorithms, including an EM algorithm for learning POMDP models.
originalAbstract: Predictive state representations (PSRs) are a recently-developed way to model discretetime, controlled dynamical systems. We present and describe two algorithms for learning a PSR model: a Monte Carlo algorithm and a temporal difference (TD) algorithm. Both of these algorithms can learn models for systems without requiring a reset action as was needed by the previously available general PSR-model learning algorithm. We present empirical results that compare our two algorithms and also compare their performance with that of existing algorithms, including an EM algorithm for learning POMDP models.

paragraphs: Predictive State Representations model controlled dynamical systems that evolve in discrete time. This paper focuses on learning these models when the system cannot be returned to a starting condition through a reset action. The previously available general learning algorithm required such an action, making reset availability an important condition on its use.

The authors introduce two learning algorithms, one based on Monte Carlo methods and another based on temporal differences. Both can learn a Predictive State Representation without requiring reset. Their shared contribution is therefore a change in the interaction conditions needed for learning, while their different learning mechanisms provide two approaches to meeting that requirement.

The paper presents empirical comparisons between the new algorithms and with existing methods, including expectation maximization for learning partially observable Markov decision process models. These comparisons place the proposed learners alongside an established alternative modeling approach. The abstract identifies the reset-free capability as the central result and reports comparative experiments without specifying a single overall winner.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms learn predictive state representations without requiring a reset action, using Monte Carlo and temporal-difference methods.

title: Learning predictive state representations in dynamical systems without reset

abstract: An anytime algorithm is capable of returning a response to the given task at essentially any time; typically the quality of the response improves as the time increases. Here, we consider the challenge of learning when we should terminate such algorithms on each of a sequence of iid tasks, to optimize the expected average reward per unit time. We provide an algorithm for answering this question. We combine the global optimizer Cross Entropy method and the local gradient ascent, and theoretically investigate how far the estimated gradient is from the true gradient. We empirically demonstrate the applicability of the proposed algorithm on a toy problem, as well as on a real-world face detection task.

paragraphs: An anytime algorithm can return an answer at essentially any point, with answer quality typically improving as it runs longer. This creates a decision about computation itself: when is the current answer good enough to stop? The paper studies learning that stopping decision across a sequence of independent, identically distributed tasks.

The objective is expected average reward per unit time. It therefore evaluates the benefit of better answers together with the time spent obtaining them. The proposed algorithm combines the Cross Entropy method for global optimization with local gradient ascent, using both broad search and local improvement to learn when computation should end.

The authors also theoretically investigate how far their estimated gradient can be from the true gradient. Empirical demonstrations include a toy problem and a real-world face detection task. These results support the applicability of learning a stopping policy, while the formulation makes the central tradeoff explicit: additional computation is useful according to how it contributes to reward relative to elapsed time.
summary.tldr: A learned stopping policy balances answer quality against computation time to optimize expected reward per unit time across repeated tasks.

title: Learning when to stop thinking and do something!

abstract: We propose a novel boosting algorithm which improves on current algorithms for weighted voting classification in striking a better balance between classification accuracy and sparsity of the weight vector. In order to justify our optimization formulations, we first consider a novel integer linear program as a model forsparse classifier selection, generalizing the minimum disagreementhalfspace problem, whose complexity has been investigated in computational learning theory. Specifically, our mixed integer problem is that of finding a separating hyperplane with minimum empirical error subject to an L0-norm penalty. We find that common soft margin linear programming formulations for robust classification are equivalent to a continuous relaxation of our model. Since the initial continuous relaxation is weak, we suggesta tighter relaxation, using novel cutting planes, to better approximate the integer solution. To solve this relaxation, we propose a new boosting algorithm based on linear programming with dynamic generation of variables and constraints. We demonstrate the classification performance of our proposed algorithm with experimental results, and justify our selection of parameters using a minimum description length, compression intrepretation of learning.

paragraphs: A weighted voting classifier combines multiple classifiers, but using more of them can make the resulting model less sparse. This paper proposes a boosting algorithm intended to improve the balance between classification accuracy and the number of nonzero voting weights. It starts by formulating sparse classifier selection as a mixed integer optimization problem.

The formulation seeks a separating hyperplane with low empirical error while applying an L0 penalty, which penalizes the number of nonzero weights. The authors show that familiar soft-margin linear programming formulations correspond to a continuous relaxation of this problem. Because that initial relaxation is weak, they introduce cutting planes to make the relaxed problem more closely approximate the integer formulation.

Their boosting algorithm solves the tighter relaxation using linear programming with dynamically generated variables and constraints. Experiments demonstrate its classification performance, while a minimum description length interpretation provides a justification for parameter selection. The contribution connects a practical ensemble-learning procedure to an explicit sparse-selection objective, explaining how stronger optimization relaxations can support the desired accuracy–sparsity balance.
summary.tldr: A boosting algorithm uses a tighter relaxation of sparse classifier selection to improve the balance between accuracy and sparse voting weights.

title: Boosting Classifiers with Tightened L0-Relaxation Penalties

abstract: We present a generic framework for parallel coordinate descent (CD) algorithms that has as special cases the original sequential algorithms of Cyclic CD and Stochastic CD, as well as the recent parallel Shotgun algorithm of Bradley et al. We introduce two novel parallel algorithms that are also special cases—Thread-Greedy CD and Coloring-Based CD—and give performance measurements for an OpenMP implementation of these.
originalAbstract: We present a generic framework for parallel coordinate descent (CD) algorithms that has as special cases the original sequential algorithms of Cyclic CD and Stochastic CD, as well as the recent parallel Shotgun algorithm of Bradley et al. We introduce two novel parallel algorithms that are also special cases—Thread-Greedy CD and Coloring-Based CD—and give performance measurements for an OpenMP implementation of these.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent approaches optimization by updating selected coordinates of a solution. This paper presents a general framework for parallel coordinate descent in large ℓ1 regularization problems. Its contribution includes a common formulation that accommodates both familiar sequential algorithms and methods designed to perform updates in parallel.

Cyclic coordinate descent and stochastic coordinate descent appear as special cases of the framework, as does the parallel Shotgun algorithm. Bringing these methods under one formulation connects different ways of organizing coordinate updates. The framework therefore provides a shared setting for describing established algorithms alongside additional parallel variants.

The authors introduce two such variants, Thread-Greedy coordinate descent and Coloring-Based coordinate descent, and report performance measurements from an OpenMP implementation. The work combines algorithmic unification with concrete implementations of new parallel methods. Its stated findings establish the breadth of the framework and provide implementation measurements; the abstract does not identify one method as uniformly fastest. The practical emphasis is on expanding the available ways to organize parallel coordinate descent.
summary.tldr: A general parallel coordinate descent framework includes existing algorithms and introduces Thread-Greedy and Coloring-Based variants with OpenMP performance measurements.

title: Scaling Up Coordinate Descent Algorithms for Large ℓ1 Regularization Problems

abstract: In this paper, a novel learning paradigm is presented to automatically identify groups of informative and correlated features from very high dimensions. Specifically, we explicitly incorporate correlation measures as constraints and then propose an efficient embedded feature selection method using recently developed cutting plane strategy. The benefits of the proposed algorithm are two-folds. First, it can identify the optimal discriminative and uncorrelated feature subset to the output labels, denoted here as Support Features, which brings about significant improvements in prediction performance over other state of the art feature selection methods considered in the paper. Second, during the learning process, the underlying group structures of correlated features associated with each support feature, denoted as Affiliated Features, can also be discovered without any additional cost. These affiliated features serve to improve the interpretations on the learning tasks. Extensive empirical studies on both synthetic and very high dimensional real-world datasets verify the validity and efficiency of the proposed method.

paragraphs: This paper addresses feature selection in very high-dimensional data, where useful predictors may belong to correlated groups. It distinguishes two outputs: Support Features, which form a discriminative and uncorrelated subset, and Affiliated Features, which are correlated features associated with each support feature. The aim is to obtain a useful prediction subset while also revealing the surrounding feature structure.

The method incorporates correlation measures directly as constraints and uses a cutting-plane strategy for efficient embedded feature selection. The authors describe it as identifying the optimal support subset under its formulation. During the same learning process, it also discovers the affiliated groups without additional cost, making group discovery part of selection rather than a separate analysis.

The paper reports significant prediction improvements over the state-of-the-art feature-selection methods included in its comparisons. Affiliated features contribute interpretation by exposing related variables around each selected support feature. Extensive studies on synthetic and very high-dimensional real-world datasets support the method’s validity and efficiency, grounding both its predictive and structural claims in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: The method selects discriminative, uncorrelated support features while discovering their correlated affiliates without additional cost during learning.

title: Discovering Support and Affiliated Features from Very High Dimensions
